~Son of Jacob and Leah.
~Brother of Simeon.
~Associated with violent revenge at Shechem.
~Ancestor figure for the Levites and priestly traditions.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Levi is one of Jacob's sons and appears most sharply in the violence at Shechem alongside Simeon. Though that episode is dark, Levi later becomes the ancestral name behind the Levites and priestly traditions in the Torah.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Levi both as a patriarchal son and as a retrojected ancestor for later priestly and Levitical identity. His importance grows dramatically beyond his limited personal narrative in Genesis.

cards.q:
~Son of Judah and Tamar.
~Born in an unusual birth scene involving twins.
~Part of the ancestry leading to David and later genealogies.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Perez is one of the twin sons born to Tamar and Judah in Genesis 38. Though a minor figure in the immediate story, he becomes important in later genealogies that lead toward David and beyond.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Perez is a strong example of how small genealogical figures can become highly significant in later biblical tradition. Scholars often note his importance in the Davidic line, especially in Ruth and Matthew.

cards.q:
~Twin brother of Perez.
~Son of Judah and Tamar.
~Associated with the unusual birth scene in Genesis 38.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zerah is the twin brother of Perez and the other child born to Tamar and Judah in Genesis 38. His significance comes mainly through the striking birth scene and later genealogical memory.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually treat Zerah as a genealogical figure whose main narrative importance lies in the dramatic twin-birth episode. He is an example of how Genesis embeds later lineage consciousness within family drama.

cards.q:
~A son of Moses.
~Associated with Moses’ family in Midian.
~One of the named children in Moses’ household traditions.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Gershom is one of the sons of Moses and Zipporah, appearing in the family traditions connected with Moses' life in Midian. His name is tied to Moses' sense of being a sojourner in a foreign land.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Gershom is mostly a genealogical and family marker rather than a developed narrative character. Scholars note such figures because they preserve traces of Moses' household tradition beyond the larger public story.

cards.q:
~Son of Aaron.
~A priestly figure.
~Succeeded Aaron in priestly leadership.
~Associated with priestly continuity in the wilderness and conquest traditions.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Eleazar is one of Aaron's sons and becomes the priestly successor after Aaron's death. He appears in priestly and conquest traditions as a sign of continuity within Aaron's line.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read Eleazar as part of the lineage-building work of priestly tradition. He is important less for personal characterization than for succession and institutional continuity.

cards.q:
~A ruler in the book of Daniel.
~Associated with the lions’ den story.
~Issued the decree that made Daniel’s prayer life dangerous.
~Part of the foreign court setting of Daniel.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Darius is the ruler in the Daniel narrative associated especially with the lions' den episode. He belongs to the book's sequence of foreign imperial courts under which Daniel remains faithful.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Darius the Mede as a historical problem because the figure does not map neatly onto known historical rulers. He is therefore important in conversations about the literary and historical shaping of Daniel.

cards.q:
~A queen in the book of Esther.
~Refused the king’s command at a banquet.
~Removed before Esther became queen.
~Part of the opening court conflict in Esther.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Vashti is the queen at the opening of Esther whose refusal of the king's command leads to her removal. Her absence creates the opening through which Esther later enters the royal story.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Vashti as a figure of resistance, royal politics, and gendered power in the Persian court narrative. Though she appears only at the beginning, she leaves a strong interpretive impression.

cards.q:
~One of the twelve disciples in the Gospel lists.
~Less developed narratively than Peter or John.
~Often linked by tradition with Nathanael.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Bartholomew appears in the apostle lists of the Synoptic Gospels and Acts but receives little developed narrative attention. Later tradition commonly links him with Nathanael from John's Gospel.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Bartholomew almost entirely in relation to questions of identification with Nathanael. He is a classic example of a named apostle whose narrative footprint is much smaller than his traditional importance.

cards.q:
~One of the twelve disciples.
~Known by a distinguishing label.
~Appears mainly in apostolic lists rather than extended narrative scenes.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Simon the Zealot is one of the twelve disciples and is known mainly from the apostolic lists. The descriptive label attached to his name distinguishes him from the many other Simons in the New Testament.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Simon the Zealot in relation to what the label may or may not mean historically. He is one of several apostles whose importance is clearer in list tradition than in developed narrative scenes.

cards.q:
~A man compelled to carry Jesus’ cross.
~Appears in the passion narrative.
~Associated with Cyrene.
~A brief but memorable figure at the crucifixion.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Simon of Cyrene is the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross in the passion narratives. Though his role is brief, he is one of the memorable named figures who enters the story at the moment of Jesus' suffering.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point to Simon of Cyrene as an example of how even a brief named appearance may preserve remembered detail from passion tradition. His identification with Cyrene also opens questions about diaspora Jewish presence in Jerusalem.

wrongAnswers: The Roman centurion at the cross

cards.q:
~Chosen in Acts to replace Judas among the twelve.
~Selected by lot.
~Part of the earliest Jerusalem community after Jesus’ ascension.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Matthias is the disciple chosen in Acts to take the place left by Judas among the twelve. His selection happens in the earliest Jerusalem community after Jesus' ascension and before Pentecost.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note Matthias because his election shows how early the symbolic fullness of the twelve mattered to the Jerusalem community. After his selection, however, he virtually disappears from the narrative.

cards.q:
~A follower of Jesus in Luke.
~One of the Emmaus road disciples.
~Met the risen Jesus without recognizing him at first.
~Named in one of Luke’s resurrection scenes.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Cleopas is the named disciple in Luke's Emmaus road resurrection narrative. He and his unnamed companion encounter the risen Jesus, fail to recognize him at first, and later understand who he is in the breaking of bread.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often focus on Cleopas because he is named while the other Emmaus disciple is not. He is significant for how Luke gives partial specificity to one of the New Testament's most literary resurrection scenes.

wrongAnswers: Cleopas's companion on the Emmaus road

cards.q:
~Followers of Jesus in Luke.
~Met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus.
~Did not recognize him at first.
~Recognized him in the breaking of bread.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The Emmaus disciples are the followers in Luke who meet the risen Jesus on the road after the resurrection. Their recognition comes only later, in the breaking of bread, making them central to Luke's resurrection theology of scripture and recognition.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss the Emmaus narrative as one of Luke's most carefully crafted resurrection scenes. Cleopas is named, but the companion is not, which has invited much later speculation.

wrongAnswers: The Roman centurion at the cross

cards.q:
~An Israelite in the conquest narratives.
~Kept banned items from Jericho.
~His action brought trouble on Israel at Ai.
~Identified and punished after the defeat.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Achan appears in Joshua after the fall of Jericho, when Israel unexpectedly loses at Ai. His hidden taking of banned spoil is identified as the reason for the defeat, and his punishment restores the community's standing before the campaign continues.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read Achan's story as a key example of collective holiness and ban ideology in Joshua. It is also frequently compared with other biblical stories where hidden wrongdoing threatens the whole community.

cards.q:
~A military commander in Judges.
~Opponent of Deborah and Barak.
~Defeated in battle.
~Fled on foot.
~Killed by Jael.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Sisera is the Canaanite commander defeated in the Deborah-Barak narrative. After the battle turns against him, he flees and seeks refuge in Jael's tent, where he meets his end. He is the military antagonist of one of Judges' major deliverance stories.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Sisera's role in Judges 4 and 5, where his death is remembered with striking dramatic and poetic force. He functions less as a rounded character than as the defeated symbol of oppressive power.

cards.q:
~A wealthy man in the David stories.
~Husband of Abigail.
~Refused David’s request for support.
~Remembered for foolishness.
~Died after the conflict with David and Abigail.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Nabal appears in 1 Samuel as the wealthy husband of Abigail whose insulting refusal provokes David toward vengeance. Abigail's intervention prevents bloodshed, and Nabal later dies, after which Abigail becomes David's wife.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that Nabal functions almost proverbially as a figure of folly, with even his name resonating with foolishness. His story helps shape David's image by placing a wise woman between him and a rash act of violence.

cards.q:
~A son of David.
~Half-brother of Tamar.
~Violated Tamar.
~Later killed by Absalom.
~Part of the tragic collapse of David’s household.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Amnon is David's son whose violation of Tamar becomes one of the darkest moments in the royal family story. His actions set in motion Absalom's revenge and deepen the internal collapse of David's house.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Amnon in the succession narrative as part of the judgment on David's household announced by Nathan. His story is central to discussions of sexual violence, royal impunity, and family catastrophe in Samuel.

cards.q:
~A king of the northern kingdom of Israel.
~Founder of an important royal line.
~Associated with Samaria.
~Father of Ahab.
~Historically significant beyond his brief biblical treatment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Omri is a king of the northern kingdom and the father of Ahab. Though the Bible treats him relatively briefly, he is associated with the establishment of Samaria and the rise of an influential dynasty.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point to Omri as a case where the Bible's theological priorities downplay major political importance. Extrabiblical sources suggest he was historically more significant than his biblical narrative footprint.

cards.q:
~A queen associated with Judah’s royal crisis.
~Seized power after dynastic upheaval.
~Tried to destroy the royal line.
~Ruled until the hidden heir was revealed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Athaliah is the royal woman who seizes power in Judah after a dynastic crisis and attempts to eliminate rival heirs. Her reign ends when the hidden child Joash is revealed and she is overthrown.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Athaliah with Jezebel because both are powerful royal women remembered negatively in the historical books. She is important for narratives of dynastic survival and temple-centered legitimacy.

cards.q:
~A prophetess in the time of Josiah.
~Consulted after the book of the law was found.
~Confirmed coming judgment and future reform significance.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Huldah is the prophet consulted in Josiah's reign after the book of the law is discovered. She confirms that judgment is coming but also explains the significance of Josiah's response. Her role is brief but decisive in the reform narrative.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Huldah is one of the notable female prophetic figures in the Bible and is often discussed for the authority she holds in a major royal crisis. Scholars also point to her importance in the validation of the law book tradition.

cards.q:
~A king of Judah in the final years before exile.
~Associated with Jeremiah’s warnings.
~Burned the prophetic scroll.
~Part of the downward spiral before Jerusalem’s fall.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jehoiakim is one of Judah's last kings before the Babylonian destruction. He appears in Jeremiah as a ruler who rejects prophetic warning, most memorably by burning Jeremiah's scroll. His reign belongs to the final phase of Judah's collapse.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Jehoiakim in relation to Jeremiah and the escalating Babylonian crisis. He is important for how prophetic resistance to royal power is dramatized in narrative form.

cards.q:
~One of Judah’s final kings.
~Ruled during Jerusalem’s last siege.
~Associated with Jeremiah.
~Failed to avert the Babylonian catastrophe.
~A tragic figure of the kingdom’s end.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zedekiah is the last king of Judah before Jerusalem falls to Babylon. His reign is marked by siege, political pressure, and repeated encounters with Jeremiah's warnings. He becomes the final royal face of Judah's collapse.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often treat Zedekiah as a tragic and pressured ruler caught between imperial realities and prophetic warning. He is a key figure in reconstructing the final years of Judah.

cards.q:
~A king of Judah.
~Associated with exile to Babylon.
~Part of the final generations of the Davidic line before the exile.
~Known by more than one name in biblical tradition.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jehoiachin, also known as Jeconiah or Coniah in some traditions, is one of Judah's last kings and is taken into Babylonian exile. His memory remains important because he belongs to the Davidic line even after royal collapse.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Jehoiachin because he appears in both exile traditions and later genealogies. He is a significant link between historical collapse and the persistence of Davidic lineage.

cards.q:
~A prophetic figure mentioned in Nehemiah.
~Associated negatively with opposition.
~Part of the resistance faced during rebuilding.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Noadiah is briefly mentioned in Nehemiah among those opposing or intimidating the rebuilding effort. She appears only in passing, but her name shows that prophetic claims were not always aligned with Nehemiah's cause.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Noadiah is one of those tiny biblical figures scholars notice because a brief mention opens a window onto competing prophetic authority in the post-exilic period. Her short appearance hints at a more complex social landscape than the main narrative foregrounds.

cards.q:
~A ruler in the book of Daniel.
~Associated with the writing on the wall.
~Presided over a banquet marked by sacrilege and doom.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Belshazzar is the ruler in Daniel 5 whose banquet ends with the writing on the wall. His use of Jerusalem's temple vessels and the sudden interpretation of doom make him a memorable figure of arrogant empire brought down.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Belshazzar is important in scholarship because the Daniel story preserves a memory not fully aligned with straightforward historical royal succession. He is often discussed in relation to the relationship between biblical narrative and Babylonian history.

cards.q:
~A foreign queen who visited Solomon.
~Came to test his wisdom.
~Associated with wealth, questions, and admiration for Solomon’s court.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The queen of Sheba is the foreign ruler who visits Solomon to test his wisdom and observe his wealth and court. Her visit becomes one of the major international scenes of Solomon's reign.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss the queen of Sheba in relation to trade networks, royal display, and later interpretive tradition. She is also important because later Jewish, Christian, and Ethiopian traditions expand her significance dramatically.

cards.q:
~An opponent of Nehemiah.
~Associated with resistance to rebuilding Jerusalem’s wall.
~A prominent adversary in the post-exilic narrative.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Sanballat is one of the main opponents in Nehemiah's rebuilding narrative, resisting the restoration of Jerusalem's wall. He functions as a key external adversary in the post-exilic political setting.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that Sanballat has historical resonance beyond the Bible, which helps anchor parts of Nehemiah in a broader Persian-period world. He is important for understanding the local politics of restoration.

cards.q:
~An opponent of Nehemiah.
~Worked with other adversaries against the rebuilding effort.
~Associated with resistance to Jerusalem’s restoration.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Tobiah is another of the named opponents in Nehemiah who resists the rebuilding and restoration work in Jerusalem. He participates in the network of pressure, ridicule, and interference surrounding the project.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Tobiah alongside Sanballat as part of the regional political complexity reflected in Nehemiah. His presence shows that restoration was contested and socially entangled.

cards.q:
~A Roman soldier present at Jesus’ crucifixion.
~Associated with a striking confession after Jesus’ death.
~A small but memorable witness in the passion narrative.
cards.a: The Roman centurion at the cross

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The centurion at the cross is the Roman witness in the crucifixion narrative who responds to Jesus' death with a notable declaration. Though a minor figure, he becomes one of the memorable outsiders in the passion story.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how the centurion functions narratively as an unexpected witness at the climactic moment of Jesus' death. His exact confession varies across Gospels, which also makes him interesting for comparison.

cards.q:
~A servant in the arrest of Jesus.
~Associated with the ear cut off in Gethsemane.
~Named in John’s Gospel.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Malchus is the servant of the high priest whose ear is cut off during Jesus' arrest scene. He is named in John's Gospel, which gives the episode a more individualized cast than some parallel accounts.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note Malchus because naming a small figure can signal remembered tradition or literary vividness. He is one of several passion figures whose brief appearance leaves a strong narrative impression.

wrongAnswers: The Roman centurion at the cross

cards.q:
~A man crucified beside Jesus.
~Associated especially with Luke’s passion narrative.
~Spoke to Jesus from the cross.
~Remembered in later tradition as the penitent thief.
cards.a: The criminal beside Jesus (penitent thief tradition)

notes.label: Context
notes.text: One of the criminals crucified beside Jesus speaks to him in Luke's Gospel and receives the promise of being with him in paradise. The scene is one of Luke's distinctive passion elements and has had a strong afterlife in Christian tradition.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss this figure as an example of Luke's special emphasis on repentance, mercy, and reversal even at the point of death. The later label 'penitent thief' comes from tradition, not the biblical text itself.

wrongAnswers: The Roman centurion at the cross

cards.q:
~Son of Boaz and Ruth.
~Part of the genealogy leading to David.
~A bridge figure between Ruth and the royal line.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Obed is the son born to Boaz and Ruth at the end of the book of Ruth. Though only briefly treated in the narrative, he is crucial as the link between that family story and the later line of Jesse and David.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often use Obed as an example of how genealogy turns a small domestic story into a text of major national significance. His importance lies almost entirely in lineage and literary connection.

cards.q:
~A Roman official in Acts.
~Associated with Corinth.
~Heard a case involving Paul.
~Dismissed the charges brought before him.
~A useful figure for situating Paul chronologically.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Gallio is the Roman proconsul before whom Paul appears in Corinth in Acts. He dismisses the case brought against Paul, and the episode helps show the movement's position in the Roman legal environment.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Gallio is especially important because his tenure can be correlated with external evidence, making him one of the most useful fixed points for Pauline chronology. Scholars often cite him when dating parts of Acts and Paul's missionary career.

cards.q:
~A member of the Herodian ruling family.
~Appeared with Agrippa II in Acts.
~Present during Paul’s later defense scenes.
~Part of the elite political setting around Paul’s imprisonment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Bernice appears in Acts with Agrippa II during the later legal scenes involving Paul. She belongs to the Herodian political world that surrounds Paul's imprisonment and hearings before elite audiences.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often mention Bernice as part of the historically grounded Herodian context of Acts. Her presence helps show how Paul's case is staged before multiple layers of political authority.

cards.q:
~A Roman military official in Acts.
~Intervened when Paul was in danger.
~Associated with Paul’s transfer for protection.
~Part of the legal and military chain in late Acts.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Claudius Lysias is the Roman tribune who intervenes when Paul is endangered in Jerusalem and later arranges his transfer for protection. He is one of the important Roman officials in the legal sequence of late Acts.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Claudius Lysias as part of Acts' portrayal of Roman administration and Paul's movement through legal channels. He helps the narrative present Rome as both threat and temporary protector.

cards.q:
~A woman connected with Roman provincial power in Acts.
~Associated with Felix.
~Present in scenes where Paul speaks before officials.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Drusilla appears in Acts as the woman with Felix when Paul is heard by the governor. She belongs to the Herodian-connected elite environment of the later trial scenes.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often mention Drusilla in reconstructing the political and dynastic background of Acts. Her appearance helps tie Paul's hearings to the broader network of regional elite power.

cards.q:
~A speaker in the book of Job.
~Appears after Job’s three friends.
~Offers additional speeches before God speaks from the whirlwind.
~A debated figure in the structure of Job.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Elihu is the younger speaker who appears in the book of Job after the three main friends have exhausted their arguments. He speaks at length before the divine speeches begin, making him a structurally unusual figure in the book.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Elihu is one of the most debated figures in Job because many scholars think his speeches may be a later addition or at least stand somewhat apart from the main dialogue structure. He is important for discussions of the book's composition history.

cards.q:
~One of Job’s friends.
~A major speaker in the dialogues.
~Argued that suffering reflects moral order.
~Part of the debate over Job’s condition.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Eliphaz is one of Job's three primary friends and among the first to respond to Job's suffering. His speeches reflect a worldview in which suffering is assumed to correspond in some meaningful way to wrongdoing or moral order.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read Eliphaz as the most rhetorically developed of Job's friends, especially in the first cycle of speeches. He helps establish the conventional wisdom position that the book will repeatedly challenge.

cards.q:
~One of Job’s friends.
~A speaker in the poetic dialogues.
~Argued from traditional wisdom and moral order.
~Part of the debate over Job’s suffering.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Bildad is one of Job's three friends and participates in the cycles of speeches that respond to Job's suffering. His arguments lean heavily on traditional moral assumptions and inherited wisdom.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Bildad as a representative of conventional wisdom whose confidence in moral order contrasts sharply with Job's lived experience. He is important as part of the book's dialogical structure.

cards.q:
~One of Job’s friends.
~A speaker in the poetic dialogues.
~Known for sharp and forceful responses to Job.
~Part of the debate over suffering and justice.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zophar is the third of Job's main friends and one of the speakers in the book's long debates. He tends to respond strongly and bluntly, insisting on divine justice against Job's complaints.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that Zophar is the least developed of the three major friends in terms of speech quantity, but he still contributes to the increasingly rigid conventional wisdom position that Job resists.

cards.q:
~Associated with Abraham’s household.
~Traditionally linked with being sent to find a wife for Isaac.
~Connected with Rebekah at the well.
~A servant figure of major narrative importance.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Abraham's servant is the key figure sent to find a wife for Isaac in Genesis 24, where he meets Rebekah at the well and helps carry the promise-line story forward. Though Genesis 24 itself does not name him, later tradition often associates him with Eliezer of Damascus.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually distinguish between the named Eliezer of Damascus in Genesis 15 and the unnamed servant in Genesis 24, even though later tradition often merges them. This is a good example of how biblical and later character traditions can converge.

cards.q:
~Servant of Elisha.
~Present in several Elisha narratives.
~Associated with Naaman’s healing story.
~Acted deceitfully after Naaman was healed.
~Struck with Naaman’s disease as judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Gehazi is Elisha's servant in several narratives of 2 Kings. He is especially remembered for secretly pursuing gifts from Naaman after Elisha had refused them, which results in judgment falling on him.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Gehazi as a foil within the Elisha cycle: while Naaman the outsider responds well, the insider servant becomes compromised by greed. His role is important for the moral contrasts built into the Elisha stories.

cards.q:
~A descendant of Saul.
~Son of Jonathan.
~Lame in his feet.
~Shown kindness by David for Jonathan’s sake.
~A figure linking Saul’s house and David’s reign.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Mephibosheth is the son of Jonathan and surviving descendant of Saul whom David treats with covenant loyalty for Jonathan's sake. His story is one of vulnerability, royal kindness, and later suspicion during political crisis.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note Mephibosheth as an important figure for showing both David's generosity and the political fragility surrounding Saul's surviving line. He is also significant in discussions of disability and dependence in biblical narrative.

cards.q:
~A figure in Saul’s court.
~Associated with the priests at Nob.
~Reported David’s presence.
~Carried out brutal violence under Saul.
~A memorable antagonist in the David-Saul conflict.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Doeg the Edomite is Saul's servant who reports David's contact with the priests at Nob and later carries out the massacre there when Saul's own men refuse. He is one of the most chilling figures in the Saul-David conflict.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read Doeg as an outsider enforcer whose willingness to perform violence highlights Saul's moral collapse. His story also became significant in later interpretation, including in Psalm superscriptions.

cards.q:
~A counselor in the David narratives.
~Known for highly valued advice.
~Later sided with Absalom.
~Associated with the rebellion against David.
~Ended his own life after his counsel was not followed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ahithophel is the renowned counselor whose advice carries enormous weight in the later David stories. During Absalom's rebellion he sides against David, and his rejected counsel becomes part of the turning point that leads to his death.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note Ahithophel as an example of how political intelligence and court strategy drive the succession narrative. He is important because his counsel is treated almost as a prophetic oraclesque force within the story.

cards.q:
~A woman in the book of Hosea.
~Associated with Hosea’s symbolic marriage.
~Part of the prophet’s family-sign narrative.
~Connected with themes of unfaithfulness and restoration.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Gomer is the woman associated with Hosea's marriage in the opening of the book of Hosea. Her relationship to Hosea functions symbolically within the prophetic portrayal of Israel's unfaithfulness and the hope of restoration.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate how literally Hosea's marriage to Gomer should be understood, since the book may reflect symbolic construction, prophetic sign-act, or some mix of memory and literary shaping. She is therefore important in both interpretation and composition debates.

cards.q:
~A woman follower of Jesus.
~Associated with support for Jesus’ ministry.
~Named among the women in Luke.
~Connected with the resurrection-witness tradition.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Joanna is one of the named women in Luke who supports Jesus' ministry and later appears among the women associated with the resurrection reports. Though not as prominent as Mary Magdalene, she is one of the significant named female followers in Luke.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note Joanna because Luke preserves her name in contexts where other traditions are more selective. She is important for understanding the visible role of women in discipleship and witness.

cards.q:
~A figure in the letter to Philemon.
~Connected with Paul during imprisonment.
~Associated with estrangement and reconciliation.
~A key person in one of the shortest Pauline letters.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Onesimus is the figure at the center of Paul's letter to Philemon. The letter concerns his relationship to Philemon and presents a deeply personal appeal involving reconciliation, changed status, and Christian fellowship.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Onesimus is central to debates about slavery, social status, and Paul's rhetoric in Philemon. Scholars often study the letter because so much hinges on this one named person's situation and Paul's careful language around it.

cards.q:
~A recipient of one of Paul’s letters.
~Connected with Onesimus.
~Part of a household-church setting.
~Central to the short letter bearing his name.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Philemon is the man addressed in Paul's short letter concerning Onesimus. He is part of a household-church setting and becomes the recipient of one of Paul's most personal and socially charged appeals.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often study Philemon because the letter to him is a major site for discussion of slavery, reconciliation, patronage, and Pauline interpersonal strategy. His role is inseparable from the letter's ethical force.

Hebrew word meaning "Law".
The first five books of the Old Testament.

notes.text:
While commonly used to mean "law," the term literally means instruction, teaching, or direction.

- Genesis (Bereshit)
- Exodus (Shemot)
- Leviticus (Vayikra)
- Numbers (Bamidbar)
- Deuteronomy (Devarim)

cards.q:
Greek word meaning "Five books".
Referring to the Greek translation of the first five books of the Old Testament.

notes.label: FYI
notes.text: Individuals might use this Greek word to refer to any language version, as it means "five books". It primarily refers to the first five books of the Bible

cards.q: The Hebrew canonical collection of Jewish scriptures, aka Hebrew Bible, aka Old Testament.
The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. Often referred to as the Greek Old Testament.

Hebrew word meaning "Prophets". 
Subdivided into "Former Prophets" (historical narratives like Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and "Latter Prophets" (prophetic books like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the 12 Minor Prophets).

notes.label: FYI
notes.text:
The books include: 

- Joshua (Yehoshua)
- Judges (Shoftim)
- Samuel (I & II are counted as one book)
- Kings (I & II are counted as one book)
- Isaiah (Yeshayahu)
- Jeremiah (Yirmiyahu)
- Ezekiel (Yehezkel)
- The Twelve (Trei Asar): Considered one book, it contains the twelve "minor" prophets (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi).

cards.q:
Hebrew word meaning "Writings".
The third section of the books of the Old Testament encompassing poetry and wisdom literature (Psalms, Proverbs, Job), the Five Megillot or Scrolls (Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther), and historical/prophetic books (Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah, Chronicles).

notes.label: FYI
notes.text:
The books include: 

- Psalms (Tehillim)
- Proverbs (Mishlei)
- Job (Iyov)
- Song of Songs (Shir HaShirim)
- Ruth (Rut)
- Lamentations (Eichah)
- Ecclesiastes (Kohelet)
- Esther
- Daniel
- Ezra-Nehemiah (Counted as one book)
- Chronicles (I & II are counted as one book)

cards.q:
Hebrew word meaning "learning" or "instruction".
It contains the Oral Tradition and Commentary on the Old Testament.

notes.label: FYI
notes.text: It is a central text of Rabbinic Judaism comprising a vast compilation of Jewish law, ethics, customs, and history. It consists of the Mishnah (oral law compiled around 200 CE) and the Gemara (commentary on the Mishnah), covering topics like rituals, civil law, and ethics.

cards.q: A late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.

notes.label: FYI
notes.text:
It was written in "Vulgar Latin"-the everyday language spoken by common people at the time.
Commissioned in 382 AD by Pope Damasus I, it was primarily the work of Saint Jerome (Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus), who aimed to provide a more accurate and unified text than the various "Old Latin" (Vetus Latina) versions then in circulation.

cards.q: Who wrote between 7 and 13 of the New Testament Epistles/Letters

notes.label: FYI
notes.text: Most scholars believe that Paul actually authored seven of the thirteen Pauline epistles: Galatians, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Philemon, Philippians, and 1 Thessalonians. However, three of the epistles attributed to Paul are widely regarded as pseudepigraphic (falsely attributed): 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus. The authorship of the remaining three epistles in Paul’s name -2 Thessalonians, Ephesians, and Colossians-remains a subject of extensive debate.

decks.name: Stories
decks.desc: Different stories and where they are in the bible

cards.q:
__**Creation**__
God creates the heavens, the earth, light, sky, land, seas, plants, animals, and human beings.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis opens by presenting God as the creator of everything that exists. The chapter describes creation in a structured sequence of six days followed by a seventh-day rest: light, sky, dry land and vegetation, heavenly lights, sea creatures and birds, land animals, and finally humans. Humans are told to multiply and to rule over the living world, and the chapter ends with God resting on the seventh day.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars commonly treat Genesis 1 as part of the Priestly material in the Pentateuch and often date its final written form to the exilic or post-exilic period, roughly the 6th–5th centuries BCE, though it may preserve older traditions. It is frequently compared with Mesopotamian creation texts such as Enuma Elish, but unlike those stories Genesis has one god creating by speech rather than through combat among rival gods.

cards.q:
__**Adam and Eve in Eden**__
Adam and Eve live in the Garden of Eden, eat from the forbidden tree, and are expelled from the garden.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the creation account of Genesis 1, the story narrows to the first human pair and the garden where they are placed. God forms the man, places him in Eden, and commands him not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The woman is then created, and in Genesis 3 the serpent persuades her to eat the fruit and she gives some to the man. Afterward they hide, are confronted by God, receive punishments, and are expelled from the garden so they cannot also eat from the tree of life.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars distinguish Genesis 2–3 from Genesis 1 and connect it with the Yahwist strand of Pentateuchal tradition, often dated in written form anywhere from the monarchic period to the exilic era, with the Pentateuch reaching final shape much later, around the 6th–5th centuries BCE. The Eden story is also compared with ancient Near Eastern paradise traditions, and the serpent is usually read in its original context as a crafty animal rather than the later Christian identification with Satan.

cards.q:
__**Noah's Ark**__
Noah builds an ark, God sends a flood, and his family and the animals survive.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As the early human world grows, Genesis describes the earth as filled with violence and corruption. God decides to wipe out life on earth but tells Noah, who is singled out as righteous, to build an ark. Noah brings his family and animals aboard, the flood destroys life outside the ark, and the waters later recede. Noah leaves the ark, offers sacrifice, and God makes a covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, with the rainbow as the sign.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The flood story is one of the clearest places where scholars compare Genesis with older Mesopotamian flood traditions such as Atrahasis and the flood episode in Gilgamesh. Many scholars think the biblical account combines multiple sources, often associated with Priestly and non-Priestly strands, and reached its present form when Genesis was compiled in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Tower of Babel**__
Humanity unites to build a city and tower, and God confuses their language and scatters them.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the flood stories and the spread of Noah's descendants, Genesis turns to a story about humanity acting together as one people with one language. People gather in one place, make bricks, and begin building a city and tower so they can make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God comes down, confuses their language so they cannot understand one another, and scatters them across the earth. The city receives the name Babel because of the confusion of languages there.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see this as an origin story explaining linguistic diversity and the name 'Babel,' while also alluding to Mesopotamian temple towers or ziggurats. Its final literary form is usually placed in the same primeval-history block of Genesis, commonly dated in compilation to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Sodom and Gomorrah**__
Angels visit Lot, the cities are judged and destroyed, and Lot escapes with his daughters.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Abraham's plea over Sodom in Genesis 18, the story shifts to Lot living inside the city as judgment approaches. Two angels enter Sodom and are hosted by Lot, but the men of the city surround the house and demand access to the visitors. Lot and his family are hurried out before fire and sulfur destroy the cities, and Lot's wife turns back and becomes a pillar of salt. The chapter ends with Lot and his daughters in the hills.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Outside the Bible, no decisive archaeological evidence has confirmed the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as told here, though the story has long been linked to the Dead Sea region. Scholars usually read Genesis 19 as part of the Abraham-Lot cycle in Genesis' final form, compiled in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Abraham and Isaac**__
God tests Abraham by telling him to offer Isaac as a sacrifice, but stops him and provides a ram instead.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Isaac has been born as the child of promise and Abraham's household tensions with Hagar's line have already played out, God tests Abraham by telling him to take Isaac to the land of Moriah and offer him there. Abraham travels with Isaac, prepares the altar, and raises the knife, but an angel stops him at the last moment. A ram is offered instead, and the promises to Abraham are reaffirmed.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The Aqedah, or binding of Isaac, has generated an enormous amount of critical discussion because it centers on child sacrifice narrowly averted. Scholars usually place the story within Genesis' final literary form of the 6th–5th centuries BCE, and some compare it with ancient Near Eastern sacrificial traditions while noting that the biblical version ends with animal substitution.

cards.q:
__**Joseph Sold by His Brothers**__
Joseph’s brothers, driven by jealousy over his dreams and their father’s favoritism, sell him into slavery and send him to Egypt.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Joseph's dreams and Jacob's favoritism intensify his brothers' hatred. They first plan to kill him, then throw him into a pit, and finally sell him to traders going to Egypt. To cover the crime, they dip Joseph's robe in blood and lead Jacob to believe he has been killed by an animal.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see the Joseph story as more novella-like and literarily unified than many earlier Genesis episodes, though debate continues about sources and additions. Its final form is still generally placed within the Pentateuch's growth toward the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Baby Moses in the Nile**__
Moses is hidden in a basket among the reeds, discovered by Pharaoh’s daughter, and preserved from death.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Pharaoh has ordered the Hebrew baby boys killed, so Moses' mother hides him and then places him in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter finds the child, Moses' sister watches from nearby, and the baby's own mother is brought in to nurse him. Moses is then raised in Pharaoh's household even though he was born a Hebrew.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare the basket story with the legend of Sargon of Akkad, another ancient Near Eastern tale about an exposed infant set in a river and later rising to prominence. The Exodus narrative in its final Pentateuchal form is usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE, though many scholars think it preserves older memories and traditions.

cards.q:
__**Moses and the Burning Bush**__
God appears to Moses in a burning bush and calls him to lead Israel out of Egypt.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While tending sheep in Midian, Moses sees a bush that burns without being consumed. God calls to him from the bush, identifies himself as the God of his ancestors, and sends him to confront Pharaoh. Moses objects repeatedly, and signs are given to equip him for the mission.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that Exodus 3–4 combines call narrative, revelation of the divine name, and miracle traditions that may have come from more than one source. In source-critical work, parts of the chapter are often associated with non-Priestly and Priestly strands within a Pentateuch finalized in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Ten Plagues and Passover**__
God sends plagues on Egypt and institutes Passover before Pharaoh finally lets Israel go.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh to demand that the Israelites be released from slavery, but Pharaoh repeatedly refuses. A series of plagues strikes Egypt, culminating in the death of the firstborn. Before that final plague, the Israelites are told to mark their doorways with lamb's blood and eat the Passover meal, so that their households will be spared. After the final plague, Pharaoh finally lets them go.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often argue that the plague narratives are composite, with repetitions and differing formulas suggesting more than one strand of tradition. The Passover material may also reflect the merging of more than one festival tradition, and the book of Exodus reached final written form as part of the Pentateuch in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Crossing the Red Sea**__
God parts the sea so Israel escapes Egypt, and Pharaoh’s army is destroyed when the waters return.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After letting Israel go, Pharaoh changes course and pursues them to the sea. God drives back the waters so Israel crosses on dry ground, then the waters return when the Egyptians follow. Israel is rescued and Egypt's army is destroyed.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars frequently note that Exodus 14–15 appears to preserve more than one sea-deliverance tradition, and that the prose account in Exodus 14 stands alongside the older poetic celebration in Exodus 15. The Hebrew name often translated 'Red Sea' more literally refers to the 'Sea of Reeds,' which affects how scholars discuss the setting.

cards.q:
__**The Ten Commandments at Sinai**__
At Mount Sinai, God gives Israel the Ten Commandments as part of the covenant.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Israel arrives at Mount Sinai, where the mountain is wrapped in thunder, smoke, and trumpet blast. The people are warned not to approach the mountain carelessly, and Moses goes up to meet God. In that setting the Ten Commandments are given to define core obligations of the covenant.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare the covenant setting and command structure with ancient Near Eastern treaty traditions, especially Hittite and Neo-Assyrian forms, though the fit is not exact. The Decalogue itself may have had a long transmission history before becoming part of Exodus in a Pentateuch finalized in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Fall of Jericho**__
Israel marches around Jericho, the walls collapse, and the city is destroyed except for Rahab's household.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Israel crosses into Canaan, Jericho becomes the first major city it faces. Israel circles the city for six days and then seven times on the seventh day while priests blow trumpets. At Joshua's command the people shout, the city falls, and it is placed under a ban of destruction. Rahab and her family alone are spared because she had hidden the Israelite spies earlier.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Jericho is one of the best-known places where archaeology and biblical narrative are debated. Excavation history has produced conflicting interpretations about whether there was a city there to match the biblical timeline, so scholars do not agree that Joshua 6 can be tied straightforwardly to a single historical destruction event. The book of Joshua likely reached written form in stages between the 7th and 5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Samson and Delilah**__
Delilah learns the secret of Samson's strength, his hair is cut, and he dies bringing down a Philistine temple.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Samson becomes involved with Delilah, who is bribed by Philistine leaders to discover the source of his strength. After deceiving her several times, he finally reveals that his hair has never been cut, and she has it shaved while he sleeps. He is captured, blinded, displayed in a temple, and dies pulling the building down on himself and the crowd.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Samson to wider folklore about strongman figures whose power is tied to a special condition or taboo. His stories are also set in the borderland struggle with the Philistines, and Judges in its present literary form is usually thought to have been compiled and edited between the monarchic and exilic periods, roughly the 8th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**David and Goliath**__
Young David volunteers to fight the giant Philistine warrior Goliath with only a sling and stones while the Israelite army cowers.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Israel and the Philistines face each other while Goliath repeatedly challenges Israel to single combat. David, sent to bring supplies to his brothers, volunteers to fight despite his youth and lack of armor. He kills Goliath with a stone, cuts off his head, and triggers a Philistine retreat.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter has long drawn scholarly attention because 2 Samuel 21:19 attributes the killing of Goliath to Elhanan in the Masoretic text, leading to debates about textual development and later harmonization. First Samuel 17 is also absent in shorter form in some textual traditions, which suggests a complex transmission history.

cards.q:
__**Elijah and the Prophets of Baal**__
Elijah challenges 450 prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel; fire falls from heaven on Elijah’s altar while Baal’s prophets fail.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After a long drought in the reign of Ahab, Elijah gathers the king, the people, and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel for a public contest. Both sides prepare sacrifices, but only Elijah's offering is consumed when fire falls from heaven after he prays. The people then side with Elijah, showing that the God of Israel, not Baal, is the one being presented as controlling rain and fertility. The scene leads directly into the breaking of the drought.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read this chapter as a polemical story aimed at condemning Baal worship in the northern kingdom under Ahab and Jezebel. The Elijah cycle is preserved within Kings, which most scholars place in a major literary edition in the late 7th century BCE with exilic shaping in the 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Esther Saves the Jews**__
Queen Esther risks her life to approach King Xerxes uninvited and foil Haman’s plot to annihilate the Jews; the Jews are delivered and the festival of Purim is established.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In the Persian court, Haman secures a royal decree to destroy the Jews, and Mordecai urges Queen Esther to intervene even though approaching the king uninvited could cost her life. Esther risks that approach, hosts banquets, exposes Haman's plot, and wins royal protection for her people. The story ends with the enemies of the Jews defeated and the festival of Purim established to remember the deliverance.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The Hebrew version of Esther never explicitly mentions God, which has made the book especially notable in scholarship and reception history. Scholars often read it as a diaspora court tale explaining the origin of Purim; Greek versions add prayers and explicit references to God that are absent from the Hebrew text. Esther is often dated to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, roughly the 4th–3rd centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the Fiery Furnace**__
The three young men refuse to bow to Nebuchadnezzar’s golden statue and are thrown into a blazing furnace; a fourth figure appears with them unharmed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image and commands all officials to bow before it when the music sounds. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse, are accused, and are thrown into an overheated furnace. They survive, and the king sees an additional figure with them before finally ordering them released.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars generally date the court tales in Daniel 1-6 later than the Babylonian period they describe, often to the Hellenistic era, with the book reaching final form around the 2nd century BCE. The stories are widely read as resistance literature designed to encourage fidelity under imperial pressure rather than as straightforward court records.

cards.q:
__**Daniel in the Lions’ Den**__
Daniel is thrown into the lions’ den for praying to God; the lions are shut and he emerges unharmed the next morning.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Daniel rises above other officials in the new imperial administration, which leads rivals to target him. They persuade the king to forbid prayer to anyone but the king for a set period, knowing Daniel will continue his practice. Daniel is thrown to the lions, survives the night, and his accusers are then punished.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Like Daniel 3, this chapter is usually read by scholars as part of a set of Jewish court tales preserved in Daniel 1-6 and finalized in the Hellenistic period, especially the 2nd century BCE. The story’s setting under Darius the Mede also draws attention because that ruler is historically difficult to identify, which is one reason critical scholars do not read the narrative as simple chronicle.

cards.q:
__**Jonah and the Great Fish**__
The prophet Jonah flees God’s call, is swallowed by a great fish, prays from inside it, and is vomited onto dry land to finally obey.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jonah is told to go to Nineveh but instead boards a ship going the other way. A violent storm threatens the vessel, Jonah is identified as the cause, and he is thrown into the sea. A great fish swallows him, he prays from inside it, and after three days he is vomited onto dry land.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Unlike many prophetic books, Jonah is almost entirely a short narrative about the prophet rather than a collection of his speeches. Many scholars date the book relatively late, often to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, roughly the 5th–3rd centuries BCE, and note its satirical tone and its focus on divine mercy toward a foreign city.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Matthew opens with Jesus' genealogy, Joseph's dream, and the birth of Jesus. Magi come from the east asking for the newborn king, Herod reacts violently, and the family flees to Egypt after another warning in a dream. After Herod's death they return and settle in Nazareth.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Matthew to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, though views vary. The infancy narrative includes motifs that echo Israel's earlier story world, especially Moses traditions, and it differs sharply from Luke's account in setting, visitors, and sequence.

cards.q:
__**Jesus’ Birth and the Visit of the Magi**__
Jesus is born, magi visit him, and the family flees Herod before later settling in Nazareth.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness calling for repentance and baptizing in the Jordan. Jesus comes to him for baptism, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a heavenly voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son. The chapter sets up Jesus' public mission immediately before the wilderness testing.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The baptism is widely regarded by scholars as one of the earliest and most historically secure elements in Jesus tradition, partly because later Christians had to explain why Jesus would submit to John's baptism. Matthew is commonly dated around 80–90 CE and reshapes the scene by adding dialogue that addresses that tension.

cards.q:
__**The Baptism of Jesus**__
Jesus is baptized by John, the heavens open, and a voice declares him to be God’s beloved Son.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jesus goes up the mountain, sits, and teaches a large gathered crowd. The sermon includes the Beatitudes, sayings about law and righteousness, instructions on almsgiving and prayer, the Lord's Prayer, warnings about judgment, and a closing call to hear and do his words. It ends with the crowd reacting to his authority.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Most scholars think Matthew has gathered and arranged teachings from different earlier Jesus traditions into one major discourse. The Gospel itself is commonly dated around 80–90 CE, and the sermon is often compared with Luke's shorter Sermon on the Plain as evidence of literary shaping.

cards.q:
__**The Sermon on the Mount**__
Jesus teaches the Beatitudes, prayer, mercy, nonretaliation, and many other core teachings in a long public discourse.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After seeking a quiet place, Jesus is met by a large crowd and responds with healing and food rather than dismissal. Five loaves and two fish are blessed, broken, and distributed by the disciples until the entire crowd eats. Twelve baskets of leftovers are collected afterward.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This is one of the very few miracle stories found in all four canonical Gospels, which makes it especially important for source criticism. Scholars often compare it with wilderness-feeding traditions in the Hebrew Bible and with Greco-Roman banquet and miracle motifs.

cards.q:
__**Feeding the Five Thousand**__
Jesus feeds a huge crowd with five loaves and two fish, and baskets of leftovers remain.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: During Passover preparation, Jesus eats with the disciples, identifies betrayal within the group, and gives bread and wine new significance tied to his body and blood. The meal is followed by the Mount of Olives, the prediction of Peter's denial, and the scene at Gethsemane. It is the final intimate gathering before arrest.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The precise relation of the Last Supper to Passover remains debated because the Synoptic Gospels and John do not present the timing in exactly the same way. Scholars usually date Matthew to the late 1st century CE and see this meal tradition as one of the central streams behind later Christian ritual practice.

cards.q:
__**The Last Supper**__
Jesus shares a final meal with his disciples, predicts betrayal, and interprets the bread and cup in relation to his death.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jesus is handed over to Pilate, condemned, mocked by soldiers, and led to Golgotha. He is crucified, bystanders taunt him, darkness falls, and he dies with dramatic signs accompanying the moment. The chapter closes with burial and the securing of the tomb.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Jesus' execution by crucifixion under Roman authority is one of the strongest points of agreement in historical Jesus research. Matthew's passion narrative, usually dated in its Gospel context to around 80–90 CE, includes distinctive elements such as the earthquake and risen holy ones that are not found in the other Gospels.

cards.q:
__**The Crucifixion of Jesus**__
Jesus is tried, crucified by Roman authority, mocked, and dies outside Jerusalem.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Women come to the tomb, an angel announces that Jesus has been raised, and they are told to notify the disciples. Guards are drawn into a counter-explanation about the body, while the disciples later meet Jesus in Galilee. The Gospel ends with the command to make disciples of all nations.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars distinguish between the broad claim that Jesus' followers very early believed he had been raised and the harder historical question of exactly what experiences generated the resurrection narratives. Matthew's version has distinctive features such as the guards at the tomb and the Galilee commissioning scene.

cards.q:
__**The Resurrection of Jesus**__
Women find the tomb empty, Jesus appears alive, and the Gospel closes with a commission to the disciples.

__**Pentecost**__
The Spirit comes upon Jesus' followers, they speak in many languages, and Peter publicly announces the message about Jesus.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While the disciples are gathered, a violent sound and divided tongues as of fire appear, and they begin speaking in other languages. A crowd gathers because pilgrims from many regions hear them in their own tongues. Peter then gives a public speech explaining the event and calling people to repent and join the movement.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Pentecost with Jewish festival traditions tied to Shavuot and with biblical theophany imagery such as wind, fire, and divine speech. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, commonly around 80–90 CE, and this scene is widely recognized as one of its major programmatic episodes.

cards.q:
__**Cain and Abel**__
Cain and Abel bring offerings to God, and Cain kills his brother Abel out of jealousy.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Cain and Abel each bring an offering to God, but God favors Abel's offering instead of Cain's. After God warns Cain about anger, Cain takes Abel into the field and kills him. God confronts Cain, places him under a curse connected to the ground, and marks him before sending him away east of Eden.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually place Genesis 4 within the early primeval-history traditions of Genesis, with its final literary form reaching the post-exilic Pentateuch in the 6th–5th centuries BCE. The story is often read as an etiological tale explaining bloodguilt, the danger of vengeance, and why Cain's descendants are associated with settled life and crafts.

cards.q:
__**Birth of Isaac and Hagar Sent Away**__
Isaac is born to Abraham and Sarah, and Hagar and Ishmael are sent away into the wilderness.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Sarah gives birth to Isaac as promised, and Abraham circumcises him. Later Sarah sees Ishmael and demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. In the wilderness they nearly die of thirst, but God hears the boy, shows Hagar water, and preserves his life.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Genesis 21 with Genesis 16 because both stories involve Hagar in crisis and divine rescue, but with different settings and emphases. The repeated Hagar material is often taken as evidence that Genesis incorporates more than one traditional version before reaching final form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Jacob Steals Esau’s Blessing**__
Jacob, with Rebekah’s help, deceives Isaac and receives the blessing meant for Esau.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Esau has already sold his birthright to Jacob, the family conflict deepens when Isaac grows old and nearly blind. Rebekah learns that Isaac plans to give the formal paternal blessing to Esau, so she and Jacob plan to secure it for Jacob instead. Jacob disguises himself with Esau's clothes and goat skins, deceives Isaac, and receives the blessing. Esau returns too late and vows revenge, forcing Jacob to flee.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This story is usually read together with Genesis 25 as part of a larger Jacob-Esau rivalry cycle shaped by family conflict and reversal of primogeniture. Scholars generally place the final form of these narratives within Genesis as compiled in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Jacob Wrestles with God**__
Jacob wrestles through the night, is blessed, and receives the name Israel.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After leaving Laban and before meeting Esau again, Jacob fears what may happen when the brothers finally come face to face. On the night before that meeting, Jacob sends his family across the stream and remains alone. A mysterious man wrestles with him until daybreak, injures Jacob's hip, and gives him the new name Israel. Jacob names the place Peniel after saying he has seen God and lived.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The identity of Jacob's opponent is debated in scholarship because the text moves between 'man,' divine blessing, and Jacob's claim to have seen God. Like other Bethel and Peniel stories, it is also read as an etiological narrative tied to names, custom, and place, within Genesis' final 6th–5th century BCE form.

cards.q:
__**Joseph Interprets Pharaoh’s Dreams**__
Joseph explains Pharaoh’s dreams, predicts famine, and is elevated to power in Egypt.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Joseph is forgotten in prison for a time, Pharaoh himself begins having disturbing dreams that no one at court can explain. Joseph is brought from prison and interprets the dreams as seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine. He advises preparation, Pharaoh elevates him to high office, and Joseph oversees the storage plan.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars frequently compare Joseph's rise in Egypt with other ancient court stories in which a gifted outsider gains royal favor through wisdom. While the story is set in Egypt, the final Hebrew literary form belongs to Genesis as shaped and compiled in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Joseph Reveals Himself to His Brothers**__
Joseph tells his brothers who he is, forgives them, and explains that God used their evil for good.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After testing his brothers and seeing Judah plead for Benjamin, Joseph can no longer hold back his identity. He sends everyone else out and tells his brothers who he is. The brothers are terrified, but Joseph reassures them and says God used the events to preserve life during famine. He then arranges for Jacob's household to come to Egypt.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is often treated as the emotional climax of the Joseph story and one of the Bible's most artfully constructed recognition scenes. Like the rest of the Joseph cycle, it is generally placed within Genesis' final compilation in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Golden Calf**__
While Moses is on the mountain, the people make a golden calf, worship it, and Moses breaks the tablets in anger.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While Moses remains on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to make them a visible god to lead them. Aaron fashions a calf, an altar is built, and the people celebrate before it. Moses comes down, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, and a violent punishment follows.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars have long connected this episode to later northern calf imagery associated with Bethel and Dan, suggesting the story may also function as a polemic against rival worship practices. In source-critical scholarship, Exodus 32 is often treated as layered material within a Pentateuch finalized in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Twelve Spies in Canaan**__
Israel sends spies into Canaan, but the fearful report leads the people to rebel and refuse to enter the land.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Moses sends twelve spies into Canaan, and they return carrying produce from the land. Although the land is described as fertile, most of the spies emphasize its fortified cities and powerful inhabitants, stirring panic among the people. Caleb and Joshua urge trust, but the rebellion ends with the generation being sentenced to die in the wilderness.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note duplications and tensions between Numbers 13 and Deuteronomy 1, suggesting the spy story circulated in more than one form before being incorporated into the Pentateuch. The book of Numbers took shape over time and is commonly thought to have reached final form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Balaam and the Donkey**__
On the way to curse Israel, Balaam's donkey sees an angel, speaks to Balaam, and saves his life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Balak, king of Moab, summons Balaam to curse the Israelites. On the journey, Balaam's donkey sees the angel of the Lord blocking the path and turns aside three times, but Balaam does not understand what is happening. The donkey speaks, Balaam's eyes are opened, and he is forced to continue only under divine constraint.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The Balaam material is especially interesting because Balaam also appears outside the Bible in the Deir Alla inscription, an Aramaic text from around the 8th century BCE that refers to 'Balaam son of Beor.' Scholars do not think the texts are identical stories, but the extra-biblical parallel is one of the clearest cases of a biblical figure also known from ancient inscriptions. Numbers in its present literary form is usually dated to final compilation in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**David Anointed by Samuel**__
Samuel goes to Jesse's house, passes over the older brothers, and anoints the young shepherd David.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Saul's rejection, Samuel is sent to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse's sons. Jesse presents the older sons first, but God rejects them. David is summoned from tending sheep and is anointed, after which the spirit of the Lord is said to come upon him.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how strongly this chapter favors the unexpected younger son motif, common in biblical narrative. It also works as the formal beginning of David's rise within a larger court-history tradition that many scholars think underwent substantial literary shaping.

cards.q:
__**David and Bathsheba**__
David sleeps with Bathsheba, arranges Uriah’s death, and takes Bathsheba as his wife.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While his army is at war, David sees Bathsheba bathing and sends for her. When she becomes pregnant, David tries to cover it by bringing Uriah home, but Uriah refuses to enjoy home comforts while the army is in the field. David then arranges for Uriah to die in battle and takes Bathsheba into his house.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars see 2 Samuel 11–12 as part of the Court History or Succession Narrative, often valued for its unusually sharp portrayal of royal abuse and moral failure. The text is notable for offering no flattering spin on David's actions.

cards.q:
__**Solomon’s Wise Judgment**__
Two women claim the same baby; King Solomon proposes cutting the child in half and the true mother reveals herself by begging for the child’s life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After becoming king, Solomon offers sacrifice at Gibeon and receives a dream in which God invites him to ask for something. Solomon asks for wisdom to govern the people well instead of long life or military victory. God grants the request, and the following judgment between two women becomes the public proof of his discernment.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars see 1 Kings 3 as part of the Solomon tradition that presents him as the ideal wise king before later narratives emphasize his failures. Kings is commonly associated with Deuteronomistic editing, with major literary shaping often dated to the exilic period in the 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Nineveh Repents**__
Jonah finally preaches in Nineveh, and the city responds with fasting and repentance so that destruction is withheld.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jonah receives the command again, goes to Nineveh, and announces that the city will be overthrown in forty days. To his displeasure, the people believe the warning, fast, and even the king and animals participate in mourning rituals. God sees their response and does not bring the announced destruction.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point out the exaggerated features of the story, including the city’s scale and the animals in sackcloth, as signs of deliberate literary humor or satire. The book is frequently read as a critique of narrow nationalism and as a late didactic narrative rather than historical report.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After his baptism, Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness and faces three tests involving bread, spectacular display, and political power. He answers each temptation with scripture and the devil leaves him. The chapter then shifts to Galilee, where Jesus begins preaching and calling disciples.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually read this story as a highly shaped theological narrative rather than a scene recoverable in detail by historical method. It is often compared with Israel's wilderness testing and Moses imagery, and Matthew's version differs in order from Luke's.

cards.q:
__**The Temptation in the Wilderness**__
After fasting in the wilderness, Jesus resists the devil’s tests and begins his public ministry.

__**Jesus Calms the Storm**__
A furious storm threatens to sink the boat while Jesus sleeps; the disciples wake him in panic and he rebukes the wind and waves, bringing sudden calm.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After teaching by the sea, Jesus crosses the lake with his disciples. A violent storm fills the boat with water while Jesus sleeps, and the disciples fear they are about to die. Jesus wakes, rebukes the wind and sea, and the disciples are left asking who he is.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Mark to around 70 CE, making it the earliest canonical Gospel in the view of many researchers. The story belongs to a cluster of sea and nature miracles that present Jesus with powers associated in Jewish scripture with God's rule over chaotic waters.

cards.q:
__**Jesus Walks on Water**__
During a storm the disciples see Jesus walking on the sea; Peter tries, begins to sink, and is saved; the wind stops when Jesus enters the boat.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the feeding of the crowd, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes to pray alone. In the night he comes to them walking on the water, and Peter briefly walks toward him before becoming afraid and sinking. When Jesus enters the boat, the wind stops.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Matthew to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE. Peter's attempt to walk on the water appears only in Matthew, which makes the episode a good example of how the Gospels often retell related material with distinct emphases.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Jesus approaches Jerusalem, he sends disciples to fetch a donkey and enters the city while crowds spread garments and branches on the road. They shout royal and messianic acclamations, and the city is stirred by his arrival. The scene launches the final Jerusalem section of the Gospel.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually read the entry as a deliberately symbolic action shaped by scriptural allusion, especially to Zechariah. Matthew's version is famous for its awkward double-animal reading, which many scholars take as the result of a very literal interpretation of the prophecy text.

cards.q:
__**The Triumphal Entry**__
Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey while crowds greet him as a king and messianic figure.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In response to a question about who counts as a neighbor, Jesus tells of a man beaten on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest and a Levite pass by, but a Samaritan stops, treats the wounds, and pays for the man's care. Jesus then turns the question back on the listener.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Luke is often dated around 80–90 CE. The Good Samaritan appears only in Luke, and scholars usually see it as part of that Gospel's strong interest in reversal, outsiders, and ethical response rather than ritual status.

cards.q:
__**The Good Samaritan**__
A Samaritan, not the expected religious figures, becomes the true neighbor by aiding a wounded man.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A younger son demands his inheritance early, leaves home, squanders everything, and is reduced to hunger and humiliation. He returns planning only to ask for servant status, but his father embraces him and throws a celebration. The older brother resists the welcome, and the story ends with tension still hanging in the air.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This parable is unique to Luke and is usually treated by scholars as one of the best examples of Luke's concern with loss, reversal, and restoration. Because it ends without resolving the older brother's response, many interpreters see it as intentionally pressing the audience rather than neatly closing the story.

cards.q:
__**The Prodigal Son**__
A younger son wastes his inheritance, returns home in ruin, and is welcomed back while his older brother resents it.

__**The Samaritan Woman at the Well**__
Jesus talks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well, reveals her life story, and offers “living water”; she becomes one of the first evangelists to her town.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Traveling through Samaria, Jesus stops at Jacob's well and asks a woman for water. Their conversation moves from ordinary water to 'living water,' worship, and the coming Messiah, and Jesus reveals details of her personal life. She goes back to town and many Samaritans come out to hear him.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date John to the late 1st century CE, often around 90–100 CE. The story is notable for crossing multiple social boundaries at once—male and female, Jew and Samaritan, teacher and outsider—and it has no close Synoptic parallel.

cards.q:
__**The Woman Caught in Adultery**__
Religious leaders bring a woman caught in adultery to Jesus; he writes on the ground and says that whoever is without sin should throw the first stone, then tells her he does not condemn her.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Scribes and Pharisees bring a woman accused of adultery and try to trap Jesus into either endorsing stoning or appearing to reject the law. Jesus bends down and writes on the ground, then challenges the sinless person to cast the first stone. One by one the accusers leave, and Jesus dismisses the woman without condemnation.

notes.label: Scholarly note
