notes.text: This is one of the most famous New Testament episodes, but it has major text-critical problems: many scholars think it was not originally part of the Gospel of John because it is absent from the earliest and best Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in some later copies. Even so, the story became deeply embedded in Christian tradition.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jesus delays before going to Bethany even though Lazarus is ill. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and Jesus speaks with Martha and Mary before going to the grave. He orders the stone removed, calls Lazarus out, and the event intensifies the move toward Jesus' own death.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This is one of the most striking examples of material unique to John, since no close parallel appears in the Synoptic Gospels. Scholars often debate whether the story is a highly symbolic Johannine construction, an expanded tradition, or something with a historical core that circulated independently.

cards.q:
__**The Raising of Lazarus**__
After Lazarus dies and is buried, Jesus calls him out of the tomb in one of John’s climactic signs.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Jesus appears to the disciples, Thomas says he will not believe unless he can see and touch the wounds. A week later Jesus appears again, invites Thomas to inspect the wounds, and Thomas responds with a direct confession. The scene closes with a statement about those who believe without seeing.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that John's resurrection scenes are tightly linked to the Gospel's stated purpose of producing belief. The Thomas episode is also frequently read as addressing later audiences who had no direct access to eyewitness experience and had to rely on testimony.

cards.q:
__**Doubting Thomas**__
Thomas refuses secondhand reports of the resurrection until he encounters the risen Jesus for himself.

__**Stephen's Martyrdom**__
Stephen is accused, gives a long speech, and is killed by a mob while Saul looks on.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Stephen is chosen among the Seven, performs signs, and is accused before the council. He gives a long retelling of Israel's history that ends in sharp accusation against his hearers. He is then dragged out and stoned, while a young Saul is present at the scene.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read Stephen's speech as a major interpretive summary of Israel's past within Luke-Acts, not just a trial defense. Acts is generally dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, and the speech likely reflects the author's theological shaping rather than a verbatim transcript.

cards.q:
__**The Conversion of Saul**__
Saul encounters a heavenly light on the road to Damascus, is struck blind, and becomes a follower of Jesus.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While traveling to Damascus to act against Jesus' followers, Saul is overwhelmed by a light and hears the voice of Jesus. He is left blind and must be led into the city. There Ananias restores his sight, Saul is baptized, and he quickly begins proclaiming Jesus.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Acts retells Paul's conversion more than once, which scholars often take as a sign of how central the event is to Luke's narrative. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, and the speeches in the retellings are generally understood as literary compositions shaped by the author.

cards.q:
__**Peter and Cornelius**__
Peter visits the Gentile centurion Cornelius, and the Spirit falls on Gentiles before they are baptized.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Cornelius receives a vision telling him to send for Peter, while Peter has a vision that challenges his food boundaries. When Peter enters Cornelius's house and speaks, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile listeners. Peter then orders that they be baptized, despite the surprise of Jewish believers present.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars see Acts 10 as one of the decisive turning points in Luke's narrative because it authorizes Gentile inclusion through visions and Spirit activity. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Council of Jerusalem**__
Leaders debate whether Gentile converts must keep the full Jewish law, and a compromise letter is sent.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A dispute over circumcision leads Paul, Barnabas, and others to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders. After debate and speeches by Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James, the gathering sends a letter asking Gentile believers to observe only certain basic restrictions. The decision is then carried back to the churches.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars regularly compare Acts 15 with Paul's own account in Galatians 2 because the two portray the Jerusalem discussions differently. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, and many scholars think Luke has shaped the scene to emphasize unity.

cards.q:
__**Manna and Quail in the Wilderness**__
The Israelites complain in the wilderness, and God provides manna in the morning and quail for meat.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Soon after crossing the sea, the Israelites complain that they have been brought into the wilderness to die of hunger. God responds by sending quail in the evening and manna in the morning, with instructions about daily gathering and the Sabbath. The story ends with manna becoming Israel's regular food in the wilderness.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often treat Exodus 16 as part of the wilderness-tradition cycle shaped over time within the Pentateuch. Some also compare manna traditions with wider ancient Near Eastern stories of divine provision in harsh landscapes, though no direct one-to-one source is agreed on. Exodus reached final written form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Crossing the Jordan**__
Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground as the ark goes before them and memorial stones are set up.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: With Moses gone and Joshua now leading, Israel comes to the Jordan River, the final barrier before entering Canaan. The priests carrying the ark step into the river and the waters stop upstream. The people cross on dry ground, and stones are taken from the riverbed to create a memorial. The crossing marks the formal entry into the land.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars frequently compare this crossing scene to the sea crossing in Exodus because both stories depict waters parted under divine action and both end with memorializing language. Many see Joshua 3–4 as a carefully shaped entry narrative within a book edited over time, with major literary formation commonly placed between the 7th and 5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Gideon Defeats the Midianites**__
God reduces Gideon's army so that Israel defeats Midian with trumpets, jars, and torches.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After another cycle of oppression in the time of the judges, Midian dominates Israel and forces people into hiding. Gideon is called while threshing in secret and repeatedly asks for reassurance. Before the battle, his army is drastically reduced so the coming victory cannot be credited to military strength. At night the men blow trumpets, smash jars, reveal torches, and throw the enemy camp into panic.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see Gideon's story as layered, since different sections present him in different tones: reluctant deliverer, cult reformer, military leader, and eventually a figure associated with problematic royal behavior. Judges is widely viewed as a compilation of older hero traditions shaped into a larger work in the monarchic and exilic periods, roughly the 8th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Ruth and Naomi**__
After great loss, Ruth stays with Naomi, goes to Bethlehem, and eventually marries Boaz.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The book of Ruth is set in the time of the judges, but instead of focusing on warfare or national crisis, it follows a family story shaped by loss and loyalty. After Naomi's husband and sons die in Moab, Ruth refuses to leave her and goes with her to Bethlehem. Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz, Naomi instructs her in how to appeal for protection, and Boaz arranges to act as kinsman-redeemer. The story ends with marriage, a child, and Ruth's connection to David's line.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read Ruth as a counterpoint to stricter attitudes toward foreign wives found in texts like Ezra-Nehemiah, because the heroine is a Moabite who is positively integrated into Israel's story. The book is frequently dated to the Persian period, often around the 5th–4th centuries BCE, though not all scholars agree.

cards.q:
__**Nathan Confronts David**__
Nathan tells David a parable about a stolen lamb, exposes his crime, and announces judgment on his house.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Nathan approaches David with a parable about a rich man who steals a poor man's lamb. When David condemns the offender, Nathan tells him he is the man. The child born from the affair dies, but David later has another son by Bathsheba, Solomon.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is often read as one of the Bible's clearest examples of a prophet confronting a king. Scholars also note how it sets in motion the later family and succession crises that dominate the rest of David's story.

cards.q:
__**Solomon Builds the Temple**__
Solomon builds the temple in Jerusalem, brings the ark into it, and dedicates it as the central place of worship.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After David's reign ends, Solomon consolidates power and undertakes the major royal project his father had prepared for but not completed. He organizes labor, gathers materials, and builds the temple in Jerusalem as the central place of worship for Israel. The project ties his kingship closely to the city's religious life.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars generally see 1 Kings as part of the Deuteronomistic History, a literary work often dated in major stages to the late monarchic and exilic periods, especially the 7th–6th centuries BCE. The temple account is also compared with ancient Near Eastern royal building inscriptions, where kings present major construction projects as proof of divine favor and legitimate rule.

cards.q:
__**Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire**__
Elijah and Elisha walk together; a chariot of fire and horses of fire appear, and Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Elijah and Elisha travel together, prophetic groups warn that Elijah is about to be taken away. Elijah parts the Jordan, and then a chariot and horses of fire appear as he is taken up in a whirlwind. Elisha picks up Elijah's cloak and continues the prophetic work.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare this departure scene with ancient traditions about exceptional figures who do not undergo an ordinary death. The Elijah-Elisha narratives are embedded in Kings, generally treated as part of the Deuteronomistic History shaped in the late monarchic and exilic periods, especially the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Naaman the Leper Healed by Elisha**__
Naaman, commander of Aram, is told by Elisha to wash seven times in the Jordan; he obeys and his skin is restored.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Naaman, a successful commander from Aram, seeks healing after a captive Israelite girl points him toward Elisha. Offended at first by the simple instruction to wash in the Jordan, he eventually obeys and is healed. The story ends with Naaman's acknowledgment of Israel's God and with Gehazi's greed being punished.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note the irony in this chapter: an Israelite king appears helpless while a foreign commander receives help and insight from an Israelite prophet. The Elisha cycle likely circulated before being woven into Kings, whose larger literary history is usually dated to the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Valley of Dry Bones**__
Ezekiel sees a valley of bones restored to life as a vision of national restoration.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In a vision, Ezekiel is taken to a valley full of dry bones and told to prophesy over them. The bones come together, are covered with flesh, and finally receive breath so that they stand as a vast army. The vision is then explained as representing the restoration of Israel from apparent death and exile.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars generally read this chapter first as a metaphor for national restoration rather than an original statement about individual resurrection, though later Jewish and Christian readers often extended it in that direction. Ezekiel 37 belongs to the exilic prophetic corpus of the 6th century BCE, preserved in a book that also shows later literary shaping.

cards.q:
__**The Writing on the Wall**__
At Belshazzar’s feast, mysterious writing appears on the wall, Daniel interprets it, and Babylon’s ruler falls that very night.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Belshazzar uses temple vessels from Jerusalem during a feast, and a hand appears writing on the wall. None of the court experts can explain it, so Daniel is summoned and reads the words as a verdict of judgment. That same night Belshazzar is killed and the kingdom passes to the Medes and Persians.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Historically, Belshazzar was not king in the way the story presents him, though he was a real Babylonian crown prince known from extra-biblical records. That mismatch is one reason scholars do not treat Daniel 5 as straightforward court history, and instead place the final shape of Daniel in the 2nd century BCE.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jairus begs Jesus to come because his daughter is dying. After an interruption on the way, messengers report that the girl has died, but Jesus continues to the house, dismisses mourners, and takes only a few witnesses inside. He speaks to the child and she rises.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point to Mark 5 as a strong example of Mark's 'sandwich' technique, since Jairus's story wraps around the healing of the bleeding woman. That literary structure is one reason many scholars see the Gospel traditions as carefully composed narratives rather than bare chronicle.

cards.q:
__**Raising Jairus’s Daughter**__
Jesus goes to raise a dying girl, declares she is not lost for good, and restores her to life.

__**Raising the Widow’s Son at Nain**__
Jesus meets a funeral procession, has compassion on the widow, touches the bier, and commands the young man to rise.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Jesus approaches Nain, he encounters a funeral procession for a widow's only son. Moved with compassion, he stops the procession, touches the bier, and tells the dead man to rise. The young man sits up and begins to speak, and fear spreads through the crowd.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Luke to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE. This scene is often compared with stories in 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 4 where prophets restore dead sons to widows, suggesting Luke is presenting Jesus in continuity with Elijah and Elisha while also intensifying the miracle.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Jesus passes through Jericho, Zacchaeus cannot see over the crowd and climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus stops, calls him down, and goes to his house despite public complaint about associating with a sinner. Zacchaeus responds by offering restitution and generosity, and Jesus declares salvation has come to the house.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Like several Lukan stories, this episode focuses on table fellowship, social stigma, and economic reversal. Scholars often see it as setting the tone for Jesus' final approach to Jerusalem in Luke's narrative.

cards.q:
__**Zacchaeus the Tax Collector**__
Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus, welcomes him joyfully, and publicly promises restitution.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: At a village wedding the wine runs out, and Jesus has stone jars filled with water. The water becomes wine, the steward praises its quality, and only a small circle knows what happened. John presents the event as the first sign through which Jesus reveals his glory.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: John is commonly dated around 90–100 CE, though some argue slightly earlier or later. Scholars often note that John calls miracles 'signs,' highlighting symbolic meaning, and Cana is a good example because the story is tied to abundance, revelation, and replacement imagery.

cards.q:
__**The Wedding at Cana**__
At a wedding in Cana, Jesus turns water into wine in the first sign of John’s Gospel.

__**The Ascension of Jesus**__
After appearing to his followers, Jesus is taken up and the disciples are told he will return in the same way.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The risen Jesus spends time with his followers, speaks about the kingdom, and tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Spirit. In front of them he is taken up, and two figures tell the disciples that he will return in the same manner. The disciples then return to Jerusalem and prepare for what comes next.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Luke and Acts are the only New Testament works to narrate the ascension explicitly, and scholars often see Acts 1 as the literary bridge between Luke's Gospel and the church story that follows. Acts is usually dated by scholars to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, though some argue for somewhat earlier or later dates.

cards.q:
__**Healing at the Beautiful Gate**__
Peter heals a man who could not walk, drawing a crowd at the temple and leading to another public speech.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Peter and John encounter a man who has long sat at the temple gate asking for alms. Peter tells him he has no silver or gold but commands him in Jesus' name to walk, and the man enters the temple leaping and praising God. The miracle gathers a crowd, and Peter uses the moment to address the people.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how Acts repeatedly pairs miracle stories with interpretive speeches, using the healing as a launch point for proclamation. Acts is commonly dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Ananias and Sapphira**__
A couple lies about money given to the community and both die after being confronted.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After others sell property and contribute proceeds, Ananias and Sapphira present only part of their money while claiming it is the full amount. Peter confronts each of them separately, and both collapse dead. Fear spreads through the community as the episode becomes known.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars view this as a severe purity-and-boundary story for the early movement, comparable in function to older judgment stories about sacred violation. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, commonly around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Philip and the Ethiopian Official**__
Philip explains scripture to an Ethiopian court official and baptizes him on the road.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Philip is directed to a road where he meets an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah in his chariot. Beginning from the passage the man is reading, Philip explains the message about Jesus. When they come to water, the official asks to be baptized, and Philip baptizes him before vanishing from sight.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often highlight this story for its geographic reach and for the way Acts uses scripture interpretation to connect Israel's texts to Jesus. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Philippian Jailer**__
After an earthquake opens the prison, a jailer is stopped from suicide and is baptized with his household.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned, they pray and sing during the night. An earthquake opens the doors and loosens the chains, but the prisoners remain there. The jailer, thinking all have escaped, is stopped by Paul, then takes the missionaries home and is baptized with his household.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point to the earthquake, prison release, and conversion sequence as a classic example of Acts combining miracle, reversal, and mission in one tightly shaped episode. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Paul in Athens**__
Paul debates in Athens and delivers a speech at the Areopagus about the 'unknown god.'

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Disturbed by the city's many idols, Paul argues in the synagogue and marketplace before being brought to the Areopagus. There he speaks about the creator God, cites lines his audience would recognize, and challenges idolatry in light of resurrection. Some mock, some remain curious, and a few join him.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This is one of the most discussed speeches in Acts because it frames Paul's message in terms suited to a Greco-Roman audience. Scholars usually date Acts to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, and generally regard the speech as Luke's literary composition rather than a stenographic record.

cards.q:
__**The Vision of the Exalted Christ**__
John sees the risen Christ among seven lampstands and receives a commission to write what he sees.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: John introduces himself as being on Patmos and says he receives a vision on the Lord's day. He hears a loud voice, turns, and sees a figure like a son of man among seven lampstands, holding seven stars. The figure speaks, identifies himself with death and life, and commands John to write to seven churches.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Revelation to the reign of Domitian, around 95 CE, though some argue for an earlier date under Nero. The opening vision draws heavily on imagery from Daniel 7, Daniel 10, and Ezekiel, showing how Revelation reworks earlier Jewish apocalyptic texts rather than inventing its symbolism from scratch.

cards.q:
__**The Scroll and the Lamb**__
A sealed scroll appears in heaven, and only the slain Lamb is found worthy to open it.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A scroll sealed with seven seals is held in the right hand of the one on the throne, and no one is initially found worthy to open it. Then the Lamb appears, described both as slain and victorious, and takes the scroll. Heaven responds with a new song and escalating worship.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note the deliberate shock of hearing about a lion and then seeing a slaughtered lamb instead. The scene is central to Revelation's symbolic logic and is usually placed within a text composed in the late 1st century CE, most often around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Four Horsemen**__
As the first seals are opened, riders bring conquest, war, famine, and death.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: When the first four seals are opened, four mounted figures appear in sequence. They are associated with conquest, violence, scarcity, and widespread death. The same chapter continues with the souls of slain witnesses and a scene of cosmic disturbance.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The horsemen are among Revelation's most famous images, but scholars still debate how individually fixed their meanings are. The imagery draws on Zechariah's horse visions and broader apocalyptic convention, and Revelation is usually dated to the late 1st century CE.

cards.q:
__**The Woman, the Child, and the Dragon**__
A radiant woman gives birth, a dragon tries to destroy the child, and war breaks out in heaven.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A woman clothed with the sun appears in labor while a dragon waits to devour her child. The child is snatched up to God, the woman flees into the wilderness, and a heavenly battle leads to the dragon's expulsion. The dragon then turns against the rest of her offspring.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is a major example of Revelation's layered symbolism, and scholars disagree over how far the woman should be read as Israel, Mary, Zion, the people of God, or some fusion of these. The chapter's dragon combat imagery has parallels in older Near Eastern and biblical chaos-combat traditions.

cards.q:
__**The Beasts from Sea and Land**__
A beast rises from the sea, another from the land, and people are pressured into worship and marked loyalty.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: John sees a beast from the sea receiving authority from the dragon and another beast from the land supporting the first. The second beast promotes worship of the first and enforces a mark connected with buying and selling. The chapter closes with the famous number 666.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Most critical scholars read the beast imagery against the backdrop of Roman imperial power, emperor worship, and especially the memory of Nero. The number 666 is widely explained through gematria, often linked to 'Nero Caesar,' though not all scholars agree on every detail.

cards.q:
__**The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne**__
Satan is bound, released, defeated, and the dead stand before a final judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: An angel binds Satan for a thousand years while the martyrs reign, after which Satan is released for a final rebellion. Fire ends the revolt, and then the dead stand before a great white throne as books are opened. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The millennium has produced enormous interpretive disagreement, and scholars usually note that early Christianity itself did not settle on one reading. Revelation 20 is one reason the book played such a volatile role in later theology and apocalyptic speculation.

cards.q:
__**The New Heaven, New Earth, and New Jerusalem**__
A renewed creation appears, the holy city descends, and the final vision ends with life-giving water and the tree of life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: John sees a new heaven and new earth and the New Jerusalem descending from heaven. The city is described in brilliant detail, with no temple because God and the Lamb are its light. The final chapter presents the river of life, the tree of life, final warnings, and the closing promise that Jesus is coming soon.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how the end of Revelation deliberately circles back to Genesis by restoring access to the tree of life while also transforming prophetic city and temple hopes. The book is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**A Wife for Isaac**__
Abraham’s servant travels to find a wife for Isaac, and Rebekah is chosen and brought back to him.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Abraham sends his servant to his kin to find a wife for Isaac rather than taking one from Canaan. At a well, the servant asks for a sign, Rebekah fulfills it by offering water to him and his camels, and her family agrees to the match. Rebekah travels back and marries Isaac.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how heavily the chapter relies on repeated dialogue and careful retelling, almost like a self-contained novella. It is part of the patriarchal material that most scholars think reached written shape over time and was incorporated into Genesis' final form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Joseph and Potiphar’s Wife**__
Joseph refuses Potiphar’s wife, is falsely accused, and is thrown into prison.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Joseph rises within Potiphar's household, but Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce him. Joseph refuses and flees, leaving his garment behind. She uses the garment as evidence in a false accusation, and Joseph is sent to prison.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This story is often compared with ancient Near Eastern court tales and with the Egyptian 'Tale of Two Brothers,' which also includes a false sexual accusation after a refusal. Scholars usually treat it as part of the Joseph novella complex in Genesis' final literary form.

cards.q:
__**Water from the Rock**__
When the people complain of thirst, Moses strikes the rock at Horeb and water comes out for them.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After complaining about hunger, the Israelites next complain that there is no water. God instructs Moses to go before the people, strike the rock at Horeb, and bring out water. The place is named Massah and Meribah because of the people's testing and quarreling.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars commonly note that Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 preserve similar but not identical water-from-rock traditions, suggesting related versions of the same type of wilderness story. These traditions were likely incorporated into the Pentateuch over a long period, with final compilation usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Rahab and the Spies**__
Rahab hides Israelite spies in Jericho and is promised protection when the city falls.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Before the attack on Jericho, Joshua sends spies into the city. Rahab hides them from the king's men, helps them escape, and asks that her household be spared when Israel comes. A scarlet cord marks the agreement.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how this chapter exalts an outsider who correctly recognizes Israel's god, a theme that complicates later ethnic boundary lines. The book of Joshua is widely thought to contain older conquest traditions shaped in a literary work that many scholars date in major stages from the late monarchic period to the exilic or post-exilic era, roughly the 7th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Deborah and Barak**__
Deborah sends Barak into battle, Sisera is defeated, and Jael kills him with a tent peg.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deborah, a prophet and judge, tells Barak to gather troops against Sisera. Sisera's army is routed, he flees on foot, and Jael kills him while he sleeps in her tent. Judges 5 then retells the victory in poetic form.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Judges 4 and 5 are often compared because the prose narrative and the Song of Deborah do not match in every detail. Many scholars consider Judges 5 one of the oldest poetic pieces in the Hebrew Bible, while the prose version may be later, and the book of Judges probably reached written form through stages from the monarchic to exilic periods, roughly the 8th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Hannah Prays for a Son**__
Hannah prays for a child, vows to dedicate him to God, and later gives birth to Samuel.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hannah is distressed because she has no child and is mocked by Peninnah. She prays at the sanctuary in Shiloh, vows that if she receives a son she will dedicate him to God, and is misunderstood by Eli as drunk. After Samuel is born and weaned, she brings him to Shiloh and leaves him there for service.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that this story introduces the rise of Samuel while also centering a woman's vow, prayer, and agency in a way that drives the larger national story forward. First Samuel is usually dated in its literary formation to the monarchic and exilic periods, with major shaping often placed between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Samuel Hears God's Call**__
As a boy serving at Shiloh, Samuel hears God call him in the night and receives a message of judgment against Eli's house.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While serving under Eli, Samuel hears his name called at night and at first assumes Eli is summoning him. After Eli realizes what is happening, he tells Samuel how to respond. Samuel then receives a revelation announcing judgment on Eli's family, and his reputation as a prophet begins to spread through Israel.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is often read as a prophetic call narrative marking the transition from Eli's failing house to Samuel's authority. Scholars commonly place the books of Samuel within a long editorial history tied to the Deuteronomistic History, with major written shaping often dated from the late monarchic to exilic periods, roughly the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Israel Asks for a King**__
Israel asks Samuel for a king like other nations, and Samuel warns them what kingship will cost.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Samuel grows old and his sons prove corrupt, the elders ask for a king to judge them like other nations. Samuel is displeased, but God tells him to listen while also warning the people. Samuel then describes how a king will draft sons, take daughters, seize property, and burden the nation.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: First Samuel 8 is central to debates about whether the book reflects pro-monarchy and anti-monarchy strands placed side by side. Many scholars see tension between texts that welcome kingship and texts that treat it as a rejection of divine rule, suggesting multiple viewpoints preserved in Samuel's final form.

cards.q:
__**Saul Chosen as King**__
Saul searches for lost donkeys, meets Samuel, is anointed, and is publicly chosen as Israel's first king.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While looking for his father's lost donkeys, Saul meets Samuel, who has already been told that a future king is coming. Samuel privately anoints Saul, gives him confirming signs, and later presents him publicly by lot before the people. Saul is then recognized as king, though not everyone accepts him.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point out that Saul's rise is narrated in more than one way, with private anointing, charismatic signs, and public selection all appearing in close proximity. These features are often taken as evidence of layered traditions brought together in Samuel's literary growth.

cards.q:
__**Saul Dies on Mount Gilboa**__
Saul and his sons die in battle against the Philistines, and Saul falls on his own sword.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Israel is routed on Mount Gilboa, Saul's sons are killed, and Saul is badly wounded by archers. Rather than be captured, he falls on his own sword, and his armor-bearer does the same. The Philistines strip the bodies, but men from Jabesh-gilead later recover and bury them.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars regularly compare this account with 2 Samuel 1, where an Amalekite claims he killed Saul, creating a well-known tension in the narrative. Such double reporting is one of many signs that Samuel preserves multiple traditions side by side.

cards.q:
__**David Becomes King over All Israel**__
After years of conflict, David is anointed king over all Israel and captures Jerusalem.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After ruling in Hebron over Judah, David is finally accepted by the northern tribes as well. He is anointed king over all Israel and then captures Jerusalem, making it his capital. His kingship is strengthened through military success and political consolidation.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often regard 2 Samuel 5 as part of the rise narrative that legitimates David's rule over both Judah and Israel. Jerusalem's capture and selection as capital also has obvious retrospective significance for later Judahite tradition.

cards.q:
__**Absalom's Rebellion**__
Absalom wins support, seizes Jerusalem, and drives David into flight before the rebellion is crushed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Absalom builds popularity among the people, declares himself king, and forces David to flee Jerusalem. David's supporters regroup while Absalom occupies the city. The revolt ends in battle in the forest, where Absalom is killed despite David's plea to spare him.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars commonly treat these chapters as core material in the Succession Narrative, a section often admired for political realism and narrative skill. The story is also important for showing that Nathan's judgment against David's house unfolds through domestic and dynastic disaster.

cards.q:
__**The Queen of Sheba Visits Solomon**__
The queen of Sheba visits Solomon, tests his wisdom, and departs impressed by his court and wealth.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Word of Solomon's wisdom spreads abroad, and the queen of Sheba comes with a large caravan to test him with hard questions. She sees his court, servants, temple arrangements, and wealth, and exchanges lavish gifts with him. The story reinforces Solomon's reputation as an internationally recognized king.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate how much, if any, direct historical memory lies behind the visit, and the identity of Sheba is usually linked with South Arabia, though some traditions place it elsewhere. Like the surrounding Solomon material, the story comes through 1 Kings in a literary history commonly dated in major form to the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Hezekiah and Sennacherib**__
When Assyria threatens Jerusalem, Hezekiah seeks deliverance and the city is spared.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As the Assyrian empire threatens Judah, King Hezekiah faces pressure from Sennacherib, who has already conquered other cities and now challenges Jerusalem. Assyrian officials mock Judah's trust in God and in Hezekiah. Hezekiah turns to prayer and to the prophet Isaiah, and the story ends with Jerusalem spared while the Assyrian campaign fails.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This episode is especially notable because it overlaps with extra-biblical Assyrian records, including Sennacherib's annals, which do confirm a campaign against Judah and Hezekiah though they present the outcome differently. Scholars usually treat Kings as part of the Deuteronomistic History, shaped in major editions during the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Esther Becomes Queen**__
Esther is taken into the Persian court and becomes queen in place of Vashti.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In the Persian court, Queen Vashti is removed after defying the king, and a search begins for a new queen. Esther, a young Jewish woman living in Persia, is brought into that process and eventually chosen, though her Jewish identity is not publicly disclosed at first. Her rise to royal position later becomes crucial when her people face danger.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The book of Esther is unusual because, in the Hebrew version, God is never explicitly mentioned. Scholars usually date its composition to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, often around the 4th–3rd centuries BCE, and debate how closely its court setting reflects actual Persian history versus later Jewish storytelling.

cards.q:
__**Isaiah’s Call**__
Isaiah sees the Lord in the temple, is purified with a coal, and is commissioned as a prophet.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: At the start of Isaiah's prophetic ministry, Judah is already facing moral and political crisis. In a temple vision, Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned, surrounded by seraphim, and becomes acutely aware of his own uncleanness. After being symbolically purified, he hears the divine commission and is sent to a people who will hear but not truly understand.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars see Isaiah 6 as a classic prophetic call narrative, though some argue it may also function as a later commissioning scene placed strategically within the book. The book of Isaiah is widely understood as a composite work shaped over several centuries, with First Isaiah rooted in the 8th century BCE and the book reaching final form much later, likely in the Persian period.

cards.q:
__**Daniel and His Friends Refuse the King’s Food**__
Daniel and his friends refuse the royal food, eat a simpler diet, and are found healthier and wiser than the others.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Taken into Babylonian service, Daniel and his companions are assigned the king's provisions and a program of training. They refuse the food and wine, request vegetables and water, and after the test appear better than the others. At the end of the training they stand out for wisdom and understanding.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars date the final form of Daniel to the 2nd century BCE, especially the Maccabean crisis, even though the book is set in the Babylonian and Persian periods. The court-tale style of Daniel 1–6 resembles diaspora wisdom narratives in which Jewish heroes remain loyal while serving foreign empires.

cards.q:
__**Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream of the Statue**__
Daniel recounts and interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of a great statue made of successive materials that is shattered by a stone.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men tell him both the dream and its interpretation. Daniel prays, receives the mystery, and describes a colossal statue of different metals broken by a stone not cut by human hands. He explains the image as a succession of kingdoms replaced by a final kingdom established by God.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read the statue as an apocalyptic schema of empires, and many argue that the sequence makes best sense from the perspective of the 2nd century BCE. Daniel's mixture of court tale and apocalypse, along with its Hebrew-Aramaic split, has made it a major case study in the development of Jewish apocalyptic literature.

cards.q:
__**Job Is Tested**__
In the heavenly court, Job loses his children, wealth, and health, but refuses to curse God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Job is introduced as prosperous and blameless. In the heavenly scene, the satan challenges whether Job is faithful only because he is protected, and permission is given for his possessions, children, and then his health to be struck. Job mourns deeply, and his friends arrive to sit with him in silence.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Most scholars date the prose frame of Job and the long poetic debates differently, often suggesting a long literary growth rather than a single composition. The book is commonly placed sometime between the 7th and 4th centuries BCE, and the heavenly-court scene is often compared with wider ancient Near Eastern depictions of divine councils.

cards.q:
__**The Lord Answers Job from the Whirlwind**__
After long speeches, God answers Job out of the whirlwind with questions about the creation and order of the world.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Job and his friends argue at length, God speaks from the whirlwind and challenges Job with a long series of questions about the earth, sea, stars, animals, and the limits of human knowledge. Job answers briefly, and the book ends with Job's fortunes being restored and his friends rebuked.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars regularly debate whether the restoration ending belongs to the same stage of composition as the poetic core, since it changes the tone sharply. The book's speeches are among the Hebrew Bible's most sophisticated poetry, and many scholars think its final form emerged over multiple stages between roughly the 6th and 4th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Sign of Immanuel**__
Isaiah confronts King Ahaz during a political crisis and announces the sign of Immanuel.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Judah fears attack from the Syro-Ephraimite coalition, Isaiah meets Ahaz and tells him not to panic or seek security through foreign alliances. When Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, Isaiah declares that a young woman will bear a son called Immanuel. The sign is tied to the immediate crisis and the downfall of Judah's enemies.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars almost always read Isaiah 7 first in its 8th-century BCE setting during the Syro-Ephraimite war, not as a text originally written about a much later period. Debate centers on the Hebrew word almah, the original historical referent of the child, and how later Jewish and Christian interpreters reapplied the passage.

cards.q:
__**Micah’s Vision of Zion and the Coming Ruler**__
Micah describes nations streaming to Zion and a future ruler emerging from Bethlehem.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After harsh judgment in the earlier section, Micah turns to visions of restoration. Nations stream to Zion for instruction, war gives way to peace, and Bethlehem is named as the origin point of a future ruler. The chapters alternate between hope for deliverance and scenes of distress and siege.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Micah 4-5 is often compared directly with Isaiah 2 because both books share the vision of nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord. Scholars debate whether one borrowed from the other or whether both drew on a common tradition, while the book's final composition likely extended beyond Micah's own time.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. There his appearance changes, Moses and Elijah appear speaking with him, and a cloud overshadows them while a heavenly voice identifies Jesus and commands the disciples to listen to him. The disciples fall down in fear before the vision ends.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate whether this passage began as a resurrection-appearance tradition, a visionary story, or a symbolic revelation scene. Matthew's Gospel is usually dated around 80–90 CE and presents the event in a way that closely ties Jesus to Moses and Elijah while also surpassing them.

cards.q:
__**The Transfiguration**__
Jesus is transformed in glory before selected disciples, and a heavenly voice tells them to listen to him.

__**Paul's Shipwreck**__
On the voyage to Rome, Paul's ship is caught in a storm, runs aground, and everyone reaches shore alive.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Despite warnings, Paul's ship sails into dangerous conditions and is battered for days by a violent storm. Cargo is thrown overboard, hope is nearly lost, and Paul relays an assurance that all aboard will survive though the ship will be lost. The vessel finally runs aground, breaks apart, and the passengers reach land safely.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Acts 27 is widely admired for its detailed sea-voyage narrative, and many scholars have noted its similarities to ancient shipwreck literature while still debating how much derives from travel memory or literary skill. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Paul on Malta and in Rome**__
After surviving a shipwreck, Paul reaches Malta, survives a snakebite, and eventually arrives in Rome under guard.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the shipwreck, Paul and the others find shelter on Malta, where Paul survives a viper bite and heals the father of Publius and others on the island. The journey then continues to Rome. Acts closes with Paul under house arrest there, preaching and receiving visitors without the narrative resolving his trial.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often emphasize the abrupt ending of Acts, which leaves Paul's legal outcome unstated and has led to many theories about the author's purpose or the state of the source material. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Abram and Sarai in Egypt**__
Because of famine, Abram goes to Egypt and tells Sarai to say she is his sister, leading to trouble with Pharaoh.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A famine drives Abram and Sarai to Egypt. Fearing he will be killed because Sarai is beautiful, Abram tells her to say she is his sister. Pharaoh takes Sarai into his house, God afflicts Pharaoh's household, and Sarai is returned before Abram is sent away. (This is the first of three similar "wife-sister" episodes in Genesis.)

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars regularly discuss this as one of the Bible's 'wife-sister' stories and compare it with Genesis 20 and Genesis 26, where a very similar plot appears with different details. The repetition is one reason many scholars think Genesis preserves parallel traditions that were woven together in the Pentateuch's final composition, usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Abram and Melchizedek**__
After rescuing Lot, Abram meets Melchizedek, who blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the rescue of Lot, Melchizedek king of Salem brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram in the name of God Most High. Abram then gives him a tenth of everything. Abram also refuses to enrich himself from the king of Sodom.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Melchizedek appears only briefly in Genesis, which has made the passage a magnet for later interpretation in Psalm 110, Hebrews, and Second Temple literature. Scholars often regard the scene as an independent tradition attached to Genesis 14, with the Pentateuch in final form usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**God’s Covenant with Abram**__
God promises Abram descendants and land, and makes a covenant with him through a solemn ritual.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Abram complains that he still has no heir, and God promises descendants as numerous as the stars. Abram prepares animals for a covenant ritual, and a smoking fire pot and flaming torch pass between the pieces. God then promises Abram's offspring a land stretching across named territories after a period of affliction.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that cutting animals and passing between the pieces resembles ancient Near Eastern covenant or treaty rituals. The chapter is commonly assigned to a non-Priestly strand within Genesis, while the Pentateuch as a whole reached final form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Hagar and Ishmael**__
Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, Hagar conceives Ishmael, conflict follows, and God speaks to Hagar in the wilderness.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Because Sarai has not borne a child, she gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram. Hagar conceives, tension erupts between the two women, and Hagar flees into the wilderness. There an angel tells her to return and announces the birth and future of her son Ishmael.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This is one of the places where Genesis preserves a strong tension between the Sarah and Hagar lines, and scholars often compare it with Genesis 21, where Hagar and Ishmael are sent away again under different circumstances. Like many patriarchal stories, it is usually taken as part of a larger literary complex shaped into final form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Abram Becomes Abraham**__
God changes Abram’s name to Abraham, Sarai’s name to Sarah, and establishes circumcision as the sign of the covenant.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: God appears to Abram, changes his name to Abraham, and changes Sarai's name to Sarah. God promises that Sarah will bear a son and establishes circumcision as the sign of the covenant for Abraham's household. Abraham then circumcises himself, Ishmael, and the males in his house.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars commonly connect Genesis 17 with Priestly writing because of its concern with covenant, genealogy, divine names, and ritual markers such as circumcision. That material is often dated in written form to the exilic or post-exilic period, roughly the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Three Visitors and the Promise to Sarah**__
Three visitors come to Abraham, promise that Sarah will bear a son, and reveal judgment against Sodom.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Abraham welcomes three visitors, offers a meal, and hears the announcement that Sarah will bear a son within the year. Sarah laughs when she overhears the promise. The visitors then turn toward Sodom, and Abraham negotiates with God over whether the city can be spared if righteous people are found there.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point out that the chapter moves fluidly between 'three men' and the LORD, suggesting that older traditions may have been combined. Its final form belongs to the Abraham cycle as shaped in Genesis, generally dated in compilation to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Jacob’s Ladder**__
Jacob dreams of a stairway between earth and heaven and receives God’s promise of land, descendants, and protection.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While fleeing, Jacob sleeps with a stone for a pillow and dreams of a stairway or ramp reaching to heaven with divine beings ascending and descending on it. God repeats the promises of land, descendants, and protection. Jacob wakes, names the place Bethel, and marks the stone.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often classify this as an etiological story explaining Bethel's sanctity and the standing stone there. The Hebrew word is often understood as stairway or ramp rather than the later image of a household ladder, and the story belongs to the Jacob cycle in Genesis' final 6th–5th century BCE literary form.

cards.q:
__**Jacob Marries Leah and Rachel**__
Jacob works for Laban to marry Rachel, is deceived into marrying Leah first, and then marries Rachel as well.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jacob arrives at Laban's household, falls in love with Rachel, and agrees to work seven years for her. On the wedding night Laban gives him Leah instead, and Jacob must work additional years to marry Rachel too. The chapter begins the long family rivalry between the sisters.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point out the ironic reversal: Jacob the deceiver is now deceived in turn. The chapter also reflects how the patriarchal narratives explain the origins of Israel's tribes through Leah, Rachel, and later their servants, within material compiled into Genesis in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Joseph Tests His Brothers**__
Joseph’s brothers come to Egypt for food, and Joseph tests their character before revealing who he is.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: When famine brings Joseph's brothers to Egypt, he recognizes them but they do not recognize him. He accuses them, detains one brother, demands that Benjamin be brought, and later arranges the silver cup test. These episodes force the brothers to face the family crime they committed years earlier.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often highlight the careful narrative pacing here: repeated journeys, staged tests, and delayed recognition build toward Judah's speech and Joseph's disclosure. This section is part of the Joseph novella complex in Genesis' final literary form.

cards.q:
__**Jacob’s Family Moves to Egypt**__
Jacob and his family leave Canaan and settle in Egypt during the famine under Joseph’s protection.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jacob learns that Joseph is alive and travels to Egypt with his entire household. God speaks to Jacob on the way, promising to go with him and bring him back. The family settles in Goshen under Joseph's protection during the famine.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that this movement to Egypt sets up the opening situation of Exodus and links the patriarchal stories to Israel's later oppression. In literary terms it is part of Genesis' transition into the Exodus story world.

cards.q:
__**The Bronze Serpent**__
As people die from snakebites in the wilderness, Moses makes a bronze serpent so that those who look at it may live.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After another round of complaints, poisonous serpents strike the people and many die. The people confess, Moses intercedes, and he is instructed to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. Those who look at it after being bitten survive.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This story later became controversial within the Bible itself: 2 Kings 18:4 says a bronze serpent called Nehushtan was destroyed in Hezekiah's reforms because people were burning incense to it. That later notice is one reason scholars often see Numbers 21 as preserving an origin story for an object known in later Judah; the Pentateuch reached final written form in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Saul and the Amalekites**__
Saul spares Agag and the best spoil instead of destroying everything, and Samuel announces that his kingdom has been rejected.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Saul is commanded to destroy Amalek completely, but he preserves King Agag and the best animals. When Samuel arrives, Saul claims the animals were spared for sacrifice, but Samuel rejects the excuse. Agag is executed, and Samuel declares that the kingdom has been torn from Saul.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is widely discussed because of both the violence of the command and its role in Saul's rejection. Scholars usually read it as a key Deuteronomistic-style explanation for dynastic change, and it also reflects the Bible's recurring hostility toward Amalek as a remembered enemy.

cards.q:
__**David and Jonathan's Covenant**__
Jonathan and David form a deep covenant bond as Saul grows increasingly hostile toward David.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After David's rise in popularity, Jonathan forms a covenant with him and gives him royal gear. Saul becomes suspicious and repeatedly tries to kill David, forcing David into flight. Jonathan warns David and helps him escape, even though it puts Jonathan at odds with his father.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate how to describe David and Jonathan's bond, but most agree the text presents it as one of the most emotionally intense relationships in the Hebrew Bible. The surrounding material also shows signs of editorial growth as David's rise and Saul's decline are narrated from different angles.

cards.q:
__**David Spares Saul in the Cave**__
David has the chance to kill Saul in a cave but spares him and only cuts off part of his robe.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While hiding in the wilderness, David finds Saul vulnerable in a cave. Urged by his men to strike, David instead secretly cuts off a corner of Saul's robe and then reveals what he has done from a distance. Saul weeps, admits David's future kingship, and departs for the time being.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare 1 Samuel 24 with 1 Samuel 26, since both tell a story in which David spares Saul under circumstances that feel strikingly similar. The pair is frequently treated as a doublet or at least as parallel traditions preserved together in Samuel.

cards.q:
__**Saul and the Medium of Endor**__
Desperate before battle, Saul visits a medium at Endor and hears a final doom message associated with Samuel.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: With the Philistines preparing for war and no answer coming through approved means, Saul secretly seeks out a medium despite having banned such practices. She summons a figure described as Samuel, who tells Saul that he and his sons will die and the kingdom will pass to David. Saul collapses in fear before returning to camp.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This passage is a major crux for scholars because it raises questions about necromancy, afterlife beliefs, and whether the text means the apparition really is Samuel. It is also notable for portraying Saul violating his own policy in a final act of desperation.

cards.q:
__**Jerusalem Falls and the Exile Begins**__
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and its temple, and many Judeans are taken into exile.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After rebellion against Babylon, Jerusalem is besieged, breached, and devastated. The temple, palace, and major buildings are burned, leaders are captured, and large numbers of people are deported. The chapter marks the collapse of the kingdom of Judah and the beginning of exile.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE is one of the best-attested events behind the biblical narrative, known both from the Bible and Babylonian sources. Scholars widely view Kings as reaching a major exilic edition in response to this catastrophe, especially in the 6th century BCE.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A paralyzed man is brought to Jesus, who first declares his sins forgiven. Some scribes inwardly accuse him of blasphemy, so Jesus heals the man physically as a visible sign of authority to forgive. The man rises and goes home while the crowd reacts with awe.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars commonly view healing controversy stories like this as early tradition that circulated in shorter units before being placed in the Gospels. Matthew's version is more compressed than Mark's and omits details such as the lowering through the roof.

cards.q:
__**Jesus Heals a Paralytic**__
Jesus forgives a paralytic’s sins, heals him publicly, and provokes controversy over his authority.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jesus arrives in Gentile territory and meets a man living among tombs who cannot be restrained. The demons identify themselves as Legion, beg to enter a herd of pigs, and the pigs rush into the sea after Jesus permits it. The man is left clothed and sane, though the local population reacts with fear.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Mark is commonly dated around 65–75 CE and is often treated as the earliest Gospel. Scholars have long discussed the name Legion, with some suggesting a Roman political undertone, though the interpretation remains debated.

cards.q:
__**The Gerasene Demoniac**__
Jesus confronts a man possessed by many demons, sends them into pigs, and leaves the man restored.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A man approaches Jesus asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus points to the commandments and then tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. The man departs sorrowful, and Jesus uses the moment to teach about wealth and the kingdom.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often treat this as one of the clearest Gospel sayings on wealth because the demand is sharp and the disciples themselves react with alarm. Mark's Gospel is usually dated around 65–75 CE, and Matthew and Luke both adapt this episode in their own ways.

cards.q:
__**The Rich Man and the Kingdom**__
A wealthy man asks about eternal life, but leaves grieving when told to surrender his possessions.

__**Peter Raises Tabitha**__
Peter restores Tabitha to life after mourners gather around her body in Joppa.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In Joppa, Tabitha dies and is laid in an upstairs room while widows mourn her. Peter is summoned, sends the mourners out, prays, and tells her to rise. She opens her eyes and is presented alive to the believers and widows.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare this scene with gospel raising stories, especially because the wording and setup resemble miracle traditions associated with Jesus. Acts is generally dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Peter Escapes from Prison**__
Peter is imprisoned by Herod, but an angel leads him out at night while the guards remain behind.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Herod arrests Peter during a wave of persecution, and the church prays while he is kept under guard. An angel appears in the cell at night, Peter's chains fall off, and he is led past the sleeping guards into the street. After realizing what has happened, Peter goes to the gathered believers.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note the ironic and almost comic details of this story, especially the confusion at the house where believers do not first accept that Peter is free. Acts is generally dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Paul and Barnabas at Lystra**__
After a healing in Lystra, crowds mistake Paul and Barnabas for gods, and then the mood swings violently against them.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Paul heals a man who could not walk, and the crowd in Lystra concludes that the gods have come down in human form. Priests prepare sacrifices for Barnabas and Paul, who tear their clothes and protest. Soon afterward Paul is stoned and dragged outside the city, though he survives.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The identification of Barnabas with Zeus and Paul with Hermes is often discussed by scholars because it reflects Greco-Roman religious expectations in a local setting. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Lydia of Philippi**__
Lydia hears Paul's message by the riverside in Philippi, believes, and opens her household to the missionaries.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In Philippi, Paul and his companions go outside the city gate to a riverside place of prayer. There they meet Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, and the Lord opens her heart to listen. She and her household are baptized, and she urges the missionaries to stay at her home.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note Lydia's importance as one of Acts' first named converts in Europe and as a woman shown with household authority and economic standing. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Riot in Ephesus**__
As Paul's movement affects local trade tied to Artemis, a crowd erupts in the theater at Ephesus.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In Ephesus, Demetrius the silversmith warns fellow craftsmen that Paul's preaching is hurting both their business and the prestige of Artemis. A crowd gathers and rushes into the theater shouting in confusion. The disturbance finally subsides when a city official dismisses the assembly.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see this story as one of Acts' clearest windows into economic and civic tensions created by the spread of the movement. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE, and the chapter is valued for its urban detail even where precise historicity is debated.

cards.q:
__**The Throne in Heaven**__
John sees God's throne, heavenly worship, and the living creatures around it.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the church messages, John is taken through an open door in heaven. He sees a throne surrounded by twenty-four elders, flashes of lightning, and four living creatures who continually praise God. Heavenly worship becomes the setting for the visions that follow.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This scene is heavily indebted to throne visions in Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6. Scholars generally view Revelation as a highly intertextual work whose author expected readers to catch these scriptural echoes, and the book is usually dated around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**Babylon the Great Falls**__
John sees Babylon portrayed as a corrupt woman and then hears laments over her sudden collapse.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A woman called Babylon rides the beast and is described in lavish, violent, and accusatory imagery. The next chapter mourns the fall of the city through a series of laments by kings, merchants, and seafarers who had profited from her. Her destruction is portrayed as sudden and final.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Most scholars identify Babylon here as a coded reference to Rome, following a convention already found in some Jewish and early Christian writings. The commercial laments of chapter 18 are especially important in scholarship because they show how Revelation attacks imperial wealth as well as imperial violence.

cards.q:
__**The Rider on the White Horse**__
Heaven opens, a rider on a white horse appears, the beast is defeated, and the birds are summoned to the aftermath.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After heavenly celebration, heaven opens and a rider on a white horse appears with armies behind him. The beast and the false prophet are seized, and the defeat of their forces is described in gruesome terms. The chapter pairs triumphal imagery with scenes of violent judgment.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often stress that Revelation 19 is full of scriptural reuse, especially from Isaiah and the Psalms, and that its warfare imagery is symbolic and polemical even when modern readers find it graphic. Revelation is commonly dated to the late 1st century CE.

cards.q:
__**Abram and Lot Separate**__
Abram and Lot separate because their households have grown too large to stay together, and Lot chooses the land near Sodom.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Abram and Lot both become wealthy, and conflict breaks out between their herders. Abram offers Lot the first choice of land, and Lot selects the well-watered Jordan plain near Sodom. After Lot leaves, God renews the promise that Abram's descendants will inherit the land.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often treat this as a land-allocation story that sets up later Sodom material and reinforces the promise to Abram. As with the rest of the patriarchal cycle, the final form of the narrative is usually dated within the larger Pentateuchal compilation of the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Abram Rescues Lot**__
After Lot is taken captive during a regional war, Abram gathers men, defeats the captors, and rescues him.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After a regional war among kings, Lot is captured when Sodom is defeated. Abram gathers trained men from his household, pursues the captors by night, defeats them, and brings back Lot, the other captives, and the goods. The rescue sets up Abram's meeting with the king of Sodom and with Melchizedek.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Genesis 14 stands out from the surrounding patriarchal stories because of its military style, long list of kings, and unusual vocabulary. Many scholars see it as a distinct tradition inserted into the Abraham cycle, and some date its composition later than nearby narratives, though it now forms part of Genesis as compiled in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Esau Sells His Birthright**__
Esau trades his birthright to Jacob for a meal, giving up a major family privilege for immediate hunger.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Esau comes in exhausted from the field and asks Jacob for some stew. Jacob uses the moment to bargain for Esau's birthright, and Esau agrees. The scene ends with Esau eating and the text remarking that he despised his birthright.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read this as a brief but pointed origin story explaining why the younger Jacob line supersedes the elder Esau line. Like the surrounding Jacob material, it is generally treated as part of Genesis' long literary growth before the Pentateuch's final compilation in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Joseph Interprets Dreams in Prison**__
While in prison, Joseph accurately interprets the dreams of Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In prison Joseph meets Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, who each have troubling dreams. Joseph interprets the cupbearer's dream as restoration and the baker's as execution, and both happen as he said. Even so, the restored cupbearer forgets Joseph for a time.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Dream interpretation is a standard motif in ancient Near Eastern literature, and scholars often note how the Joseph cycle uses it to move the plot from prison to court. The Joseph material is commonly seen as one of the later and more polished narrative blocks in Genesis.

cards.q:
__**Moses Strikes the Rock Again**__
At Meribah, Moses strikes the rock to bring out water, but he is told he will not lead Israel into the promised land.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Near the end of the wilderness journey, the people again complain that there is no water. God tells Moses to address the rock, but Moses strikes it before the assembly and water still comes out. Because of this act, Moses and Aaron are told they will not bring the people into the promised land.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars regularly compare this episode with Exodus 17, where Moses also brings water from a rock, and many view the two passages as related variants preserved side by side. Numbers 20 in its present form belongs to the Pentateuch's long editorial history, usually placed in its final stage in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Moses Sees the Promised Land and Dies**__
Moses views the promised land from afar and dies before Israel enters it.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the wilderness years, Moses climbs Mount Nebo and is shown the land Israel is about to enter. He dies there, is buried in an unknown location, and Joshua assumes leadership. The book closes by marking Moses as a unique prophet within Israel's memory.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Because Deuteronomy reports the death of Moses, scholars have long used this chapter in arguments against Mosaic authorship of the entire Pentateuch in its present form. Deuteronomy is often linked to traditions from the late monarchic period onward, with substantial shaping in the exilic and post-exilic periods, roughly the 7th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Ark Brought to Jerusalem**__
David brings the ark to Jerusalem with celebration, but Uzzah dies when he touches it and Michal despises David's dancing.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: David first attempts to move the ark, but Uzzah dies after touching it and the effort is halted. After a period at Obed-edom's house, David tries again with sacrifice and celebration. David dances before the ark as it enters Jerusalem, while Michal criticizes him afterward.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see 2 Samuel 6 as important for linking David's kingship with the central sanctuary tradition in Jerusalem. The story also continues the ark tradition already seen in 1 Samuel 4–6, though now reframed around Davidic rule.

cards.q:
__**The Kingdom Divides**__
After Solomon's death, the kingdom splits in two under Rehoboam and Jeroboam.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: When Rehoboam refuses to lighten the burdens imposed under Solomon, the northern tribes break away and follow Jeroboam. Rehoboam remains king over Judah, and the united monarchy is permanently divided. Jeroboam then establishes alternative centers of worship in the north.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually regard the division of the kingdom as a major turning point preserved in the Deuteronomistic History, whose principal composition is often placed in the late 7th century BCE with exilic revision in the 6th century BCE. The story is also shaped to explain later rivalry between northern Israel and Judah.

cards.q:
__**Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath**__
During a famine, Elijah stays with a widow at Zarephath; her jar of meal and jug of oil do not run out as long as the drought lasts.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After announcing a drought, Elijah first survives by the brook Cherith and then goes to Zarephath, where a widow provides for him despite severe scarcity. Her flour and oil continue through the famine, and when her son dies, Elijah stretches himself over the child and he revives. The story combines famine, provision, and a dramatic healing episode.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The Elijah stories are often treated by scholars as a cycle of prophetic narratives that circulated before being incorporated into Kings. The books of Kings belong to the Deuteronomistic History, commonly dated in main literary stages to the 7th–6th centuries BCE, though the Elijah traditions may preserve older narrative material.

cards.q:
__**Elijah at Horeb**__
After fleeing into the wilderness, Elijah encounters God at Horeb in wind, earthquake, fire, and a quiet sound.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the Carmel victory, Jezebel threatens Elijah, who flees south into the wilderness and asks to die. Strengthened by food, he travels to Horeb, where he experiences wind, earthquake, fire, and then a quiet sound before receiving new instructions. The story shifts from public confrontation to isolation and recommissioning.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is frequently discussed for its contrast with the dramatic Carmel scene and for the difficult Hebrew phrase often rendered 'still small voice' or 'sound of sheer silence.' Like the surrounding Elijah material, it is preserved in Kings, whose major written shaping is commonly dated to the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Josiah Finds the Book of the Law**__
A book of the law is discovered in the temple, and Josiah launches sweeping reforms.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: During temple repairs, a scroll described as the book of the law is found and read to King Josiah. Disturbed by its contents, Josiah consults the prophet Huldah and then begins extensive reforms, removing rival cult objects and centralizing worship in Jerusalem. The discovery becomes the catalyst for a national religious overhaul.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars regard the discovered 'book of the law' as closely related to some form of Deuteronomy or an early Deuteronomic law collection. That connection is one reason Josiah's reign is so central in theories about the composition of Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomistic History, often dated in key stages to the late 7th and 6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Return from Exile Begins**__
After Babylon falls, Cyrus allows exiled Judeans to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the house of God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the exile, Cyrus king of Persia issues a decree allowing Judeans to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. Temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar are returned, and a group of exiles heads back under Sheshbazzar. The chapter opens the restoration period after the destruction of Jerusalem.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The decree is often compared with broader Persian repatriation policies, though scholars debate how closely Ezra 1 reflects an exact historical edict in its present wording. Ezra-Nehemiah is usually dated in its final literary form to the Persian period, often the 5th–4th centuries BCE, while drawing on older archival and narrative material.

cards.q:
__**Rebuilding the Temple**__
The returned exiles rebuild the altar and temple despite opposition from surrounding peoples.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The returned community rebuilds the altar and begins laying the temple foundation, prompting both celebration and weeping. Work is later hindered by opposition and official intervention, but prophetic encouragement helps restart it. The temple is eventually completed and dedicated, and Passover is kept again in Jerusalem.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that Ezra 3-6 combines narrative with letters and administrative-style materials, which suggests the book preserves different kinds of sources. The rebuilding is commonly placed in the late 6th century BCE in the story world, while the book’s final composition is usually dated to the Persian period, roughly the 5th–4th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Nehemiah Rebuilds Jerusalem’s Wall**__
Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem, organizes the people, and rebuilds the city wall despite intense opposition.

notes.label: Context
