notes.text: After hearing that Jerusalem’s walls are broken down, Nehemiah receives permission from the Persian king to go to Judah. He inspects the damage at night, mobilizes the people to rebuild, and faces mockery, threats, and plots from opponents. In spite of the pressure, the wall is completed quickly.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Nehemiah’s first-person memoir style stands out from much surrounding biblical prose and is one reason scholars think Ezra-Nehemiah incorporates older documents or memoir sources. The work is usually dated in final form to the Persian period, often the 5th–4th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Hezekiah’s Illness and Recovery**__
Hezekiah becomes deathly ill, prays for more time, and receives a sign that his life will be extended.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hezekiah is told to set his house in order because he is about to die, but he prays bitterly and weeps. Isaiah returns with the message that fifteen more years will be added to his life and that Jerusalem will be delivered from Assyria. As a sign, the shadow moves backward, and the chapter also includes a thanksgiving poem attributed to Hezekiah.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This story appears in parallel with 2 Kings 20, one of several signs that the Hezekiah material circulated in more than one literary setting. Scholars usually date the Isaiah traditions behind these chapters to the late 8th century BCE, while the book in its present form took shape through later editorial growth.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah’s Call**__
Jeremiah is called as a prophet from youth and is appointed over nations to uproot and to plant.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah is told that he was known and appointed before his birth, but he protests that he is too young to speak. God touches his mouth, places words there, and sets him over nations and kingdoms. Visions of an almond branch and a boiling pot underline that judgment is coming from the north.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually treat Jeremiah 1 as a programmatic call narrative introducing the book’s themes of judgment, uprooting, and future restoration. The book of Jeremiah is textually complex, surviving in significantly different Hebrew and Greek forms, and most scholars think it grew over time from the late 7th century BCE into the exilic and post-exilic periods.

cards.q:
__**Ezekiel’s Vision of the Divine Chariot**__
By the Kebar Canal, Ezekiel sees fiery creatures, wheels within wheels, and a radiant throne vision.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Among the exiles by the Kebar Canal, Ezekiel sees storm wind, fire, four living creatures, intersecting wheels, and a brilliant throne-like form above them. The scene is mobile, dazzling, and overwhelming, and Ezekiel falls facedown. This vision introduces his prophetic commission in exile.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Ezekiel 1 is one of the most elaborate visionary openings in the Hebrew Bible and has generated centuries of interpretation, including mystical readings in later Judaism. Scholars usually date Ezekiel’s core activity to the early 6th century BCE in Babylon, though the book shows signs of later shaping as well.

cards.q:
__**Jonah and the Plant**__
Outside Nineveh, Jonah becomes angry over God’s mercy and learns a lesson from a fast-growing plant.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jonah is angry that Nineveh has been spared and sits outside the city to see what will happen. A plant grows to shade him, but it quickly dies after a worm attacks it, leaving Jonah furious again. The book ends with God confronting Jonah over his pity for the plant versus God’s concern for Nineveh and its inhabitants.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The ending of Jonah is intentionally unresolved, which scholars often view as a literary strategy that turns the question back on the reader. Like the rest of the book, Jonah 4 is commonly dated to the Persian or early Hellenistic period and is frequently read as wisdom-like satire in narrative form.

cards.q:
__**Micaiah and Ahab**__
Micaiah predicts disaster for Ahab, a heavenly council is described, and Ahab dies in battle despite disguising himself.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ahab and Jehoshaphat plan war against Aram and summon prophets for guidance. Micaiah first mocks the court consensus, then describes Israel scattered and a heavenly scene in which a lying spirit deceives Ahab's prophets. Ahab disguises himself for battle but is struck anyway and dies by evening.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point to 1 Kings 22 as one of the Hebrew Bible's clearest scenes of a divine council, comparable to council imagery in texts from Ugarit and other ancient Near Eastern sources. Kings is commonly understood to have been shaped within the Deuteronomistic History, with major composition in the exilic period, especially the 6th century BCE, though older court traditions likely underlie parts of the story.

cards.q:
__**Elisha and the Widow’s Oil**__
A destitute widow follows Elisha’s instructions, and her single jar of oil multiplies until all her borrowed vessels are filled.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A widow of one of the prophets fears losing her sons to debt-slavery. Elisha tells her to gather empty vessels, shut the door, and pour from her small amount of oil. The oil keeps flowing until every vessel is full, allowing her to sell it, pay the debt, and live on the remainder.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Miracle stories about prophets providing food or resources are common in the Elijah-Elisha cycles, and scholars often compare this one with 1 Kings 17 and other ancient tales of wonder-working holy figures. Many scholars think the Elisha stories circulated independently before being incorporated into Kings, whose major editorial shaping is usually dated to the exilic 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Elisha Raises the Shunammite’s Son**__
After the promised son of a Shunammite woman dies, Elisha goes to the child and restores him to life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A wealthy woman from Shunem had earlier shown hospitality to Elisha and unexpectedly received a son after his promise. When the boy later collapses and dies, she travels urgently to find the prophet. Elisha comes, prays, stretches himself over the child, and the boy revives.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually compare this story with Elijah's raising of the widow's son in 1 Kings 17, since the narrative patterns are strikingly similar. Such parallels are often taken as evidence that the Elijah and Elisha cycles were shaped as companion traditions before being incorporated into Kings in the exilic period.

cards.q:
__**Jehu’s Revolt**__
Jehu is anointed, kills Joram and Jezebel, and violently overthrows the house of Ahab.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A prophetic messenger secretly anoints Jehu and commissions him against Ahab's dynasty. Jehu rides to Jezreel, kills King Joram, orders Jezebel thrown from the window, and then has Ahab's descendants and supporters slaughtered. He also eliminates the worshipers of Baal in a bloody purge.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars note that Jehu is also known from the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, an Assyrian monument from the 9th century BCE that depicts him or his envoy paying tribute. The biblical account in Kings, however, was shaped much later in the Deuteronomistic History, especially in the exilic period.

cards.q:
__**Joash Crowned in the Temple**__
The priests reveal the hidden heir Joash, crown him in the temple, and overthrow Athaliah.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After hiding Joash for years, Jehoiada the priest organizes a coup inside the temple precincts. Guards are stationed, the boy is brought out, crowned, and acclaimed by the people. Athaliah is executed, and a covenant is renewed while Baal's temple is torn down.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see this chapter as preserving temple-centered royal traditions that elevate priestly involvement in legitimate kingship. Its present literary form comes through the books of Kings, generally associated with exilic Deuteronomistic editing in the 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Nebuchadnezzar Humbled**__
Nebuchadnezzar boasts over Babylon, loses his sanity, lives like an animal, and regains his kingdom only after acknowledging heaven’s rule.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Nebuchadnezzar has a troubling dream of a great tree cut down but not destroyed. Daniel warns that the dream points to the king's coming humiliation if he does not change, and later the judgment falls while he is boasting. After a period of madness and animal-like life, he lifts his eyes to heaven and his rule is restored.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The chapter is unusual because much of it is presented as a royal proclamation by Nebuchadnezzar himself. Scholars generally see Daniel 4 as one of the court tales adapted into the book's later apocalyptic setting, with the final compilation of Daniel commonly dated to the 2nd century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Daniel’s Vision of the Four Beasts**__
Daniel sees four monstrous beasts rise from the sea, followed by heavenly judgment and the transfer of dominion.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Daniel dreams of four beasts emerging from the sea, each representing a kingdom or empire. He then sees thrones set in place, the Ancient of Days seated in judgment, and one like a son of man receiving dominion. The vision is interpreted as a sequence of oppressive kingdoms followed by divine vindication.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Daniel 7 is one of the foundational texts for Jewish and Christian apocalyptic imagination. Most scholars date its composition to the Maccabean era in the 2nd century BCE, when symbolic visions of beastly empires made immediate political sense under persecution.

cards.q:
__**Paul and Barnabas on Cyprus**__
On Cyprus, Paul confronts the magician Elymas and the Roman proconsul responds to the message.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: During their mission on Cyprus, Paul and Barnabas meet a Jewish magician named Elymas who opposes them before the proconsul Sergius Paulus. Paul denounces him, and Elymas is struck blind for a time. The proconsul is impressed by what he sees and hears.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read this as a symbolic turning point in Acts, since Saul is now more consistently called Paul and the mission visibly engages Roman officials. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, commonly around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Eutychus Falls from the Window**__
During a long night meeting, Eutychus falls from an upper window and is restored after being taken up for dead.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Paul speaks late into the night in an upper room, a young man named Eutychus sitting in the window falls asleep and drops from the third story. He is taken up apparently dead, but Paul goes down, embraces him, and the group is comforted when he is found alive. The meeting then continues.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note the vivid and almost anecdotal quality of this story, which differs in tone from some of Acts' large public scenes. Acts is usually dated to the late 1st century CE, often around 80–90 CE.

cards.q:
__**Abraham and Abimelech**__
Abraham tells Abimelech that Sarah is his sister, but God warns Abimelech in a dream and Sarah is returned unharmed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Abraham settles in Gerar and again says that Sarah is his sister. Abimelech takes Sarah, but God warns him in a dream that she is married. Abimelech returns Sarah, rebukes Abraham, and compensates him, and Abraham then prays so Abimelech's household can bear children again.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars almost always compare this story with Genesis 12 and Genesis 26 as another version of the same 'wife-sister' motif. The cluster is one of the strongest arguments used in source criticism and tradition criticism for multiple parallel stories being preserved in Genesis, whose final form is usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Jacob and Laban Part Ways**__
After years of conflict and growing wealth, Jacob secretly leaves Laban, and the two finally make peace.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After years of tension over wages and livestock, Jacob secretly leaves with his family and possessions. Laban pursues him, but after accusation, searching, and argument, the two agree to a covenant marked by a heap of stones. They separate with a boundary and mutual warning not to cross it for harm.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read the stone heap and place-naming as etiological elements explaining a remembered border or memorial site. The final narrative form belongs to the Jacob cycle as incorporated into Genesis, usually dated in compilation to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Deaths of Jacob and Joseph**__
Jacob blesses his family before dying, and Joseph later dies in Egypt after reminding Israel of God’s future promise.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jacob blesses Joseph's sons, gives final words over his own sons, and dies in Egypt. Joseph later reassures his brothers again after Jacob's death and eventually dies as well, asking that his bones be carried up when God brings Israel out of Egypt. Genesis ends with Joseph's body in a coffin in Egypt.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read the close of Genesis as deliberately unfinished because it points forward to the exodus still to come. The end of Genesis and start of Exodus are tightly linked in the Pentateuch's final literary design, usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Sun Stands Still**__
In battle against a coalition of kings, Joshua prays and the sun is said to stand still until Israel wins.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: When Gibeon is attacked, Joshua leads Israel on an all-night march to defend it. In the battle, hailstones strike the enemy, and Joshua speaks the famous command for the sun and moon to stand still until the victory is complete. The chapter ends with a chain of military defeats for the opposing kings.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The line about the sun standing still is often thought to quote or echo an older poetic source, since the chapter refers to the Book of Jashar. Scholars debate whether the language was originally poetic, metaphorical, or intended more literally, but most place the book's written shaping between the 7th and 5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Ezra Reads the Law**__
Ezra publicly reads the law to the returned community, leading to mourning, instruction, and covenant renewal.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the wall is finished, the people gather and ask Ezra to bring out the law. He reads it publicly while Levites explain it, and the crowd first weeps and then celebrates. The people keep the Festival of Booths and later confess their sins and renew the covenant.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often discuss Ezra-Nehemiah as a key witness to the growing public authority of written Torah in the Persian period. The exact relationship between Ezra and Nehemiah’s missions is debated, and some scholars think the material has been arranged thematically rather than strictly chronologically in its final 5th–4th century BCE form.

cards.q:
__**Ezekiel Eats the Scroll**__
Ezekiel is given a scroll full of lamentation to eat before being sent to speak to a resistant people.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ezekiel is commanded to stand, listen, and accept a difficult commission to a stubborn house. A scroll covered with words of lament and woe is given to him, and he eats it; in his mouth it tastes sweet. He is then sent to the exiles and appointed as a watchman responsible to deliver the warning he has received.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Ezekiel’s eaten scroll with later scenes such as Revelation 10, though Ezekiel is the earlier text. The book’s repeated concern with prophetic responsibility and symbolic action fits what many scholars see as a carefully shaped exilic prophetic collection.

cards.q:
__**Elisha and the Siege of Samaria**__
During a brutal siege, Elisha predicts sudden relief, and the Aramean camp is miraculously abandoned overnight.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Samaria is besieged so severely that famine becomes extreme. Elisha announces that food prices will collapse by the next day, despite disbelief at court. During the night the Arameans hear a phantom army and flee, and lepers discover the abandoned camp, bringing news that ends the siege.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read this as part of a larger block of Elisha traditions in which prophetic speech is vindicated through unexpected reversals. Kings in its current form is widely regarded as a literary history shaped in the exilic period, though specific miracle stories may be considerably older.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah at the Potter’s House**__
Jeremiah watches a potter remake spoiled clay, and the image is used to warn Judah that its future can still be reshaped.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah is told to go to a potter's house, where he sees a vessel ruined in the potter's hands and then remade into a different vessel. God applies the image to Judah, saying that announced judgment or blessing can change depending on a nation's response. The message is met with resistance rather than repentance.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The potter image is one of Jeremiah's best-known symbolic scenes and has often been studied as a flexible metaphor for national destiny rather than mechanical predestination. Much of Jeremiah is associated with the late 7th and early 6th centuries BCE, though the book exists in notably different Hebrew and Greek editions, showing a complex textual history.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah Wears a Yoke**__
Jeremiah places a yoke on his neck to symbolize that Judah and its neighbors must submit to Babylon.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah is commanded to make yoke-bars and straps and to wear them as a public sign. He sends similar yokes and messages to surrounding kings, warning them that resistance to Babylon will bring disaster. The act dramatizes his claim that Babylon's rule is, for the moment, unavoidable.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars frequently note that Jeremiah 27 is textually tangled, with some manuscripts and versions preserving confusing royal names and editorial seams. The broader Jeremianic material comes from the late monarchic and exilic periods, but its present book form reflects substantial later arrangement and expansion.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah’s Letter to the Exiles**__
Jeremiah sends a letter telling the exiles in Babylon to settle there, build houses, and wait for a long exile.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah sends a message from Jerusalem to the people already carried off to Babylon. Instead of promising an immediate return, he tells them to build, plant, marry, and seek the welfare of the city where they have been sent, because the exile will last for generations. The letter also attacks prophets who are giving false hope.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually regard this chapter as one of the clearest windows into competing prophetic messages during the exile. The letter is anchored in the early 6th century BCE, although the surrounding book was edited and expanded over time.

cards.q:
__**Ezekiel Sees Abominations in the Temple**__
In a vision, Ezekiel is taken to Jerusalem and shown idolatrous practices inside the temple precincts.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: While with the elders in Babylon, Ezekiel is seized in a vision and brought to Jerusalem. There he is shown a sequence of detestable practices inside the temple complex, including image worship, secret rites, and sun worship. The vision explains why judgment is about to fall on the city and sanctuary.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars generally date Ezekiel's core visions to the early 6th century BCE among exiles in Babylon. Ezekiel 8 is studied as part of a tightly linked temple-judgment sequence, though the exact historical practices behind each scene remain debated.

cards.q:
__**The Glory Departs from the Temple**__
Ezekiel sees divine judgment strike Jerusalem and the glory of God leave the temple and the city.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the temple-abominations vision, executioners mark and strike the inhabitants of the city, while judgment begins at the sanctuary. Ezekiel sees the divine glory move from the inner sanctuary to the threshold and then out toward the east of the city. The departure shows that Jerusalem is being abandoned to destruction.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The movement of the divine glory is one of Ezekiel's most distinctive images and is often read as the theological center of the temple-judgment sequence. Scholars usually place this material in the early exilic period of the 6th century BCE, even though the book continued to be shaped editorially afterward.

cards.q:
__**Ezekiel’s Temple Vision**__
Ezekiel is shown a vast future temple, its measurements, and the return of divine glory.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In a vision set years after Jerusalem's fall, Ezekiel is taken to a high mountain and shown an idealized temple complex in meticulous detail. A heavenly guide measures gates, courts, and chambers, and eventually the glory of the Lord returns from the east to fill the temple. The vision looks beyond destruction to a reconstituted sacred order.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate whether Ezekiel 40-48 was meant as a practical architectural plan, a utopian vision, or a priestly thought experiment. These chapters are usually dated to the exilic period of the 6th century BCE and are often seen as influential for later temple and apocalyptic traditions.

cards.q:
__**Daniel’s Vision of the Ram and the Goat**__
Daniel sees a ram, a he-goat, and a violent little horn in a vision interpreted as a sequence of empires and oppression.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Daniel sees a powerful ram overtaken by a swift goat whose great horn is broken and replaced. From one of the later horns a smaller horn grows arrogant, attacks the sanctuary, and interrupts regular worship. Gabriel explains the imagery in imperial terms and presents the oppression as limited in duration.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Most critical scholars date Daniel 8 to the 2nd century BCE, especially the period of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, because the vision maps closely onto events up to that era. The chapter is one of the strongest examples of apocalyptic symbolism functioning as coded interpretation of recent history.

cards.q:
__**Daniel’s Prayer and the Seventy Weeks**__
Daniel prays over Jeremiah’s prophecy, and an angel gives him the vision of the seventy weeks.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Reading Jeremiah's prophecy about desolation, Daniel offers a prayer of confession and appeal for Jerusalem. Gabriel then arrives and reinterprets the period as seventy weeks of years, laying out a much longer sequence involving restoration, crisis, and desecration. The response transforms a short timetable into a larger apocalyptic scheme.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars widely read Daniel 9 as a reinterpretation of Jeremiah for a later crisis, not as a prediction written centuries in advance in its final form. The chapter is usually dated to the 2nd century BCE and is central to debates about apocalyptic chronology in Jewish and Christian interpretation.

cards.q:
__**Daniel’s Vision by the Tigris**__
Daniel sees a radiant heavenly figure by the Tigris and is told of conflict among spiritual powers and earthly kingdoms.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After a period of fasting and mourning, Daniel sees an overwhelming figure near the Tigris River. He collapses in fear and is strengthened by an angelic messenger who says he was delayed by the prince of Persia until aided by Michael. The vision opens into a larger revelation about heavenly conflict behind imperial history.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Daniel 10 is one of the clearest biblical texts presenting national powers as mirrored by supernatural beings. Like the rest of Daniel's apocalyptic visions, it is usually dated by scholars to the Maccabean crisis in the 2nd century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Question about Fasting**__
Delegates ask whether the old fasts should continue, and Zechariah answers with a rebuke about empty ritual and injustice.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Representatives come to ask the priests and prophets whether they should keep mourning fasts associated with Jerusalem's destruction. The response challenges whether the fasts were ever truly for God and recalls the earlier prophets' demands for justice and mercy. The later oracle turns the old fasts toward a future of restoration and joy.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually distinguish the early vision cycle in Zechariah 1-6 from the oracular material in chapters 7-8, though both are commonly dated to the Persian period. The exchange reflects a community trying to redefine its ritual life after exile and partial restoration.

cards.q:
__**Hosea Marries Gomer**__
Hosea is told to marry Gomer, whose unfaithfulness becomes a sign-act about Israel’s betrayal and future restoration.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hosea is told to marry Gomer and name their children with symbolic names tied to judgment. Gomer later leaves, but Hosea is told to seek her again and buy her back. The marriage is used as a lived parable about Israel's unfaithfulness and the possibility of restoration.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see Hosea 1-3 as combining autobiographical material, symbolic narrative, and later literary shaping. Hosea's activity is usually placed in the 8th century BCE, but the book reached its present form through later editing, likely extending into the exilic or post-exilic period.

cards.q:
__**Joel’s Locust Plague and the Day of the Lord**__
A devastating locust plague is described as a sign of coming judgment, and the people are called to lament and repent.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Joel opens with an agricultural disaster in which locusts strip the land bare and leave the community in crisis. Priests, elders, and the people are called to mourn, fast, and cry out. The plague becomes the basis for warnings about the approaching day of the Lord and a summons to return to God.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Joel is difficult to date, and scholars have proposed settings from the monarchic period to the Persian era, though many now place much of the book in the post-exilic period, often around the 5th-4th centuries BCE. The locust imagery is debated: some read it as a literal plague, while others see it as blended with military and apocalyptic imagery.

cards.q:
__**Joel’s Locust Plague and the Day of the Lord**__
A devastating locust plague is described as a sign of coming judgment, and the people are called to lament and repent.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Joel has described devastation like a locust plague and called the people to repentance, the book turns from crisis toward restoration. The land is renewed, God's presence is promised among the people, and God's spirit is said to be poured out broadly on sons, daughters, old, young, and others across social lines. Cosmic signs and judgment on hostile nations then follow in the book's closing vision.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually read this section as part of Joel's movement from disaster to restoration and judgment. The book's final form is often dated to the Persian or early Hellenistic period, and the universal scope of the spirit passage has made it especially influential in later Jewish and Christian interpretation.

cards.q:
__**Joel’s Locust Plague and the Day of the Lord**__
A devastating locust plague is described as a sign of coming judgment, and the people are called to lament and repent.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Amos has already been announcing judgment against Israel's injustice and false security, the book shifts into a series of symbolic visions. Amos sees locusts and then consuming fire threatening the land, and in those first visions he pleads for Jacob to survive. The announced destruction is relented from at first, but the chapter then moves into a harder image of judgment that will not be turned back.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Amos prophesied in the 8th century BCE, but the book appears to have been arranged and expanded over time. Scholars often see the vision reports in Amos 7-9 as a distinct literary cluster that preserves prophetic symbolism in a relatively concentrated form.

cards.q:
__**Amos and Amaziah at Bethel**__
After Amos announces judgment, the priest Amaziah tells him to leave Bethel, and Amos replies with a final oracle.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In the middle of Amos's vision material, Amaziah the priest of Bethel sends word to the king and tells Amos to go prophesy somewhere else. Amos answers that he was not a professional prophet but was taken from shepherding and sent by God. He then pronounces judgment on Amaziah and on Israel.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often highlight this scene because it dramatizes conflict between a prophet and an official sanctuary. The confrontation also helps anchor Amos's message in the northern kingdom before its fall in 722 BCE, though the book as preserved reflects later literary shaping.

cards.q:
__**Amos’s Basket of Summer Fruit**__
Amos sees a basket of ripe fruit, a wordplay that signals Israel is ripe for its end.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Amos is shown a basket of summer fruit, and the vision becomes a pun announcing that the end has come for Israel. The chapter then attacks exploitative merchants and describes social and cosmic collapse. It closes with the image of a famine, not of food, but of hearing the words of the Lord.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note the importance of Hebrew wordplay in this vision, where 'summer fruit' and 'end' sound alike. The chapter is commonly read as part of Amos's final vision cycle, a section whose literary arrangement likely postdates the prophet's own lifetime.

cards.q:
__**Amos’s Basket of Summer Fruit**__
Amos sees a basket of ripe fruit, a wordplay that signals Israel is ripe for its end.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After severe judgment imagery, the closing lines of Amos shift to restoration. The fallen booth of David is said to be raised up, ruined cities are rebuilt, and agricultural abundance returns. The ending reverses the destruction language that dominates much of the book.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The hopeful ending of Amos is frequently debated in scholarship because some think it may be a later addition softening an otherwise harsh prophetic book. Whether original or appended, it is widely read as part of the book's final literary shaping, probably completed well after Amos's 8th-century activity.

cards.q:
__**Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira**__
The risen Christ addresses four churches with praise, warnings, and promises.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: John is told to deliver messages to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira. Each message addresses local strengths and failures, including lost devotion, suffering, compromise, and toleration of false teaching. Each ends with a promise to the one who conquers.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read these letters as tailored to real congregations in Roman Asia while also functioning as literary types for broader audiences. Their repeated structure suggests careful composition, and the whole book is usually dated in the late 1st century CE, often around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**Letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea**__
Three more churches receive messages of warning, endurance, and rebuke.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The messages continue to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Sardis is accused of appearing alive while being dead, Philadelphia is encouraged to endure, and Laodicea is condemned for being lukewarm. The chapter closes with the famous image of Christ standing at the door and knocking.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Laodicea's warning is often discussed alongside the city's wealth and water supply, which may help explain the language of lukewarmness and self-sufficiency. Revelation 2–3 is usually read as reflecting concrete social pressures in western Asia Minor near the end of the 1st century CE.

cards.q:
__**The Sealing of the 144,000 and the Great Multitude**__
A symbolic group is sealed, and John then sees an immense multitude from every nation before the throne.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the opening judgments of Revelation have begun and fear rises over what will happen next, the narrative pauses before more destruction unfolds. Servants of God are sealed on their foreheads, marking them out before the next stage of judgment. John hears the number 144,000 from the tribes of Israel and then sees a huge multinational crowd in white robes praising God. An elder explains that they have come through great tribulation.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The contrast between what John hears and what he sees has become a major topic in Revelation scholarship. The unusual tribal list and the symbolic number are widely treated as literary and theological constructions rather than a census, in a book usually dated to the late 1st century CE.

cards.q:
__**The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet**__
Two witnesses prophesy, are killed, rise again, and the seventh trumpet announces God's reign.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As Revelation continues through its trumpet visions, John is first told to measure the sanctuary, setting up a scene of contested worship and prophetic testimony. The focus then turns to two witnesses who prophesy, are killed by the beast, and lie exposed before being raised and taken up. A great earthquake follows, and the seventh trumpet then sounds, announcing God's reign and the judgment of the dead.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The two witnesses have been interpreted as Moses and Elijah, law and prophets, or a symbolic image of faithful witness more broadly. Scholars usually see Revelation's use of such paired figures as symbolic and literary rather than biographical reportage, in a book dated to the late 1st century CE.

cards.q:
__**The Seven Bowls of Wrath**__
Seven bowls are poured out, bringing sores, blood, darkness, and gathering for final conflict.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Heaven prepares for the last cycle of judgments as seven angels receive bowls filled with wrath. When the bowls are poured out, a sequence of disasters strikes the earth, sea, rivers, sun, throne of the beast, and the Euphrates. The nations are gathered for the climactic conflict associated with Armageddon.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The bowl sequence is often compared to both the Exodus plagues and earlier seal and trumpet cycles, with scholars debating whether Revelation intends strict chronology or repeated recapitulation. The book is usually dated around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**Noah’s Drunkenness and His Sons**__
Noah becomes drunk, an incident occurs involving his sons, and Noah speaks blessings and curses over their lines.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the flood, Noah plants a vineyard, drinks wine, and lies uncovered in his tent. Ham sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers; Shem and Japheth cover Noah without looking. When Noah learns what happened, he pronounces a curse on Canaan and blessings connected to Shem and Japheth.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read this passage as an etiological story meant to explain later relationships among peoples linked to Noah's sons, especially Israel and Canaan. Like the surrounding Genesis primeval material, its final form is usually placed within the Pentateuch's exilic or post-exilic compilation, roughly the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Amalek Attacks Israel**__
Amalek attacks Israel, and Joshua fights while Moses holds up his hands until Israel prevails.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Soon after the water-from-the-rock episode, Israel faces its first major external attack after leaving Egypt. Amalek attacks the Israelites at Rephidim, and Joshua leads the battle while Moses stands on the hill with the staff of God. When Moses' hands are held up, Israel prevails, so Aaron and Hur support his arms until sunset. After the victory, an altar is built and the conflict with Amalek is marked as an ongoing memory.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars see this scene as an etiological war tradition explaining lasting hostility between Israel and Amalek. The memorial language and command to record the event may reflect later editorial framing within a text whose final Pentateuchal form is usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Korah's Rebellion**__
Korah and his allies challenge Moses and Aaron, and the earth opens and swallows the rebels.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After repeated wilderness tensions over leadership, obedience, and the people's resistance to Moses, a new rebellion breaks out directly against Moses and Aaron. Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and others challenge their authority. Moses sets up a test, and the rebellion ends in dramatic judgment: the ground opens beneath some of the rebels, while fire consumes others. A further plague breaks out when the community protests the punishment.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often treat Numbers 16 as a composite chapter because the rebels, accusations, and punishments do not line up neatly throughout the narrative. Many see the chapter as preserving different traditions about challenges to priestly and leadership authority, edited together in the Pentateuch's final formation in the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Achan's Sin and the Battle of Ai**__
After Achan takes banned spoil from Jericho, Israel is defeated at Ai until the offense is exposed and punished.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Jericho falls, Israel expects continued success in taking the land, but the next campaign goes badly. Israel unexpectedly loses a battle at Ai, and Joshua learns that someone kept goods from Jericho in violation of the ban of destruction. The guilty party is identified as Achan, and after Achan and his household are executed, Israel returns and captures Ai by ambush.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars read Joshua 7 and 8 as a tightly linked pair explaining both a surprising defeat and a subsequent victory. Questions are often raised about the historicity of Ai because the site traditionally identified with it presents archaeological difficulties, making the story a regular point of discussion in biblical archaeology. Joshua as a book is usually dated in major literary stages between the 7th and 5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**The Ark Captured by the Philistines**__
Israel brings the ark into battle hoping for victory, but the Philistines win, the ark is captured, and Eli's family is devastated.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After defeats by the Philistines, Israel brings the ark from Shiloh into battle, expecting it to secure victory. Instead Israel is routed, the ark is captured, Eli's sons die, and Eli himself dies when he hears the news. The ark is taken into Philistine territory, where disasters begin to strike their cities and temples.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often refer to 1 Samuel 4–6 as the 'Ark Narrative' and many think it once circulated as a relatively independent story unit before being incorporated into Samuel. Its written form is usually placed somewhere within the larger Deuteronomistic editing process of the monarchic and exilic periods.

cards.q:
__**The Ark Returned to Israel**__
After plagues and panic in Philistine territory, the ark is sent back to Israel with offerings and arrives at Beth-shemesh.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the ark has been captured and disasters strike Philistine cities and temples, the Philistines decide they cannot keep it. They place it on a cart with guilt offerings and let cows carry it toward Israelite territory. The ark arrives at Beth-shemesh, where it is received with sacrifice, but more deaths follow when people treat it carelessly.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that the ark story portrays the god of Israel acting independently of Israel's army, striking Philistines and even Israelites who mishandle the ark. The narrative is commonly treated as part of the Ark Narrative block, likely shaped before or during the broader Samuel compilation in the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Naboth's Vineyard**__
Ahab covets Naboth's vineyard, Jezebel arranges Naboth's death, and Elijah announces judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ahab wants Naboth's vineyard because it lies near his palace, but Naboth refuses to sell ancestral land. Jezebel then arranges false charges that lead to Naboth's execution, and Ahab takes possession of the vineyard. Elijah confronts Ahab there and proclaims coming judgment on his house.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often see this chapter as a strong royal-abuse narrative that criticizes seizure of family land and abuse of legal process. It belongs to the Ahab-Elijah complex within Kings, a work whose major composition is usually dated to the 7th–6th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Fire from Heaven on Ahaziah’s Men**__
When Ahaziah sends soldiers to arrest Elijah, fire comes down from heaven on two groups before a third approaches humbly.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After being injured, Ahaziah seeks an oracle from Baal-zebub instead of from Israel's god. Elijah intercepts the king's messengers and announces that Ahaziah will die. Two military captains and their fifty men are consumed by fire from heaven, while a third captain pleads for mercy and is spared.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often read this chapter as a harsh prophetic-authority story and as part of the Elijah cycle's emphasis on contest between rival sources of divine power. The books of Kings are usually dated in major editorial form to the exilic period of the 6th century BCE, though many narratives likely draw on older royal and prophetic traditions.

cards.q:
__**Athaliah Seizes the Throne**__
After the royal family is attacked, Athaliah takes power in Judah, but one heir is hidden away in the temple.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After turmoil in Judah's royal house and the death of Athaliah's son, she acts quickly to seize power for herself. She moves to destroy the royal line and rule Judah herself, but Jehosheba rescues the infant Joash and hides him in the temple for years. Athaliah governs until the hidden heir can later be brought forward.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often observe that Athaliah is the only woman portrayed as ruling Judah in her own right, though the narrative is strongly hostile to her. The story is usually read as part of the larger royal-history framework of Kings, whose major editorial shaping is commonly placed in the 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Vision of the Lampstand and Olive Trees**__
Zechariah sees a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, and the vision is tied to Zerubbabel’s role in rebuilding.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah is shown a lampstand with a bowl and lamps, supplied continuously by two olive trees. The interpreting angel explains the vision in relation to Zerubbabel, stressing that the rebuilding work will be completed not by military strength but by divine spirit. The chapter also identifies the two anointed figures standing before the Lord.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date the early vision reports in Zechariah 1–8 to the Persian period, specifically the late 6th century BCE. The imagery belongs to the symbolic, angel-interpreted style that became increasingly common in late prophetic and apocalyptic literature.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Flying Scroll**__
Zechariah sees a giant flying scroll that carries a curse against thieves and false swearers across the land.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A massive scroll flies through the air, and Zechariah is told that it represents a curse going out over the whole land. It enters the houses of thieves and perjurers and consumes them. The vision presents judgment as mobile, invasive, and unavoidable.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Like the other night visions in Zechariah 1–8, this scene is usually dated by scholars to the Persian period of the late 6th century BCE. The imagery is highly symbolic and is often studied as a bridge between classical prophecy and later apocalyptic modes.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Woman in the Basket**__
Zechariah sees a woman called Wickedness sealed inside a basket and carried away to the land of Shinar.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In a second vision from the same chapter, Zechariah sees an ephah basket with a woman inside identified as Wickedness. She is forced back under a lead cover, and two winged women carry the basket away to Shinar to build her a house there. The scene relocates impurity away from Judah.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note the strange and highly visual symbolism of this passage, which has prompted a wide range of interpretations about personified wickedness, exile, and ritual removal. The vision belongs to the Persian-period Zechariah material, usually dated to the late 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Four Chariots**__
Zechariah sees four chariots coming from between bronze mountains, sent out as divine agents to patrol the earth.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Four chariots drawn by differently colored horses emerge from between two bronze mountains. The angel explains that they are heavenly agents going out toward the points of the compass, especially toward the north. The vision closes the sequence of night visions with a picture of divine oversight over the nations.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars generally read these chariots in connection with the mounted patrols and other symbolic messengers earlier in Zechariah's visions. The early chapters of Zechariah are usually placed in the Persian period, in the late 6th century BCE, though later chapters of the book come from different times and settings.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Horsemen Among the Myrtle Trees**__
Zechariah sees horsemen among myrtle trees and hears that the earth is at rest while Jerusalem still awaits restoration.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In the first of the night visions, Zechariah sees a rider standing among myrtle trees with other horses behind him. They report that the earth is quiet, prompting a plea for mercy on Jerusalem and Judah. The vision frames the rebuilding period against a backdrop of imperial calm and local frustration.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The night visions in Zechariah are usually dated quite specifically to the Persian period in the late 6th century BCE. Scholars often compare their angelic interpreters and symbolic imagery with later apocalyptic literature, while still noting their roots in prophetic restoration oracles.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Man with a Measuring Line**__
Zechariah sees a man going to measure Jerusalem, but the city is promised a different future than one bounded by walls.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: A man with a measuring line goes out to measure Jerusalem, apparently to define its rebuilt size. Another message interrupts him, declaring that Jerusalem will be inhabited like unwalled villages because of the number of people and animals, and that God himself will be a wall of fire around it. The vision turns from measurement to expansion and protection.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually read this vision against the early Persian-period reality of a damaged and vulnerable Jerusalem. Its imagery of measurement, expansion, and divine protection belongs to the same late 6th-century BCE vision cycle as Zechariah's other early night visions.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Shepherd Sign-Act**__
Zechariah acts out the role of a doomed shepherd, breaks two staffs, and is paid thirty pieces of silver.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah takes up the role of a shepherd over a flock marked for slaughter. He carries two staffs, symbolically breaks them, and rejects the flock after mutual frustration and breakdown. His wages are set at thirty pieces of silver, which are then thrown into the house of the Lord.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually place Zechariah 9-14 later than chapters 1-8 and often date much of this material to the late Persian or early Hellenistic period, roughly the 5th-3rd centuries BCE. The shepherd sign-act is one of the most debated passages in the book because its symbolism is dense and its historical referents remain unclear.

cards.q:
__**Amos’s Basket of Summer Fruit**__
Amos sees a basket of ripe fruit, a wordplay that signals Israel is ripe for its end.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The book accuses Edom of pride, betrayal, and violence against its brother nation Judah, especially in the wake of Jerusalem's disaster. Edom is warned that its mountain strongholds will not save it and that as it has done, so it will be done to it. The book ends by turning toward Zion's restoration and the Lord's kingship.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Most scholars connect Obadiah with the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall in 586 BCE or with later memory of Edom's behavior during that crisis. The book is one of the clearest prophetic reactions to the Babylonian destruction from the perspective of Judah's neighbors.

cards.q:
__**Micah Announces Judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem**__
Micah describes the Lord coming in judgment against Samaria and Jerusalem for violence, corruption, and injustice.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Micah opens with a dramatic vision of the Lord coming down in judgment as mountains melt and valleys split. Samaria and Jerusalem are both targeted, and later chapters condemn leaders, prophets, and judges for exploitation and corruption. The section builds toward the warning that Zion itself can be plowed like a field.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Micah is usually associated with the late 8th century BCE, roughly contemporary with Isaiah of Jerusalem, but the book contains material from more than one period. Scholars often think its final form preserves both pre-exilic warnings and later editorial shaping.

cards.q:
__**Micah’s Vision of Zion and the Coming Ruler**__
Micah describes nations streaming to Zion and a future ruler emerging from Bethlehem.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Nahum opens with a divine warrior hymn and then moves into vivid scenes of siege, flooding, battle, and humiliation aimed at Nineveh. The city is portrayed as doomed, exposed, and beyond healing. The book ends by imagining the nations clapping over Assyria's fall.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually place Nahum before the historical fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE or close enough to that event for it to shape the book's rhetoric. The book is notable for its fierce anti-Assyrian tone and for offering little ethical critique of Judah compared with prophets like Amos or Micah.

cards.q:
__**Micah’s Vision of Zion and the Coming Ruler**__
Micah describes nations streaming to Zion and a future ruler emerging from Bethlehem.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Habakkuk opens with a complaint about violence, wrongdoing, and failed justice. In response, God says the Chaldeans are being raised up, which creates a deeper crisis because an even more ruthless power will be used as punishment. The chapter ends with Habakkuk questioning how such a plan can be just.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually place Habakkuk near the rise of Babylon in the late 7th century BCE. The book is distinctive because it preserves a dialogue in which the prophet openly challenges God's handling of history rather than simply delivering speeches to the people.

cards.q:
__**Habakkuk Writes the Vision**__
Habakkuk is told to write the vision plainly, and a series of woes is pronounced against the arrogant oppressor.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Habakkuk stands watch for an answer and is told to write the vision so it can be read clearly. The chapter then delivers a series of taunts and woes against the greedy, violent, and idolatrous oppressor. The waiting of the righteous is contrasted with the downfall of the proud.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: The line about the righteous living by faithfulness has made this chapter especially influential, but in context it sits within a larger anti-imperial taunt. Scholars often read Habakkuk 2 as a carefully shaped poetic unit from the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, later preserved in the prophetic collection.

cards.q:
__**The Day of the Lord on Jerusalem**__
Zechariah imagines a climactic attack on Jerusalem, cosmic upheaval, and the Lord’s kingship over all the earth.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The chapter describes the nations gathering against Jerusalem, the city suffering, and then the Lord intervening in dramatic cosmic fashion. The Mount of Olives splits, living waters flow from Jerusalem, and the Lord becomes king over all the earth. The closing lines mix victory, plague, pilgrimage, and holiness.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Zechariah 14 is one of the most apocalyptic chapters in the Hebrew Bible and has been interpreted in many different historical and symbolic ways. Scholars generally place it in the late prophetic material of Zechariah, often dated somewhere in the Persian or early Hellenistic period.

cards.q:
__**The Martyrs and the Shaking of Heaven and Earth**__
The fifth and sixth seals reveal slain witnesses calling for justice and a scene of cosmic collapse.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Under the altar John sees those who have been killed and hears them cry out for judgment. They are given white robes and told to wait a little longer. When the next seal opens, the earth shakes and the sky and mountains are thrown into terrifying disarray.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point out that Revelation combines persecution imagery with stock apocalyptic descriptions of cosmic collapse. Such language also appears in prophetic texts like Isaiah and Joel, and Revelation is usually dated around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets**__
Silence falls in heaven, trumpets begin to sound, and disasters strike earth, sea, waters, and sky.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: When the seventh seal is opened, there is silence in heaven before a new sequence of judgments begins. Incense rises with the prayers of the holy ones, and then the first trumpets sound. Hail, fire, a blazing mountain, poisoned waters, and darkened heavenly lights affect creation in stages.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare the trumpet sequence with the Exodus plagues because both feature escalating disasters involving water, darkness, and devastation. Revelation's final composition is usually dated to around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets**__
Locust-like tormentors and a vast mounted force are released as the trumpet judgments intensify.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The fifth trumpet releases locust-like creatures from the abyss to torment people, and the sixth unleashes mounted forces associated with widespread death. Despite the suffering, the chapter says many do not repent. The imagery is surreal and deliberately overwhelming.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is one of the places where readers most clearly see Revelation's dependence on symbolic monstrosity rather than plain narrative realism. Scholars usually interpret these figures through Jewish apocalyptic convention, not as simple newspaper prediction, in a book dated most often to the late 1st century CE.

cards.q:
__**Dinah and Shechem**__
After Dinah is violated, her brothers deceive the men of Shechem and violently take revenge.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Shechem sexually assaults Dinah (Jacob's only daughter) and then asks to marry her. Jacob's sons deceive Shechem and his city by demanding circumcision, then attack while the men are weakened, killing them and plundering the town. Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi for putting the family at risk.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Modern scholarship often treats this chapter as one of the Bible's starkest narratives of sexual violence followed by retaliatory massacre. It is sometimes analyzed for how little access the reader is given to Dinah's own voice, and it belongs to Genesis' final literary form, usually dated to the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Judah and Tamar**__
Tamar secures justice by disguising herself after Judah fails to give her the protection and family line she was owed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After Judah fails to provide Tamar with the levirate protection he owes, Tamar disguises herself and sleeps with Judah without his recognizing her. When Judah later condemns her apparent pregnancy, she proves he is the father by producing his seal, cord, and staff. Judah admits that she has been more righteous than he has.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note that Genesis 38 interrupts the Joseph story but also deepens Judah's character before he reappears later. The chapter is frequently discussed in relation to levirate custom, vulnerability of widows, and family-line preservation, within Genesis' final 6th–5th century BCE form.

cards.q:
__**Saul's Unlawful Sacrifice**__
Saul offers the sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel, and Samuel tells him his kingdom will not endure.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Facing Philistine pressure and watching his troops scatter, Saul grows impatient while waiting for Samuel. He offers the burnt offering himself just before Samuel arrives. Samuel rebukes him and says his kingdom will not continue because he did not keep the command he was given.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This scene is one of several texts that build Saul's downfall through acts of disobedience. Scholars often read it together with 1 Samuel 15 as part of a theological explanation for why Saul loses the dynasty, within a narrative shaped by Deuteronomistic concerns about obedience and kingship.

cards.q:
__**Babylonian Envoys Visit Hezekiah**__
After his recovery, Hezekiah shows Babylonian visitors his treasures, and Isaiah predicts future Babylonian plunder.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Envoys from Babylon arrive after hearing of Hezekiah’s recovery, and Hezekiah proudly shows them his storehouses, armory, and treasures. Isaiah confronts him and announces that the time will come when all these riches, and even some royal descendants, will be carried off to Babylon. The chapter closes with Hezekiah’s subdued response.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This short episode also appears in 2 Kings 20 and is often read by scholars as a bridge from Assyrian crisis to Babylonian exile. In literary terms it helps pivot Isaiah from 8th-century Jerusalem to the later catastrophe that dominates much of the prophetic tradition.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah and the Broken Jar**__
Jeremiah shatters a jar in the Valley of Hinnom as a sign that Judah and Jerusalem will be broken beyond repair.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah takes elders and priests to the Valley of Hinnom, where he announces coming disaster because of idolatry and bloodshed. He then smashes a clay jar before them to symbolize how Jerusalem and its people will be shattered. The sign-act is followed by open proclamation in the temple courts.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Jeremiah’s sign-acts are a major feature of the book and are often compared with similar symbolic actions in Ezekiel. Scholars generally date the core of Jeremiah’s preaching to the late 7th and early 6th centuries BCE, while the book’s final literary shape emerged through substantial later transmission and editing.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah Threatened in the Temple**__
After proclaiming judgment at the temple, Jeremiah is nearly put to death but is defended by some of Judah’s leaders.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah stands in the temple court and warns that if the people do not change, the temple and city will become like Shiloh. Priests and prophets accuse him of deserving death, but officials hear the case and some elders recall earlier prophetic warnings. Jeremiah is spared, though another prophet, Uriah, is later killed by the king.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare Jeremiah 26 with the sermon material in Jeremiah 7 and see the two chapters as related but not identical versions of the same controversy. That sort of duplication is one reason Jeremiah is widely regarded as a layered book with multiple editions and editorial stages.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah and Hananiah**__
Hananiah predicts a quick end to Babylonian rule, but Jeremiah counters him and Hananiah dies that year.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hananiah publicly breaks Jeremiah’s yoke and declares that Babylon’s power will be broken within two years. Jeremiah first leaves, then returns with a message that Hananiah has replaced a wooden yoke with an iron one and has spoken rebellion against God. Hananiah dies that same year, as Jeremiah predicted.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter gives a rare direct clash between rival prophetic claims and is often used by scholars to show that 'prophecy' in ancient Judah was contested from within, not just rejected from outside. The narrative belongs to Jeremiah’s early-6th-century setting but survives in a book shaped by later editors and scribes.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah Buys a Field**__
While Jerusalem is under siege, Jeremiah buys a field as a sign that land will one day be bought again in Judah.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Even while imprisoned during the Babylonian siege, Jeremiah is instructed to buy a field from his cousin at Anathoth. He carefully weighs the silver, signs the deeds, and has them stored in an earthenware jar for preservation. The purchase serves as a sign that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be possessed in the land.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often point to this episode as one of Jeremiah’s strongest enacted messages of future restoration in the midst of collapse. The chapter likely reflects exilic or post-exilic shaping as the book balances doom against eventual return.

cards.q:
__**King Jehoiakim Burns the Scroll**__
After Jeremiah’s words are written down and read at court, King Jehoiakim cuts up the scroll and burns it.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah dictates his prophecies to Baruch, who writes them on a scroll and later reads them publicly when Jeremiah himself is barred from the temple. The scroll reaches the royal court, where King Jehoiakim listens as sections are read and then cuts them off and burns them piece by piece. Jeremiah then dictates the words again, with further additions.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is especially important to scholars because it shows prophetic words moving through dictation, scribal copying, public reading, destruction, and rewriting. It offers a rare window into how biblical books may have developed over time, and Jeremiah as a whole shows unusually clear signs of literary growth and edition history.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah Thrown into the Cistern**__
Jeremiah is lowered into a muddy cistern during the siege, but is rescued by Ebed-melech.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Because Jeremiah keeps urging surrender to Babylon, officials accuse him of weakening morale and persuade the king to hand him over. He is lowered into an empty cistern where he sinks into the mud. Ebed-melech the Cushite intervenes and pulls him out, and Jeremiah later has a final private interview with Zedekiah.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often note how the Jeremiah narratives preserve vivid scenes of court intrigue during Jerusalem’s final days. Ebed-melech’s positive role is also striking, since an outsider to Judah acts more justly than many of Jerusalem’s own leaders.

cards.q:
__**Ezekiel’s Siege Sign-Act**__
Ezekiel acts out the siege of Jerusalem, lies on his side for long periods, and eats rationed food as a sign of coming catastrophe.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ezekiel engraves Jerusalem on a brick, stages a siege against it, and then lies on his side for extended periods to symbolize Israel and Judah’s punishment. He also eats measured food and uses dramatic signs involving his hair to represent famine, sword, and scattering. The acted symbolism portrays what Jerusalem is about to suffer.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Ezekiel’s sign-acts are among the strangest performances in biblical prophecy and have led many scholars to ask whether they were fully enacted, partly symbolic, or stylized literary presentations. However understood, they fit an exilic prophetic book usually associated with the early 6th century BCE and later editorial development.

cards.q:
__**Haggai Calls for Temple Rebuilding**__
Through Haggai, the returned community is urged to stop neglecting the temple and to begin rebuilding it.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Haggai rebukes the returned community for living in finished houses while the temple remains in ruins. He links their poor agricultural conditions to this neglect and calls them to resume the work. The people respond, rebuilding begins, and promises are given about the temple’s future significance.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Haggai is one of the easiest prophetic books to date because it contains precise regnal dates from the Persian period, specifically 520 BCE. Scholars often treat it as a relatively direct witness to the early restoration community and the push to complete the Second Temple.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Vision of Joshua the High Priest**__
Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest accused by the satan, then cleansed and reclothed as a sign of restored leadership.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In a night vision, Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments while the satan accuses him. He is rebuked, his dirty clothes are removed, and he is dressed in clean garments as a sign that guilt has been taken away. The vision points to restored priestly leadership in the post-exilic community.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Zechariah 1–8 is generally dated alongside Haggai to the Persian period, especially around 520–518 BCE. Scholars often note that the figure called 'the satan' here is not yet the later fully developed devil of Christian tradition, but an accuser within the heavenly court.

cards.q:
__**Elisha and the Floating Axe Head**__
When an iron axe head sinks into the Jordan, Elisha throws in a stick and the iron floats so it can be recovered.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: As a prophetic group expands its dwelling place, one man loses a borrowed iron axe head in the Jordan River. Distressed because it was borrowed, he tells Elisha where it fell. Elisha cuts a stick, throws it in, and the iron floats to the surface so the man can retrieve it.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often classify this as one of the shorter folk-like miracle tales in the Elisha cycle, notable for focusing on a small everyday loss rather than national crisis. The story likely belonged to a body of Elisha traditions later gathered into Kings during the wider editorial growth of the Deuteronomistic History.

cards.q:
__**Isaiah Walks Naked and Barefoot**__
Isaiah performs a shocking sign-act by going stripped and barefoot to symbolize the coming humiliation of Egypt and Cush.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah is instructed to remove his sackcloth and sandals and to walk stripped and barefoot for an extended period. The sign-act is then interpreted as a warning that Egypt and Cush will be led away humiliated by the king of Assyria. Judah is meant to see that reliance on those powers is futile.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Prophetic sign-acts like this are often compared with symbolic actions in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where the prophet's body becomes part of the message. Scholars usually place the core of First Isaiah in the 8th century BCE, though the book as a whole reached written form through multiple stages extending into the Persian period.

cards.q:
__**Jeremiah’s Linen Belt Sign-Act**__
Jeremiah hides a linen belt by the Euphrates, and when it is ruined, he uses it as a sign of Judah’s coming corruption and ruin.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah is told to buy a linen belt, wear it, and later hide it in a crevice near the Euphrates. When he retrieves it, the belt is ruined and useless. God explains that this acted-out sign represents how Judah and Jerusalem, once meant to cling closely to him, have become spoiled through stubbornness.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate whether the text originally referred to the Euphrates or to a closer location with a similar name, since the long journey raises practical questions. Jeremiah's sign-acts are often studied as symbolic street theater from the late 7th to early 6th century BCE, though the book's final form reflects substantial later editing.

cards.q:
__**Ezekiel’s Wife Dies as a Sign**__
God tells Ezekiel that his wife will die suddenly and forbids him to mourn publicly as a sign to the people.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: On the same day that Jerusalem's siege begins, Ezekiel is told that his wife, described as the delight of his eyes, will die. He is commanded not to perform public mourning rites, and when the people ask why, he explains that they too will be stunned into silence when the temple falls. The personal loss becomes part of Ezekiel's prophetic sign.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often regard Ezekiel 24 as one of the book's starkest passages because the prophet's private life is made into a public sign-act. The chapter is tied internally to the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem in 588 BCE, though the final book reflects later arrangement and transmission.

cards.q:
__**Daniel’s Final Vision of Resurrection and the End**__
Daniel’s last vision ends with a time of distress, resurrection language, and the sealing up of the book until the end.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The final section of Daniel's vision describes unparalleled distress, deliverance for the faithful, and many sleeping in the dust awakening to different fates. Daniel is told to seal the words until the end and hears symbolic numbers attached to the period of suffering. He is then told to go his way until his own end and future rest.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Daniel 12 to the same 2nd-century BCE setting as the surrounding apocalyptic chapters. The resurrection language here is among the clearest in the Hebrew Bible and is often treated as evidence of developing Jewish ideas about final judgment and life after death.

cards.q:
__**Zechariah’s Four Horns and Four Craftsmen**__
Zechariah sees horns that scattered Judah and craftsmen sent to cast those horns down.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah sees four horns representing powers that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. He then sees four craftsmen or smiths who come to terrify and cut down those horns. The short vision presents the downfall of the forces that had shattered the people.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: As with the other early visions in Zechariah, scholars usually place this material in the late 6th century BCE during Persian rule. The imagery is compact and symbolic, and interpreters debate whether the horns should be linked to specific empires or treated more generally as hostile powers.

cards.q:
__**The Crowning of Joshua**__
A symbolic crown is placed on Joshua the high priest in a sign-act tied to temple rebuilding and future leadership.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the visions, Zechariah is told to make a crown from donated silver and gold and place it on Joshua the high priest. The act is linked with the figure called the Branch and with the rebuilding of the temple. The crown is then kept as a memorial in the temple.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars debate whether the sign-act originally pointed to Joshua, Zerubbabel, or a more ideal future ruler, because the text's royal and priestly features sit in some tension. The passage is commonly dated to the Persian period in the late 6th century BCE.

cards.q:
__**Habakkuk’s Prayer of Theophany**__
The book ends with a prayer-poem describing God as a warrior coming through storm and earthquake.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Habakkuk 3 shifts into hymn-like poetry in which God appears in overwhelming power from the south, with pestilence, earthquake, and cosmic disturbance in his wake. The prophet trembles, waits for trouble, and yet declares resolve even if crops and herds fail. The ending combines fear, endurance, and trust amid disaster.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Many scholars treat Habakkuk 3 as a distinct liturgical poem attached to the earlier dialogue chapters. Its musical notations and style have led some to think it circulated separately before being incorporated into the book.

cards.q:
__**Habakkuk’s Prayer of Theophany**__
The book ends with a prayer-poem describing God as a warrior coming through storm and earthquake.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: In Zechariah's later visions, Jerusalem becomes the center of conflict and mourning. The people look upon one who has been pierced and grieve deeply, and the following chapter speaks of a cleansing fountain and the removal of impurity and false prophecy. The section blends lament, purification, and conflict.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually place Zechariah 9-14 later than chapters 1-8 and often treat chapters 12-14 as another distinct block within that later material. The dating is debated, but many proposals place much of it in the late Persian or early Hellenistic period, roughly the 5th-3rd centuries BCE.

cards.q:
__**Habakkuk’s Prayer of Theophany**__
The book ends with a prayer-poem describing God as a warrior coming through storm and earthquake.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 13 moves from cleansing imagery to violence and testing. The sword is called to strike the shepherd, the flock is scattered, and only a remnant remains after severe judgment. Those who survive are pictured as refined and brought into restored relationship with God.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: This chapter is part of the difficult later Zecharian material whose historical setting remains uncertain. Scholars often read the shepherd imagery here alongside Zechariah 11, but the exact figures and events behind the symbolism are still heavily debated.

cards.q:
__**Corrupt Priests Rebuked in Malachi**__
Malachi attacks priests who dishonor the altar and people who treat covenant obligations lightly.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: By the time of Malachi, the temple has long since been rebuilt, but the post-exilic community is marked by religious complacency and corruption. The book opens by confronting priests who dishonor God through defective sacrifices and careless worship. The rebuke sets the tone for Malachi's wider critique of the community's failures.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars usually date Malachi to the Persian period, often the 5th century BCE, after temple worship had been restored. The book's anonymous title simply means 'my messenger,' and some scholars think it may be a descriptive heading rather than a personal name.

cards.q:
__**Corrupt Priests Rebuked in Malachi**__
Malachi attacks priests who dishonor the altar and people who treat covenant obligations lightly.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Malachi announces a messenger who will prepare the way and portrays the Lord's coming as a refining and purifying fire. The chapter then condemns sorcery, exploitation, and withholding from the temple, while also speaking of a book of remembrance for those who fear God. The people are repeatedly challenged to return.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Malachi 3 became especially important in later Jewish and Christian interpretation because of the messenger imagery. In its original literary setting, however, the chapter addresses concrete post-exilic concerns about worship, justice, and covenant loyalty in Persian-period Judah.

cards.q:
__**Corrupt Priests Rebuked in Malachi**__
Malachi attacks priests who dishonor the altar and people who treat covenant obligations lightly.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Malachi closes by looking ahead to a coming day of judgment that will both destroy the arrogant and vindicate those who fear God. Before that day arrives, Elijah is said to come as a forerunner figure who will call for repentance and restoration. The book therefore ends not with a completed resolution, but with expectation of future reckoning and renewal.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: These closing verses function as the canonical ending of the Twelve in the Hebrew prophetic collection. Scholars generally date them, with the rest of Malachi, to the Persian period, and they became especially important because they leave the prophetic corpus looking forward to a future messenger figure.

cards.q:
__**The Mighty Angel and the Little Scroll**__
John receives a small scroll from a mighty angel and is told to eat it before prophesying again.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: After the terrifying visions of the fifth and sixth trumpets, Revelation pauses before moving on to the next major judgment scene. In that pause John sees a mighty angel and receives a little scroll that he must eat, just as prophets in earlier biblical visions had taken in God's message before speaking it. The episode prepares for renewed prophetic witness before the final trumpet sounds.

notes.label: Scholarly note
notes.text: Scholars often compare this scene with Ezekiel eating a scroll in Ezekiel 2–3. Revelation repeatedly adapts older prophetic call imagery, and the book is commonly dated around 95 CE.

cards.q:
__**The Lamb on Mount Zion and the Three Angels**__
The Lamb stands with the redeemed, angels announce judgment, and earth's harvest is gathered.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The chapter opens with the Lamb on Mount Zion with the redeemed, then presents angelic proclamations about judgment, Babylon, and endurance. It closes with a pair of harvest scenes, one of grain and one of grapes, with the latter ending in a blood-soaked winepress image.
