The field is connected to different agents in the two accounts.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Judas was the indirect purchaser because the money was his, even though the priests carried out the transaction. The problem is that the two passages still assign the acquisition in different ways and tell the story from noticeably different angles.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of the larger divergence between Matthew's and Acts's Judas traditions. The field story appears to have developed in different narrative forms rather than as one consistent remembered event.

cards.q:
__**Who was Joseph's father?**__

Matthew and Luke give different names for Joseph's father in Jesus's genealogy.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Both Matthew and Luke give genealogies connected to Jesus, and both lines pass through Joseph. Matthew says Joseph was the son of Jacob. Luke says Joseph was the son of Heli. The genealogies do not agree on Joseph's father.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one genealogy gives Joseph's legal line while the other gives Mary's line, even though Luke still names Joseph. The problem is that this explanation is not stated in either Gospel and is supplied to reconcile the difference.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars understand Matthew and Luke as preserving different genealogical constructions shaped by different theological aims. The lines are not usually treated as historically reconcilable in a simple way.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus tell his disciples to take a staff or not?**__

One Gospel allows a staff for the journey, while others forbid taking one.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: These passages all describe Jesus sending out his disciples on mission. In Mark, they are told to take nothing for the journey except a staff. In Matthew and Luke, they are told not to take a staff. The instructions do not line up neatly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one version means they may keep an existing staff but must not acquire extra supplies, while the others forbid taking additional gear. The problem is that the plain wording still sounds like Mark permits what Matthew and Luke prohibit.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a straightforward Synoptic variation in missionary instructions. The differences are usually explained as part of the way each evangelist edited inherited tradition for literary or theological purposes.

cards.q:
__**How many generations were there from the exile to Jesus?**__

Matthew presents a neat numerical scheme, but his own genealogy appears not to fit it exactly.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Matthew says there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile, and fourteen from the exile to the Messiah. But if you count the names in Matthew 1:12-16, the final section does not fit the scheme neatly. The summary number and the genealogy list create tension.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Matthew is counting generations in a stylized way, perhaps double-counting or compressing certain names for literary effect. The problem is that the text still presents the pattern as a numerical summary of the genealogy, so the mismatch remains visible in the list as written.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars view Matthew's genealogy as a deliberately shaped literary construction rather than a raw archival list. The neat three-fold structure of fourteen appears to matter more to the author than strict numerical consistency.

cards.q:
__**Did Paul receive his gospel from the apostles or not?**__

One passage stresses that he did not receive it from humans, while another shows him being taught and endorsed within the church.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Galatians, Paul insists that he did not receive his gospel from any human source but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. In Acts, Ananias instructs him after his conversion, and Paul is integrated into the believing community. The tension is over how independent Paul's gospel and commissioning really were.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the core gospel came directly by revelation, while later instruction and fellowship came through the church. The problem is that Acts presents human mediation more prominently than Galatians does, so the two accounts leave different impressions about Paul's dependence on others.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a difference in rhetorical emphasis between Paul's own self-defense and Luke's narrative portrayal. Galatians magnifies apostolic independence, while Acts places Paul more smoothly within the continuity of the Jerusalem-centered church.

cards.q:
__**Were animals created before humans or after the man?**__

One creation account has animals before humanity, while another seems to place the animals after the man is formed.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis 1 presents the creation sequence with land animals made before humankind on the sixth day. Genesis 2 says that after the man is formed and found to be alone, God forms the animals and brings them to him. The order of events appears different between the two accounts.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the verb in Genesis 2 can be translated as 'had formed,' making the animal creation earlier rather than later. The problem is that the narrative flow in Genesis 2 still naturally reads as though the animals are being formed in response to the man's loneliness.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars regard Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 as distinct creation traditions placed side by side. One is more structured and cosmic, while the other is more earthy and narrative, and they do not fully agree on sequence.

cards.q:
__**Was circumcision an everlasting requirement or not?**__

One text calls it an everlasting covenant, while later Christian texts treat it as unnecessary.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis presents circumcision as an everlasting covenant sign given to Abraham's descendants, with severe consequences for refusing it. In Galatians and Acts, early Christians argue that Gentile believers do not need to be circumcised. The tension is between an apparently perpetual requirement and a later decision that sets it aside for many followers of Israel's God.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the command remains valid for the old covenant community, while the new covenant changes its role for Gentiles in Christ. The problem is that Genesis describes the requirement in sweeping, enduring terms, so the later limitation still feels like a major shift rather than a simple clarification.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as one of the clearest examples of early Christianity reworking inherited Jewish covenant markers. The debate reflects a major historical struggle over continuity, identity, and the inclusion of Gentiles.

cards.q:
__**Did the women tell anyone about the empty tomb or not?**__

One Gospel says they said nothing to anyone, while others have them reporting what they saw.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark's shorter ending, the women flee from the tomb trembling and say nothing to anyone because they are afraid. In Matthew and Luke, the women leave the tomb and report the news to the disciples. The accounts do not agree on whether they spoke or remained silent.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Mark means they said nothing to anyone on the way, but later did tell the disciples. The problem is that Mark's wording presents silence as the dramatic end of the scene, while the other Gospels move directly to active reporting.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars take this as one of the most important resurrection narrative tensions in the Gospels. Mark's abrupt ending creates a different literary effect from Matthew's and Luke's more resolved accounts.

cards.q:
__**Did Paul's companions hear the voice or not?**__

One account says they heard the voice, while another says they did not hear it.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Acts tells Paul's conversion story more than once. In Acts 9, his companions are said to hear the voice but see no one. In Acts 22, Paul says the men with him saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one speaking to him. The accounts do not line up cleanly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the companions heard the sound but did not understand the words. The problem is that the text itself still presents one account as hearing and the other as not hearing, so the distinction has to be read into the wording.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a small but telling variation among Acts's retellings of Paul's conversion. It shows that even within one book, repeated narrations of the same event may not fully agree in detail.

cards.q:
__**How did the purchase of a burial field happen?**__

One passage says Abraham bought a burial field for Sarah, while another speech credits Jacob with buying the burial place.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis says Abraham bought the cave and field at Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place for Sarah. In Acts 7, Stephen's speech refers to a tomb that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. The burial purchase traditions do not line up cleanly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says two different purchases and burial traditions are being compressed together in Stephen's speech. The problem is that Acts still blends names, places, and transactions in a way that reads like a conflation rather than a careful distinction.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a classic case of compressed retelling in Stephen's speech, where separate patriarchal traditions have been merged. It is often discussed as a historical or rhetorical inconsistency within Acts.

cards.q:
__**Should followers answer a fool or not?**__

Two adjacent proverbs give opposite instructions about answering a fool.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Proverbs 26:4 says not to answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself. Proverbs 26:5 says to answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes. The two adjacent proverbs give opposite instructions.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the two sayings apply in different situations, so wisdom lies in knowing when each one fits. The problem is that the text still deliberately places contradictory advice side by side rather than resolving the tension for the reader.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a characteristic feature of wisdom literature rather than an accidental contradiction. The juxtaposition itself teaches that proverbial truth is situational and cannot always be reduced to a single universal rule.

cards.q:
__**Did David buy Araunah's threshing floor for fifty shekels or six hundred?**__

One account gives a small payment, while another gives a much larger amount for what appears to be the same purchase.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Both passages describe David purchasing Araunah's threshing floor after the census plague, in connection with building an altar. 2 Samuel says David paid fifty shekels of silver. 1 Chronicles says he paid six hundred shekels of gold. The amounts do not match.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one text refers only to the threshing floor and oxen, while the other refers to the entire site. The problem is that the passages still read like parallel reports of the same purchase, and the numbers remain dramatically different.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as another numerical discrepancy between Samuel and Chronicles. It fits a broader pattern in which Chronicles revises, expands, or reshapes earlier material from Samuel-Kings.

cards.q:
__**Did God command human sacrifice or condemn it as something he never commanded?**__

One passage has God command Abraham to offer Isaac, while another says such sacrifices were never commanded and never entered God's mind.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Genesis 22, God commands Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering, though the act is stopped before completion. In Jeremiah 7, God condemns child sacrifice in Judah and says it is something he did not command and did not even enter his mind. The tension is that one text depicts God issuing such a command, while another denies that this is the sort of thing God commands at all.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Genesis 22 was a unique test that God never intended to be completed, whereas Jeremiah condemns actual pagan child sacrifice. The problem is that the original command in Genesis still takes the form of a divine demand for child sacrifice, so the moral tension remains even if the outcome changes.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of a broader development in Israelite theology about sacrifice, divine testing, and the rejection of child sacrifice. The tension may preserve traces of older traditions later reevaluated by prophetic critique.

cards.q:
__**How many horsemen did David capture?**__

One account gives seven hundred horsemen, while another gives seven thousand.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Both passages describe David's victories over Hadadezer and list the military captives taken. In 2 Samuel, David captures seven hundred horsemen. In 1 Chronicles, he captures seven thousand horsemen. The figures do not match.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one text may count chariot units while the other counts individual men. The problem is that the passages are close enough as parallel reports that the numbers still look like competing textual figures rather than clearly different categories.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a typical numerical discrepancy between Samuel and Chronicles. Variations of this kind are common in the historical books and are often explained by transmission differences or editorial reshaping.

cards.q:
__**Did Baasha die before Jehoshaphat, or was he still acting as king years later?**__

Kings places Baasha earlier, but Chronicles appears to mention him in a later reign.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: 1 Kings says Baasha began reigning over Israel in Asa's third year and reigned for twenty four years, which would place his death before the later part of Asa's reign and before Jehoshaphat. But 2 Chronicles 16:1 seems to describe Baasha coming against Judah in Asa's thirty sixth year. The chronology does not line up cleanly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Chronicles may be counting from the division of the kingdom rather than from Asa's own regnal years. The problem is that the verse reads like a standard regnal notice tied to Asa, so the alternative system has to be imported to make the timing work.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a chronological problem in Chronicles, likely reflecting either a textual corruption or a redactional confusion. It is often cited as one of the clearer dating tensions in the royal narratives.

cards.q:
__**Was man made before plants, or after them?**__

One creation passage has vegetation appearing before humans, while another says no plant had yet sprung up when the man was made.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis 1 says vegetation appears on the third day, before humankind is created on the sixth day. Genesis 2 says that when the man was formed, no shrub of the field had yet appeared and no plant had yet sprung up because there was no one to till the ground. The order of plants and humans appears different between the two accounts.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Genesis 2 refers only to cultivated field plants, not all vegetation. The problem is that the passage still sounds like a general statement about the earth's plant life at that stage of the narrative, so the distinction is not obvious from the wording alone.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as another sign that Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 preserve distinct creation traditions with different assumptions and narrative sequences. The tension is usually treated as literary rather than accidental.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus ascend on Easter day, or after forty days?**__

Luke's ending reads as if the ascension happens the same day, while Acts places it forty days later.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: At the end of Luke's Gospel, Jesus appears to the disciples, leads them out toward Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven with no explicit long delay in the narrative flow. In Acts, written by the same author, Jesus appears over a period of forty days before ascending. The two presentations create a tension about the timing of the ascension.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Luke 24 simply compresses events and does not mean the ascension happened that same day. The problem is that the Gospel's narrative sequence strongly encourages that reading, while Acts gives a more extended timetable.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a literary tension between Luke's Gospel ending and Acts's opening. The same author appears to shape the ending of the Gospel and the beginning of Acts differently for narrative effect.

cards.q:
__**Did Solomon build the Temple because David was barred by war, or because David simply was not the chosen builder?**__

Different passages frame the reason David did not build the Temple in different ways.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In 1 Kings, Solomon says David could not build the house for the Lord because of the wars around him until God gave rest. In 1 Chronicles, David says God told him he could not build the house because he had shed much blood and fought great wars. The explanations overlap, but they are framed differently enough to create tension about the reason David was barred.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the two passages are simply giving complementary reasons for the same restriction. The problem is that Chronicles sharpens the issue into a moral or symbolic disqualification connected with bloodshed, which is stronger than the more circumstantial explanation in Kings.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a good example of Chronicles reshaping earlier material from Samuel-Kings. The Chronicler often moralizes and theologizes David's story more explicitly than the earlier history does.

cards.q:
__**Did Elijah go to heaven, or does John say no one has ascended to heaven?**__

One text says Elijah went up by whirlwind into heaven, while another says no one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: 2 Kings says Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. John 3:13 says no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. The statements create tension about whether Elijah counts as someone who ascended to heaven.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Elijah was taken into the sky or to God's presence in a special way, but not in the same sense John means about heavenly origin and authority. The problem is that the wording in both passages still sounds broad enough to invite direct comparison.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a tension created by different theological frameworks rather than by two texts trying to answer the same question. Elijah's story belongs to prophetic narrative, while John is making a christological claim about unique heavenly knowledge and authority.

cards.q:
__**Was the law given by God directly, or through angels?**__

Some passages speak as if God gave the law directly, while others say it was mediated by angels.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Exodus introduces the commandments by saying God spoke all these words. Later texts in Acts and Galatians describe the law as ordained or delivered through angels. The tension is over whether the giving of the law is portrayed as direct divine speech or as angelic mediation.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says God was the ultimate giver while angels served as intermediaries in the process. The problem is that Exodus itself does not mention angelic mediation in that scene, so the later explanation adds a layer not plainly present in the original narrative.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as evidence of later interpretive development around Sinai traditions. Jewish and early Christian thought often elaborated earlier texts by introducing heavenly intermediaries and expanded revelatory frameworks.

cards.q:
__**Did Judas return the betrayal money or keep it?**__

One passage says he threw the silver into the temple, while another speaks as if the money remained his reward.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Matthew, Judas returns the betrayal silver by throwing it into the temple, and the chief priests then use it to buy the field. In Acts, the field is connected to Judas as acquired with the reward of his wickedness. The stories leave tension over whether the money was relinquished by Judas or still counted as his in the purchase.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the money remained Judas's in a legal or moral sense even though the priests handled the purchase. The problem is that Matthew and Acts still narrate the money's path in noticeably different ways.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as part of the larger divergence between Matthew's Judas tradition and the version preserved in Acts. The tensions concern not only Judas's death but also the money and the field attached to it.

cards.q:
__**Did God want sacrifices, or not?**__

Some passages command sacrifice directly, while others say God does not desire or require sacrifice in the same way.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Leviticus opens with God giving detailed commands for burnt offerings and other sacrifices. Psalm 40 says sacrifice and offering God did not desire. Hosea 6 says God desires mercy and not sacrifice. The tension is that some texts prescribe sacrifice in detail, while others relativize or critique it sharply.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the prophets and psalmist are not rejecting sacrifice itself, only empty sacrifice without obedience or mercy. The problem is that the wording in these critiques is still broad and forceful enough to create real tension with the detailed sacrificial legislation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see these texts as preserving competing or evolving theological emphases within Israelite religion. Priestly texts center sacrificial order, while prophetic and poetic texts often subordinate sacrifice to ethics, covenant loyalty, or inward devotion.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus permit divorce for sexual immorality, or forbid remarriage after divorce without exception?**__

Matthew includes an exception clause, while Mark and Luke do not.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Matthew, Jesus says divorce and remarriage count as adultery except in a case involving sexual immorality. In Mark and Luke, Jesus states the rule against divorce and remarriage without giving that exception. The teachings do not line up in the same way across the Gospels.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Matthew preserves the fuller saying while Mark and Luke abbreviate it. The problem is that the exception clause changes the practical meaning of the teaching, so its absence in Mark and Luke is not a minor detail.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a significant example of Gospel variation in Jesus tradition. Matthew often adapts material for a more explicitly Jewish-Christian setting, and the exception clause is frequently discussed in that light.

cards.q:
__**Was Jehoiachin eighteen years old when he began to reign, or eight?**__

Kings and Chronicles give different ages for the same king.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Both verses report the age of Jehoiachin when he began to reign in Judah. 2 Kings says he was eighteen years old. 2 Chronicles says he was eight years old. The numbers do not match.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one text may refer to a co-regency or a different stage of royal status. The problem is that the verses read like straightforward accession notices, so the simplest impression is still that they disagree.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most scholars and textual critics treat this as a scribal or transmission error, with Kings generally preserving the more historically plausible figure in context.

cards.q:
__**How long did the flood last?**__

Some flood details suggest one timeline, while others suggest another when the days and months are added together.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis says the waters prevailed upon the earth for one hundred fifty days. Other flood notices in Genesis 8 describe the ark resting in the seventh month and the earth drying out only much later in Noah's six hundred first year. When readers try to total the chronology, the timeline can feel layered and difficult to reconcile cleanly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says all the dates can be arranged into one sequential flood calendar if one carefully distinguishes prevailing waters, receding waters, and final drying. The problem is that the flood narrative still feels like it combines overlapping chronological systems rather than one transparently simple timeline.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see the flood chronology as a classic example of combined source material. Different time schemes appear to have been woven together, which is why the narrative sometimes reads as both repetitive and chronologically uneven.

cards.q:
__**Were the Israelites in Egypt for four hundred years, or four hundred thirty?**__

Different passages give different totals for the period of sojourning and oppression.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis tells Abraham that his descendants will be afflicted for four hundred years. Exodus says the Israelites' sojourn lasted four hundred thirty years. Galatians also uses the figure of four hundred thirty years in discussing the time before the law. The totals do not line up exactly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one number is rounded and the other more exact, or that one includes a broader sojourning period beyond Egypt itself. The problem is that the texts still present the figures in ways that invite direct comparison, so the tension remains.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see these differences as the result of variant chronological traditions. The numbers may reflect distinct textual histories and different ways later interpreters counted Israel's ancestral and Egyptian periods.

cards.q:
__**Did Abraham justify his action about Sarah by saying she was his sister, or is that exactly the kind of deception God condemns?**__

Genesis reports Abraham twice passing Sarah off as his sister, while other texts condemn lying and deceptive speech strongly.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Genesis, Abraham presents Sarah as his sister in dealings with foreign rulers, apparently to protect himself. Other biblical texts, such as Proverbs and the Psalms, condemn lying lips and deceptive speech. The tension is not a direct contradiction of event detail, but a moral tension between revered patriarchal behavior and later ethical teaching.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Abraham acted out of fear in a dangerous setting, and the narrative records his action without approving it. The problem is that Abraham still remains a central exemplary figure, so the moral ambiguity is never fully removed by the text itself.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a tension built into biblical narrative itself. The patriarchal stories often preserve morally troubling actions without resolving them neatly, which later wisdom and ethical texts can make feel even sharper.

cards.q:
__**Did Moses write all the law, or did later generations add to it?**__

Some passages attribute the law directly to Moses, while others suggest a more layered process when read critically.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy says Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests. Yet the same book also contains the account of Moses's death and burial in Deuteronomy 34. The tension is that the book presents itself as Mosaic while also including material that appears to come from after Moses's death.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Moses wrote the law itself and a later inspired editor added only the final obituary-like section. The problem is that once post-Mosaic addition is admitted there, it raises the wider question of how much else in the text may reflect later shaping.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see Deuteronomy as a text with strong Mosaic framing but substantial later editorial development. The death narrative is one of the clearest internal signs that the final form of the book is not simply a direct document from Moses's own hand.

cards.q:
__**Did God dwell in the Temple, or does God not dwell in houses made by human hands?**__

Some passages celebrate the Temple as God's dwelling, while others deny that God lives in handmade structures.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In 1 Kings, Solomon dedicates the Temple and speaks of building a lofty house for God to dwell in forever. In Acts, Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in houses made with human hands and quotes Isaiah in support. The texts pull in different directions about the Temple as God's dwelling place.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says God was specially present in the Temple but not confined by it. The problem is that Stephen's wording is still a pointed rejection of identifying divine presence too closely with a man-made sanctuary.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a theological tension between temple-centered worship and later critiques of temple ideology. The Bible preserves both strong pro-Temple voices and sharp warnings against domesticating God within sacred architecture.

cards.q:
__**Did Ahaziah die in Megiddo, or in Samaria?**__

Kings and Chronicles narrate the king's death with different place details.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In 2 Kings, Ahaziah is wounded while fleeing Jehu, reaches Megiddo, and dies there. In 2 Chronicles, Jehu's men capture Ahaziah while he is hiding in Samaria, bring him to Jehu, and kill him. The details about where and how his death occurs do not line up neatly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Ahaziah was captured in the Samaria region, wounded, then taken or fled onward before dying at Megiddo. The problem is that the narratives still present the sequence differently enough that the reconciliation depends on stitching together details not explicitly integrated by either account.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars regard this as another example of Chronicles retelling Kings with altered narrative detail. The differences fit a larger pattern in which the Chronicler reworks earlier royal narratives rather than merely copying them.

cards.q:
__**Was Jesus's lineage traced through Solomon or through Nathan?**__

Matthew and Luke trace Jesus's ancestry through different sons of David.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Matthew traces the Davidic line through Solomon. Luke traces it through Nathan, another son of David. The genealogies diverge sharply after David, raising tension about which Davidic line is being presented for Jesus.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one line is Joseph's and the other is Mary's, even though both are presented through Joseph in the text. The problem is that this explanation is not stated in either Gospel and is supplied afterward to reconcile the two lines.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat Matthew's and Luke's genealogies as theological constructions serving different narrative purposes. The divergence after David is one of the clearest signs that the two lists are not operating as a single harmonizable family record.

cards.q:
__**Did Israel ask for meat because of craving, or because of nostalgia for Egypt?**__

The wilderness complaints overlap but are framed differently in different retellings.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Numbers says the people complained in the wilderness because they craved meat and remembered the foods of Egypt. Psalm 78 retells the complaint in a more accusatory theological way, emphasizing that they tested God by demanding food and doubting his ability to provide. The details overlap, but the framing shifts enough to create tension in emphasis and motive.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the texts describe the same complaint from different angles, one historical and one poetic. The problem is that the later retelling intensifies and reshapes the earlier narrative, so the motive and theological weight are not exactly the same.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars would treat this as a tension of interpretation rather than a strict contradiction of event detail. Biblical retellings often recast earlier narratives in more polemical or theological terms.

cards.q:
__**Did Noah send out a raven first, or only doves?**__

One account includes a raven before the dove sequence, while some retellings and memories focus only on the dove.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis says Noah first sent out a raven after the floodwaters began to recede. It then narrates the sending of the dove, including repeated releases of the dove in search of dry land. The tension is not a flat contradiction between two books, but an internal narrative layering where the raven can be overshadowed by the more famous dove sequence.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says there is no contradiction because Noah simply sent out both birds in sequence. The problem is that the narrative still feels composite and repetitive, which is why readers often remember the dove cycle while barely noticing the raven at all.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see the flood bird sequence as another sign of layered flood traditions. The raven and dove episodes may preserve overlapping versions that were combined into a single narrative.

cards.q:
__**Did David spare Saul because Saul was the Lord's anointed, or did he later accept an Amalekite's claim to have killed Saul?**__

One narrative emphasizes David's refusal to harm Saul, while another has David respond to a report of Saul's death after the fact.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In 1 Samuel, David refuses to kill Saul because Saul is the Lord's anointed. In 2 Samuel, David hears an Amalekite claim that he killed Saul at Saul's own request, and David has the man executed for striking the Lord's anointed. The tension is not that David changes his principle, but that the narrative depends on a second, disputed report of Saul's death that complicates the overall story.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says David remained perfectly consistent: he would not kill Saul himself and he condemned anyone else who claimed to have done so. The problem is that this still leaves unresolved the clash between the earlier account of Saul's suicide and the later claim brought to David.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of the politically careful storytelling around David's rise. The texts work hard to distance David from Saul's death, even while preserving variant traditions about how Saul died.

cards.q:
__**Did Moses receive water from the rock by striking it once, or by striking it twice?**__

Different wilderness water stories look similar, but the details and consequences differ.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Exodus describes Moses striking the rock at Horeb and water coming out for the people. Numbers later describes a similar water-from-the-rock event in which Moses strikes the rock twice, and that act becomes part of the reason he is barred from entering the land. The stories overlap in theme but differ in detail and outcome.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says these are simply two separate events at different times and places. The problem is that their similarities are strong enough that many readers experience them as doubled or parallel versions of the same basic tradition.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat these as related wilderness traditions that have been preserved in distinct forms. The repetition with altered details is often seen as part of the Pentateuch's layered narrative history.

cards.q:
__**Did God harden Pharaoh's heart, or did Pharaoh harden his own heart?**__

Exodus alternates between divine hardening and Pharaoh hardening himself.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In some Exodus passages, Pharaoh hardens his own heart or his heart is described as becoming hard. In others, the text says the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart. The tension is over who is ultimately responsible for Pharaoh's resistance.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Pharaoh first hardened his own heart, and God later confirmed him in that chosen rebellion. The problem is that Exodus still alternates the agency language in a way that leaves the moral and theological tension fully in view.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a deliberate theological tension rather than an inconsistency to be erased. Exodus strongly emphasizes both Pharaoh's culpability and God's sovereignty, even though those emphases remain difficult to reconcile.

cards.q:
__**Did the disciples understand Jesus's resurrection prediction, or not?**__

Some passages say they understood, while others stress that the meaning was hidden from them.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Matthew shows Jesus predicting his death and resurrection, and Peter responds strongly enough that Jesus rebukes him. Luke later says the disciples did not understand the prediction at all and that the meaning was hidden from them. The tension is over how much the disciples actually grasped when Jesus spoke about his coming death and rising.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the disciples heard the words but did not truly understand their full meaning. The problem is that the narratives still give different impressions, with Matthew portraying active response and Luke emphasizing near-total incomprehension.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of each Gospel's larger portrayal of the disciples. Luke often highlights hidden understanding and delayed comprehension, while Matthew gives more room for direct interaction even when it leads to misunderstanding.

cards.q:
__**Was the Passover meal before Jesus's death, or had the Passover not yet been eaten?**__

The Synoptics present the Last Supper as a Passover meal, while John places Jesus's death before the Passover meal is eaten.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark, Jesus's final meal with the disciples is prepared on the day when the Passover lamb is sacrificed, and the supper is presented as a Passover meal. In John, the authorities avoid defilement so that they may still eat the Passover, and Jesus is sentenced on the day of Preparation for the Passover. The two chronologies do not line up cleanly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the groups followed different calendars or that the terms are being used more flexibly. The problem is that each Gospel's timeline is coherent on its own, and the tension remains when the two are placed side by side.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as one of the most significant chronological differences in the Passion narratives. John's timeline is often understood as theologically shaped so that Jesus dies in closer alignment with Passover symbolism.

cards.q:
__**Did David wear a linen ephod, or was that priestly attire for others?**__

Narratives and legal texts create tension around who may wear priestly garments and handle sacred roles.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: 2 Samuel says David danced before the Lord wearing a linen ephod during the ark procession. Numbers emphasizes that priestly service at the sanctuary belongs to Aaron and his sons, and that outsiders who approach may be put to death. The tension is that David sometimes appears to take on roles or symbols associated with priestly activity even though he is not a priest.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says wearing a linen ephod did not make David a priest and did not violate the law. The problem is that David's broader cultic behavior in the ark narratives still pushes close to priestly space, which is exactly why the tension is felt.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see the David narratives as elevating David in royal and quasi-priestly ways that sit awkwardly beside stricter priestly boundaries elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible. The tension reflects competing models of authority and cultic leadership.

cards.q:
__**Did Jehu destroy Baal worship completely, or did later texts still speak of Baal in Israel?**__

One narrative sounds total, while later prophetic material implies the issue continued.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: 2 Kings says Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel after the massacre of Baal's prophets and the destruction of the temple. Hosea, speaking later about Israel's unfaithfulness, still speaks as though devotion to the Baals remains a living issue. The tension is between the totalizing language of Jehu's purge and the later prophetic reality.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jehu eliminated one major state-backed Baal cult, but later Baal practices returned or persisted in other forms. The problem is that 2 Kings still uses sweeping language that naturally gives the impression of finality.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a difference between ideological royal narrative and prophetic social reality. Triumph language in Kings does not necessarily map neatly onto what later prophets saw among the people.

cards.q:
__**Did God regret making humans, or is God not a being who changes his mind?**__

Genesis says God regretted making humanity, while other texts deny that God repents or changes like humans do.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis says the Lord regretted that he had made human beings on the earth and was grieved to his heart. Numbers says God is not a human being that he should lie or repent. 1 Samuel says the Glory of Israel will not lie or repent, for he is not a man that he should repent. The tension is over whether God is portrayed as changing his mind or not.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the regret language is anthropopathic, using human terms to describe God's response without implying literal change in God. The problem is that the narrative language still presents God as reacting, grieving, and regretting in ways that are hard to flatten into mere figure of speech.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a major theological tension within the Hebrew Bible itself. Some texts portray God in strongly relational and emotionally responsive ways, while others stress divine constancy and transcendence.

cards.q:
__**Did the disciples immediately leave everything and follow Jesus, or were some of them already connected to him beforehand?**__

The calling scenes in the Gospels do not always present the first meetings in the same way.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark, Jesus sees fishermen by the sea, calls them, and they immediately leave their nets and follow him. In John, Andrew and another disciple encounter Jesus through John the Baptist first, spend time with him, and then Andrew brings Simon to Jesus. The narratives do not present the first stage of discipleship in the same way.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says John's account records an earlier introduction and Mark records the later decisive call to full-time following. The problem is that each Gospel still tells the beginning of discipleship in a self-contained way, so the combined sequence has to be constructed by the reader.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as another example of Gospel traditions preserving different narrative emphases rather than one harmonized biographical timeline. Mark favors sudden authority and response, while John favors gradual recognition and witness.

cards.q:
__**Did God visit the sins of the fathers on the children, or did each person die only for his own sin?**__

Some texts speak of inherited punishment, while others reject that principle explicitly.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Exodus says God visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to later generations. Deuteronomy says parents shall not be put to death for children, nor children for parents, but each shall die for his own sin. Ezekiel develops the same principle by insisting that the son shall not bear the guilt of the father. The texts pull in different directions on inherited punishment.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Exodus refers to the consequences of family sin across generations, while Deuteronomy and Ezekiel refer to direct legal or moral guilt before God. The problem is that Exodus still sounds like God himself is actively extending punishment across generations, so the tension is not removed just by distinguishing consequence from guilt.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a genuine theological development within the Hebrew Bible. Earlier covenant language often assumes corporate solidarity across generations, while later texts such as Ezekiel stress individual moral responsibility more sharply.

cards.q:
__**Was Jesus's tomb open before the women arrived, or opened in front of them by an angel?**__

The resurrection accounts frame the stone's movement in different ways.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark, the women arrive at the tomb and see that the stone has already been rolled back. In Matthew, there is an earthquake and an angel rolls back the stone in the scene. The accounts create tension over whether the stone was already open on arrival or dramatically opened in front of the witnesses.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Matthew includes the earlier event and Mark simply picks up after it has happened. The problem is that each Gospel narrates the moment in its own way, and Matthew's version reads as a visible dramatic event rather than background information assumed by the others.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a standard resurrection narrative variation. Matthew often heightens supernatural drama, while Mark's shorter account is more abrupt and restrained in scene-setting.

cards.q:
__**Were there one or two angels at the empty tomb?**__

The Gospels do not all describe the same number of heavenly messengers at the tomb.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Mark describes the women seeing one young man in a white robe at the tomb. Luke describes two men in dazzling clothes. John later describes two angels in white. The resurrection accounts differ on the number of heavenly figures present.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says there were two angels, but Mark mentions only the one who spoke. The problem is that the texts still present the scene differently enough that the variation remains visible rather than disappearing into a single report.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as one of many resurrection narrative variations that reflect the independence and literary shaping of the Gospel traditions. The differences matter because they show the accounts are not simply identical retellings.

cards.q:
__**Did the centurion confess Jesus as the Son of God, or only as an innocent or righteous man?**__

The crucifixion accounts give the centurion different words.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark, the centurion at the cross says, 'Truly this man was God's Son.' In Luke, the centurion says Jesus was innocent or righteous. The confessional wording is not the same in the two accounts.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the centurion may have made more than one statement, with each Gospel preserving a different line. The problem is that each evangelist presents the saying as the climactic reaction at the cross, so the difference still carries interpretive weight.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars view this as a theologically meaningful variation. Mark's wording highlights christological recognition, while Luke's version fits his emphasis on Jesus's innocence and unjust suffering.

cards.q:
__**Did Joseph's family go to Egypt because of famine, or because of Herod?**__

Different Joseph stories involve going down into Egypt for very different reasons.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis describes Jacob and his family, including Joseph's household, going down into Egypt during the famine in Joseph's story. Matthew describes Joseph, Mary, and Jesus fleeing to Egypt because of Herod's threat. The tension is not that the passages narrate the same event, but that the Bible contains different foundational Joseph-and-Egypt stories serving very different theological purposes.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says there is no contradiction because the passages concern completely different Josephs and different eras. The problem is that the recurring Israel-to-Egypt pattern is still theologically loaded, and later texts consciously echo earlier ones rather than standing in isolation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars would treat this less as a contradiction card and more as a literary and thematic tension card. Matthew's infancy narrative often echoes Israel's earlier storylines, and the Joseph-to-Egypt pattern is part of that deliberate reuse.

cards.q:
__**Did God command sacrifice at Sinai immediately, or say later that he did not speak to the ancestors about sacrifices when he brought them out of Egypt?**__

Exodus and Leviticus give sacrificial commands, but Jeremiah seems to speak very differently.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Exodus gives instructions for altar and sacrifice close to the Sinai covenant setting, and Levitical material develops those commands extensively. Jeremiah says that when God brought the ancestors out of Egypt, he did not speak to them or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices, but about obedience. The wording creates a strong tension over sacrifice's place in the original covenant demand.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jeremiah means obedience was primary, not that sacrifice was never commanded at all. The problem is that Jeremiah's language is still blunt enough to sound like a denial, not just a statement of priority.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a major tension between prophetic critique and priestly sacrificial theology. Jeremiah may preserve a polemical stance that deemphasizes or contests sacrificial centrality in a way later ritual texts do not.

cards.q:
__**Was Jesus recognized immediately after the resurrection, or not?**__

Some scenes present delayed recognition, while others move much more directly.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In John, Mary Magdalene initially does not recognize Jesus and mistakes him for the gardener until he speaks her name. In Matthew, Jesus meets the women and they appear to recognize him directly, taking hold of his feet and worshiping him. The post-resurrection recognition scenes do not unfold in the same way.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says these are different appearances to different people and so the recognition process need not be identical. The problem is that the resurrection narratives still create different overall impressions about how immediately recognizable Jesus was after rising.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat delayed recognition as a literary motif in some resurrection narratives, especially in John and Luke. The differences are often read as theological storytelling rather than attempts to preserve one uniform sequence.

cards.q:
__**Did God show Moses his back, or did no one ever see God?**__

One text says Moses saw something of God, while another says no one has ever seen God.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Exodus says Moses may not see God's face, but may see God's back after the divine presence passes by. John says no one has ever seen God. The passages create tension over whether Moses's encounter counts as seeing God or not.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Moses saw only a partial manifestation, not the full divine essence that John has in mind. The problem is that Exodus still presents the encounter in direct visual terms, so the distinction is doing a lot of interpretive work after the fact.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of the wider biblical tension between anthropomorphic encounter language and later claims about God's invisibility or transcendence. Different texts imagine divine presence in very different ways.

cards.q:
__**Did Judas kiss Jesus at the arrest, or does Jesus identify himself and step forward without that signal?**__

The arrest scenes do not all use the same identifying moment.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark, Judas arranges a signal and identifies Jesus with a kiss. In John, Jesus steps forward, asks whom the crowd seeks, and identifies himself, with no kiss functioning as the key identifying act. The arrest scenes are framed differently.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Judas may still have kissed Jesus even if John chose not to mention it. The problem is that John's version deliberately shifts the dramatic center from Judas's signal to Jesus's own self-disclosure and control of the scene.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a strong example of Johannine reshaping of a Synoptic arrest tradition. John's narrative often heightens Jesus's agency and composure compared with the more vulnerable framing in Mark.

cards.q:
__**Did the law promise life through obedience, or say that no one is justified by the law?**__

Some texts say the one who does the commandments will live by them, while later texts deny justification through law.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Leviticus says the person who does the statutes and ordinances shall live by them. In Galatians, Paul argues that no one is justified by works of the law and contrasts law with faith. The tension is between law as a path to life in Torah and Paul's insistence that law does not justify.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Leviticus describes the covenant framework of Israel, while Paul addresses the impossibility of attaining final justification through law in light of sin. The problem is that Paul still reads the law in a much more sharply negative soteriological way than Leviticus itself does.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as one of the central theological tensions between Torah-based covenant language and Paul's gospel argument. The issue is not merely proof-text disagreement, but a major reconfiguration of how law, life, and righteousness relate.

cards.q:
__**Did Saul inquire of the Lord before his death, or did he not?**__

One passage says the Lord did not answer Saul, while another summary says Saul did not inquire of the Lord.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In 1 Samuel, Saul inquires of the Lord before the battle, but the Lord does not answer him by dreams, Urim, or prophets. In 1 Chronicles, Saul's death is explained by saying he did not seek guidance from the Lord. The statements create tension over whether Saul inquired but received no answer, or failed to inquire at all.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Saul went through the outward act of inquiry but did not genuinely seek the Lord in faithful obedience. The problem is that Chronicles still turns the issue into a much sharper retrospective judgment than the Samuel narrative itself states.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of Chronicles's tendency to moralize earlier narratives from Samuel-Kings. The Chronicler often reframes events with clearer theological verdicts than the older account provides.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus perform many signs openly, or did he refuse to give a sign?**__

Some passages emphasize signs strongly, while others present Jesus rejecting sign-seeking.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: John says Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of the disciples, and the Gospel is written so people may believe through them. In Mark, Jesus refuses the Pharisees' demand for a sign and says no sign will be given to that generation. The tension is between a Gospel that foregrounds signs and a saying in which Jesus resists sign-seeking.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jesus refused hostile demands for signs, not all miraculous signs or evidences. The problem is that the contrast still matters because the texts encourage very different impressions about the role of signs in belief.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a difference in Gospel theology and rhetoric. John builds belief around selected signs, while Mark often stresses misunderstanding, secrecy, and the inadequacy of demand-driven sign seeking.

cards.q:
__**Did the animals go into the ark two by two, or seven by seven?**__

The flood story gives a simple pair formula in one place and larger clean-animal numbers in another.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Genesis 7:8-9 describes clean and unclean animals, birds, and creeping things going into the ark two by two, male and female. But Genesis 7:2-3 says Noah was to take seven pairs of clean animals and birds, while only two of the unclean. The internal descriptions do not line up neatly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the clean animals still entered the ark in male-female pairs, just in a greater total number of pairs. The problem is that the repeated two-by-two language still sounds like a simpler competing scheme rather than a careful restatement of the seven-pair instruction.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as another sign that multiple flood traditions have been woven together. The story preserves both a simpler pair-based formula and a priestly clean-versus-unclean counting system.

cards.q:
__**Was Jesus's kingdom not of this world, or was he expected to restore the kingdom to Israel?**__

Some texts spiritualize the kingdom strongly, while others preserve national-restoration expectations.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In John, Jesus tells Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world. In Acts, after the resurrection, the disciples ask whether he is at this time restoring the kingdom to Israel, and Jesus does not directly deny the expectation but redirects them. The tension is over whether the kingdom is framed primarily as transcendent or as tied to Israel's hoped-for restoration.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jesus's kingdom is spiritual in origin but can still have future historical implications for Israel. The problem is that the two passages still give quite different immediate impressions about what kind of kingdom is in view.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a tension between Johannine theology and the more restoration-shaped expectations preserved in Acts. Early Christian writings do not always frame the kingdom theme in the same way.

cards.q:
__**Did people carry Jesus to Egypt because of prophecy, or because of danger?**__

Matthew frames the flight to Egypt as both a response to Herod and a fulfillment of scripture, raising questions about how the motive is being told.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Matthew says Joseph takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt because an angel warns him that Herod is seeking the child. Matthew then says this fulfills 'Out of Egypt I called my son.' In Hosea, that line refers to Israel's past exodus, not to a future messianic prediction. The tension is over how Matthew is using Hosea's text.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Hosea's line can function typologically, with Israel as a pattern fulfilled in Jesus. The problem is that Hosea itself is clearly looking backward to Israel's history, so Matthew's use is not a straightforward predictive fulfillment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a classic example of Matthew's creative scriptural rereading. Rather than quoting a direct prediction, Matthew repurposes Israel's story as a typological template for Jesus.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus's ministry last about one year, or several years?**__

The Synoptics can read like a shorter ministry, while John includes multiple Passovers.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Mark tells Jesus's ministry in a fast-moving narrative that can easily be read as unfolding over roughly a single year. John explicitly mentions multiple Passovers during Jesus's ministry, implying a longer span. The tension is over how long Jesus's public ministry is understood to have lasted.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Mark simply omits many chronological markers, while John preserves more festival anchors. The problem is that the two Gospels still encourage different impressions of the ministry's timespan when read on their own.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a chronological difference produced by distinct narrative strategies. John uses festival structure to shape Jesus's ministry over multiple years, while Mark is less interested in constructing that kind of extended public timetable.

cards.q:
__**How many bath measures could the molten sea hold?**__

Kings gives one capacity, while Chronicles gives a larger one for the same Temple vessel.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Both passages describe the great bronze sea in Solomon's Temple. 1 Kings says it held two thousand baths. 2 Chronicles says it held three thousand baths. The numbers do not match.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says one number may refer to normal working capacity and the other to maximum brim capacity. The problem is that the texts themselves do not make that distinction explicit, so it reads like an interpretive rescue rather than a clear explanation from the wording.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as another numerical discrepancy between Kings and Chronicles. Large numerical variations of this sort are common in the historical books and are often linked to transmission or redaction.

cards.q:
__**How many men did David kill of the Arameans in one battle?**__

Samuel and Chronicles give different totals for the chariot forces destroyed.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Both passages describe David's battle against the Arameans. 2 Samuel says David killed the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen. 1 Chronicles says he killed the men of seven thousand chariots and forty thousand foot soldiers. The figures and categories do not line up neatly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the texts may be counting different military units or troop types. The problem is that the passages are close enough as parallels that the divergent figures still look like competing textual reports.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as another typical numerical difference between Samuel and Chronicles. Such discrepancies are common in parallel military accounts and are often explained through transmission or editorial revision.

cards.q:
__**What were Jesus's last words from the cross?**__

Different Gospels present different final sayings as the climactic end of the crucifixion scene.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Luke presents Jesus's final words as 'Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.' John presents 'It is finished.' Mark's climactic cry centers on 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' The Gospels do not preserve the same final saying at the point of death.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jesus spoke several sayings from the cross, and each Gospel preserves a different final line from the sequence. The problem is that each Gospel still presents its chosen wording as the climactic end of the moment, so the accounts do not function like one shared transcript.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see the last sayings as literary and theological choices shaped by each evangelist's portrait of Jesus. Luke emphasizes trustful surrender, John emphasizes completion, and Mark emphasizes abandonment and lament.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus tell the healed man to tell no one, or to go tell others?**__

Different healing stories show sharply different instructions about publicity.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Mark, after healing a leper, Jesus sternly tells the man to say nothing to anyone and instead show himself to the priest. In John 9, the healed blind man is drawn into public testimony and open confession about Jesus. The tension is not that these are the same miracle, but that the Gospels often frame healed people's publicity very differently.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jesus gave different instructions in different situations, so there is no contradiction. The problem is that the broader pattern still matters: Mark frequently emphasizes secrecy, while John often turns miracles into open public witness.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars would treat this as a tension in Gospel narrative strategy rather than a flat contradiction of a single event. Mark is famous for secrecy motifs, while John builds public revelation around signs and testimony.

cards.q:
__**Did Judas die before the field was bought, or is the field part of his own story of death?**__

Matthew and Acts tie Judas, the money, the field, and his death together in different sequences.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Matthew says Judas regretted betraying Jesus, returned the silver, left, and died, after which the chief priests used the money to buy the potter's field. Acts says Judas acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness and died there in a gruesome way. The sequencing of Judas, the money, the field, and the death does not line up neatly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the priests carried out the purchase, but the field still counted as Judas's because it was bought with his money after his death. The problem is that Matthew and Acts still tell the field story with different agents and a different narrative flow.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as part of the broader divergence between Matthew's Judas tradition and the version preserved in Acts. The traditions overlap in theme but differ enough that they are usually not treated as one straightforwardly unified report.

cards.q:
__**Did Abraham inherit the land in his lifetime, or not even enough to set his foot on?**__

Some passages speak as if the promise is already his, while others stress that he never actually possessed it.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Genesis, God promises the land to Abraham and his offspring, speaking in sweeping terms as though the grant is his. In Acts, Stephen says God gave Abraham no inheritance in it, not even enough ground to set his foot on. The tension is between promised possession and actual non-possession.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Genesis records the legal or covenant promise, while Acts emphasizes that Abraham never physically possessed the land during his lifetime. The problem is that the language of gift and possession in Genesis still sounds stronger than a merely future abstract promise.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a tension between promise theology and historical reality. Acts leans into Abraham's status as a sojourner, while Genesis can speak of the land as already granted in covenant language.

cards.q:
__**Was the old covenant inadequate and fading, or was the law perfect and enduring?**__

Some texts celebrate the law's perfection, while others speak of covenant obsolescence and weakness.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Psalm 19 says the law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul. Hebrews says the first covenant is becoming obsolete and speaks of a former commandment being set aside because of its weakness and uselessness. The tension is between celebration of Torah and the later claim that part of the old order has been surpassed.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the psalm praises God's law in its proper purpose, while Hebrews is speaking specifically about the old covenant's inability to bring final perfection. The problem is that Hebrews still uses language of weakness and obsolescence that sounds much sharper than the Psalm's affirmation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see Hebrews as a major reinterpretation of Israel's covenantal and priestly framework in light of Christ. That creates real tension with earlier texts that praise the law without qualification.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus cleanse the temple at the end of his ministry, or near the beginning?**__

John places the temple action early, while the Synoptics place it near the final week.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: John places Jesus's temple action near the beginning of his public ministry, shortly after the wedding at Cana. Mark places the same kind of dramatic temple cleansing in Jesus's final visit to Jerusalem, during the climactic last week. The chronology does not line up if the passages refer to one event.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Jesus may have cleansed the temple twice, once early and once late. The problem is that the scenes are so similar in character and function that many readers experience them as differently placed versions of one major episode.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a deliberate chronological relocation by John for theological and narrative purposes. The temple scene serves different structural roles in John and in the Synoptic tradition.

cards.q:
__**Did Solomon's workers number thirty thousand, or more than one hundred fifty thousand?**__

Different building accounts give very different workforce totals around the Temple project.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: 1 Kings says Solomon drafted thirty thousand men from Israel and also lists additional labor supervisors and burden-bearers. 2 Chronicles emphasizes a much larger labor force involving one hundred fifty thousand men from the resident foreigners, plus overseers. The workforce descriptions do not align simply when compared at face value.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says the passages are counting different labor pools, one mainly Israelite and the other mainly non-Israelite. The problem is that the totals still feel hard to compare cleanly because the narratives present the project scale in noticeably different ways.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as another example of Chronicles reshaping or expanding figures from Kings. Temple-building numbers are especially prone to variation in these parallel accounts.

cards.q:
__**Did Moses fear Pharaoh when he fled, or did he leave Egypt without fearing the king's anger?**__

Exodus and Hebrews frame Moses's departure in different emotional terms.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Exodus says Moses became afraid when his killing of the Egyptian was known, and then fled from Pharaoh. Hebrews says Moses left Egypt without fearing the king's anger. The two texts frame Moses's departure very differently.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Exodus refers to one early flight, while Hebrews is highlighting Moses's later faith-filled departure connected with the exodus. The problem is that Hebrews still sounds like a broad retelling of Moses leaving Egypt, which is why the tension is noticed.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see Hebrews as offering a stylized theological retelling of Israel's past, one that can reshape narrative detail in service of exemplary faith. That makes it different from the more psychologically direct Exodus narration.

cards.q:
__**Did the blind men near Jericho approach Jesus while entering the city, or while leaving it?**__

The Synoptics do not all place the healing at the same point relative to Jericho.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Luke places the blind man's encounter with Jesus as he was drawing near to Jericho. Matthew and Mark place the scene as Jesus was leaving Jericho. The location framing does not line up cleanly.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says there may have been old and new Jericho sites, or multiple related healings near the area. The problem is that the texts still naturally read as variant placements of what seems like the same memorable event.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars treat this as a standard Synoptic variation in narrative setting. It is one of several examples where parallel miracle stories preserve different spatial details.

cards.q:
__**Was the priesthood changed because the law changed, or was the law itself already perfect?**__

Hebrews links priesthood change with law change, which creates tension with stronger Torah affirmations elsewhere.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Hebrews says that when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change in the law as well. Psalm 19 celebrates the law of the Lord as perfect, and Deuteronomy warns against adding to or taking away from God's commands. The tension is between a framework that affirms fixed divine law and a text that argues for law change tied to a new priestly order.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Hebrews is speaking about covenant administration and priestly application, not about abolishing God's moral will. The problem is that Hebrews still uses remarkably strong language about change and replacement, which presses beyond a minor adjustment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see Hebrews as reconfiguring Israel's cultic law around a new high-priestly christology. That creates a real interpretive tension with texts that celebrate Torah's stability and completeness.

cards.q:
__**Was Joseph planning a quiet divorce because Mary was pregnant, or does Luke's account present the conception without that tension at all?**__

Matthew and Luke frame the beginning of the infancy story very differently.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: Matthew introduces the infancy story by saying Mary was found to be pregnant before she and Joseph came together, and Joseph considers divorcing her quietly. Luke presents the annunciation to Mary with no focus on Joseph's suspicion or divorce plan. The narratives begin the conception story from very different angles.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says Luke simply omits Joseph's internal struggle while Matthew includes it. The problem is not a direct contradiction of one event, but a strong narrative difference in how the conception and its human fallout are framed.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see Matthew's and Luke's infancy narratives as highly distinct literary constructions with different emphases, sources, and theological aims. Their overlap is limited, and their framing choices are often as important as their shared claims.

cards.q:
__**Did Jesus curse the fig tree before entering the temple, or after the temple action?**__

Matthew and Mark arrange the fig tree and temple episodes in different orders.

notes.label: Tension Context
notes.text: In Matthew, Jesus curses the fig tree and it withers in close sequence before the temple controversies continue. In Mark, the fig tree is cursed before the temple action, but the withering is noticed only afterward, creating a sandwich structure around the temple episode. The ordering and dramatic presentation are not the same.

notes.label: Harmonization
notes.text: A common harmonization says both accounts describe the same sequence, with Matthew simply compressing what Mark spreads across two days. The problem is that Matthew's arrangement still reads more immediate and Mark's version more layered, so the narrative logic differs.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many scholars see this as a deliberate editorial difference. Mark's intercalation links the fig tree symbolically with temple judgment, while Matthew streamlines the material into a more direct miracle scene.

cards.q:
__**Did the centurion come to Jesus himself, or send others?**__

Matthew has the centurion speak directly, while Luke has him act through messengers.

notes.label: Tension Context
