notes.text: Many critical scholars note that this is a softer kind of Old-Testament-in-the-New-Testament reuse than the better-known prophecy debates. The verse is not being used as prediction or controversy material, but as devotional and formative language. Scholars often describe 1 Peter 2:3 as later spiritual appropriation of a psalm of trust.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT passage in a discussion about tongues and intelligibility.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a judgment scene in which foreign speech becomes a sign against people who refused to listen.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 28:11–12 is part of a prophecy against dismissive and intoxicated leadership. The people have refused straightforward instruction, so Isaiah says that foreign lips and strange tongues will become a sign of judgment to them. In context, this is not about Pentecostal speech or Christian worship practices. It is about refusal to hear God and the consequence of that refusal. Paul later reuses the passage in 1 Corinthians to make a point about speech, signs, and understanding in the assembly.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Paul’s use of Isaiah 28:11–12 is one of his more surprising interpretive moves. They note that he takes a prophetic judgment text about foreign speech and relocates it into a discussion of tongues and intelligibility in church life. Scholars often describe this as a later analogical reuse of a judgment passage rather than the original intended meaning of Isaiah 28:11–12.

cards.q:
NT: Paul and another New Testament writer use this OT line to describe people who were once “not my people” becoming God’s people.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language about Israel after judgment and broken covenant, not originally about a later Christian community.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hosea 2:23 comes after Hosea’s harsh judgment language and turns toward reversal, mercy, and renewed relationship. The line says that the one once called “not my people” will again be called “my people.” In context, this is about Israel’s damaged covenant status being reversed after punishment. It is part of Hosea’s symbolic family language, where names of judgment are turned into names of restoration. The original passage is about Israel’s own story, not about Gentile Christians or the church in a direct way.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hosea 2:23 originally referred to Israel’s restoration after judgment, not to a future Christian community. They note that Paul and 1 Peter reuse the verse by extending Israel-restoration language into a new setting of communal identity. Scholars often describe this as later identity transfer or reappropriation of restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT verse to support an argument about who can be called children of the living God.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language for Israel after rejection and covenant rupture.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hosea 1:10 follows the naming of Hosea’s children with symbolic names tied to judgment, including “not my people.” Then the tone shifts. The passage says that those once rejected will again be numerous and will be called children of the living God. In context, this is still about Israel’s own broken covenant relationship being reversed. It is not originally a statement about Gentile inclusion in Christianity. Paul later takes that restoration line and uses it in a much broader argument about belonging and divine calling.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hosea 1:10 originally addressed Israel’s restoration, not the later church or Gentile believers directly. They note that Romans 9:26 gives the verse a wider theological use than it has in Hosea itself. Scholars often describe this as a later reinterpretation in which Israel-restoration language is extended into an argument about a newly configured people of God.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic sermon uses this OT warning at the end of a speech to warn hearers not to dismiss what God is doing.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to a prophetic complaint about shocking divine judgment in the prophet’s own time.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Habakkuk 1:5 is part of a prophetic exchange about violence, injustice, and how God is going to respond. The response is disturbing: God says something is happening that would seem unbelievable, namely the rise of a foreign power as an instrument of judgment. In context, the verse is about shocking historical judgment in Habakkuk’s own setting, not about Jesus or a synagogue audience in Acts. Acts later uses the verse as a warning not to ignore a surprising act of God in a new situation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 13:41 reuses Habakkuk 1:5 as a warning text, not because Habakkuk originally had that sermon setting in mind, but because both settings involve people failing to recognize a disturbing divine action. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of a prophetic judgment warning in a new historical and theological context.

cards.q:
NT: One major speech uses this OT passage to accuse Israel of false worship and resistance to God.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a prophetic attack on hollow worship, idolatry, and coming exile.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Amos 5:25–27 appears in a section where the prophet attacks empty ritual, injustice, and idolatry. The passage questions whether Israel’s wilderness worship was really faithful and then points toward exile as judgment. In context, Amos is not giving a speech about Jesus or the temple trials in Acts. He is confronting his own society with the charge that religious observance can coexist with deep rebellion. Stephen later uses that same passage to accuse his audience of continuing the same pattern of resistance.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Acts 7 uses Amos 5:25–27 polemically, as part of a long speech about Israel’s repeated resistance to God. They also point out that Acts follows the Greek textual tradition closely here. Scholars often describe this as a later rhetorical reuse of prophetic judgment language in order to intensify Stephen’s accusation.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line in an argument about whether the message has gone out widely enough to be heard.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a poem about creation’s witness, not originally to missionary preaching.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 19 celebrates the heavens and the created world as declaring God’s glory. The line about their voice going out through all the earth belongs to poetic language about creation’s universal witness. In context, it is not about preachers traveling the world or about the spread of the gospel. Paul later takes that cosmic-witness language and uses it in Romans 10 to speak about the wide reach of the message he is discussing.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 10:18 is one of Paul’s freer and more suggestive uses of scripture. They note that he takes language about the heavens and applies it to proclamation in a way that goes well beyond the Psalm’s original setting. Scholars often describe this as analogical or metaphorical reuse rather than as a direct continuation of the Psalm’s original meaning.

cards.q:
NT: Two New Testament writings use this OT line to say that vengeance belongs to God, not to human beings.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a covenant warning song and is part of a larger passage about judgment and divine justice.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 32:35 appears in the Song of Moses, a long poem about Israel’s future unfaithfulness and God’s right to judge. The line about vengeance and recompense is not a slogan about personal feelings. In context, it belongs to a much larger covenant warning in which God alone has the authority to judge and repay. Romans later uses that principle to forbid personal revenge, while Hebrews uses it in a severe warning passage.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30 reuse Deuteronomy 32:35 in different ways. Romans turns it into an ethical reason not to seek private revenge, while Hebrews uses it to underscore the seriousness of divine judgment. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of covenant-judgment language in both moral exhortation and warning.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT proverb to explain suffering as discipline rather than abandonment.
OT: In its original setting, the lines belong to wisdom instruction about correction and growth, not to a later Christian persecution setting.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Proverbs 3:11–12 tells the learner not to despise the Lord’s discipline, because correction can be a sign of care rather than rejection. In context, this is wisdom teaching meant to shape a person’s understanding of hardship, learning, and moral formation. It is not originally a sermon about Christian endurance under pressure. Hebrews later applies it to a community under strain, using the proverb to interpret suffering as something formative rather than meaningless.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 12 is a strong example of wisdom literature being reused pastorally. They note that the original proverb is general moral instruction, while Hebrews applies it to a concrete communal situation of fatigue and suffering. Scholars often describe this as later pastoral reuse of sapiential teaching.

cards.q:
NT: In the Synoptic Gospels, Jesus uses this OT verse in debate about how the messiah can be both David’s son and David’s lord.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to royal enthronement language and does not originally present a later Gospel debate scene.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 110:1 says, “The Lord said to my lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.” In context, the verse belongs to royal psalm language about enthronement, status, and divine backing for a ruler. It is not originally phrased as a puzzle about messianic identity. In the Gospels, however, Jesus uses the verse argumentatively to pressure common assumptions about the messiah and Davidic descent.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the Synoptic use of Psalm 110:1 here is different from later Christian uses that focus mainly on exaltation after resurrection. In these debate scenes, the verse is used to complicate simplistic messianic expectations. Scholars often describe this as a strategic rereading of royal-psalm language in a controversy setting.

cards.q:
NT: Two New Testament writings use this OT proverb to say that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to wisdom teaching about moral posture, arrogance, and favor.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Proverbs 3:34 is part of wisdom instruction about how pride and humility affect a person’s standing before God. In context, it belongs to a larger section about learning, discipline, and walking in wisdom. The line is not predictive and is not tied to one later crisis. It expresses a general moral principle. James and 1 Peter later apply that same principle to conflicts, pride, and submission within their communities.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say James and 1 Peter are carrying forward the original wisdom principle of Proverbs 3:34 rather than radically changing its meaning. At the same time, they note that the verse becomes more pointed when used in concrete community disputes and exhortations. Scholars often describe this as direct sapiential reuse in a new pastoral setting.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus uses this OT verse to criticize outward religion that is disconnected from the heart.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to prophetic critique of worship that sounds pious but is empty in practice.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 29:13 says that people honor God with their lips while their hearts are far away. In context, the verse is part of a prophetic attack on hollow worship and humanly manufactured religion in Isaiah’s own setting. It is not originally about first-century Pharisaic debates. Even so, the contrast between outward speech and inward reality made the verse highly portable. In the Gospels, Jesus uses it against practices he sees as missing the point of true devotion.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Jesus’s use of Isaiah 29:13 is a strong example of later prophetic reuse rather than original prediction. They note that the verse already attacked empty religiosity in Isaiah’s own time, which made it easy to apply again in later religious controversies. Scholars often describe this as a portable prophetic critique that could be reused whenever external piety and internal reality came apart.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus quotes this OT line in dispute scenes to argue that mercy matters more than ritual performance.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic critique of shallow covenant loyalty and empty religious acts.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hosea 6:6 says, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” or in some translations, “steadfast love, not sacrifice.” In context, Hosea is criticizing Israel for outward religious activity that is not matched by real loyalty to God. The problem is not sacrifice by itself, but sacrifice without faithfulness, justice, or lasting covenant commitment. The passage belongs to Hosea’s larger message that ritual can become hollow when the people’s actual life is corrupt or unstable. Jesus later uses the line in conflict scenes to challenge religious priorities that ignore compassion.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hosea 6:6 originally criticized Israel’s own shallow worship in Hosea’s time, not first-century Pharisaic debates. They note that Jesus reuses the line because it already expresses a prophetic principle: mercy and covenant loyalty matter more than empty ritual performance. Scholars often describe this as later prophetic reuse of an existing critique rather than a prediction about Jesus’s controversies.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus and Paul both use this OT creation line in arguments about marriage, sex, and union.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the creation story and explains why man and woman are joined as one flesh.
cards.a: Matthew 19:5, Mark 10:7–8, 1 Corinthians 6:16, Ephesians 5:31 vs Genesis 2:24

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 2:24 comes near the end of the Eden creation narrative. It says that a man leaves his father and mother, joins his wife, and the two become one flesh. In context, the line explains human pair-bonding and union inside the creation story. It is not originally a legal code verse or a later church rule, but a foundational statement about human relationship in the narrative world of Genesis. That is why later New Testament writers could use it in more than one way: in marriage debates, in sexual ethics, and in symbolic language about deeper union.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Genesis 2:24 already functioned as a foundational anthropology text before the New Testament reused it. They note that Jesus uses it in divorce debate, Paul uses it in sexual ethics, and Ephesians uses it in a more symbolic ecclesial direction. Scholars often describe this as direct reuse of a creation text whose original importance made it especially portable in later interpretation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing applies this OT royal psalm to the Son in strongly exalted language.
OT: In its original setting, the lines belong to a royal wedding or enthronement setting for a human king, not originally to a later Christian statement about Jesus.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 45 is a royal psalm celebrating a king, most likely in a wedding or enthronement setting. Verses 6–7 speak of the king’s throne, righteousness, and anointing above companions. In context, this is courtly royal language, full of praise and honor for the ruler. It is not originally a Christian text about Jesus. But because the language is elevated and striking, Hebrews later uses it in a much more exalted way when speaking about the Son.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Psalm 45:6–7 originally referred to a human king in a royal celebration setting. They note that Hebrews 1:8–9 gives the passage a much higher christological reading than it had in its first context. Scholars often describe this as an intensified rereading of royal psalm language, where court language for a king is expanded into language about the Son.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing applies this OT creation passage to the Son.
OT: In its original setting, the words are addressed to God as the unchanging creator whose years do not fail.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 102 is a prayer from someone overwhelmed by suffering and weakness, but in the second half of the psalm the focus shifts to God’s permanence and power. Verses 25–27 say that God laid the earth’s foundations, created the heavens, and remains the same even when creation wears out. In context, these lines are about God, not about a messiah or a future king. Hebrews later takes words originally said of God and applies them to the Son.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars point to Hebrews 1:10–12 as one of the strongest examples of high christological reuse in the New Testament. They note that the original Psalm addresses God directly, yet Hebrews applies it to the Son without hesitation. Scholars often describe this as a major case of language first used for God being reassigned to Jesus in a later theological context.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT father-son covenant line in relation to Jesus.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to God’s promise about David’s royal line and is tied to Solomon and later kings in that dynasty.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: 2 Samuel 7 records God’s promise to David that his line will continue and that his son will build the house for God’s name. Verse 14 says, “I will be his father, and he shall be my son.” In context, this is dynastic covenant language about the Davidic monarchy. It most immediately concerns the royal line beginning with Solomon, not a direct statement about Jesus in its first setting. Hebrews later lifts that father-son language into a christological argument about the Son’s superiority.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say 2 Samuel 7:14 originally referred to the Davidic king, especially Solomon and the royal line after him. They note that Hebrews 1:5 reuses the verse as part of a larger argument that Jesus fulfills and surpasses royal-son language from Israel’s monarchy. Scholars often describe this as later dynastic promise language being reread christologically.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT passage in the same resurrection climax as another prophetic text, turning it into a taunt against death.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a judgment context and is not originally framed as a triumphant resurrection slogan.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hosea 13 is a judgment passage against Israel. Verse 14 is difficult and has been translated in more than one way, especially in Hebrew and Greek. In its original context, the verse is tied to death, Sheol, and divine judgment, not to a simple celebration of resurrection victory. Paul, however, uses wording from this passage in 1 Corinthians 15:55 as part of a triumphant challenge directed at death itself. That means the original setting and Paul’s later use sound very different in tone.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Hosea 13:14 is one of the clearest places where Paul’s later use sounds more triumphant than the original passage. They also point out that the Greek textual form helps explain how Paul can turn the line into a taunt against death. Scholars often describe this as a highly creative later reuse of a difficult prophetic text.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT ascent text when speaking about Christ’s exaltation and gifts.
OT: In its original setting, the verse celebrates divine victory and ascent, but the wording about gifts is handled differently later than in the Hebrew text.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 68 is a victory psalm full of movement, procession, divine triumph, and royal imagery. Verse 18 speaks of ascending on high after victory and of receiving gifts among people. In context, the verse is about divine triumph, not a straightforward prediction of Christ’s ascension. Ephesians 4:8 uses the verse in a noticeably adapted way, because instead of speaking about receiving gifts, it speaks about giving gifts. That difference matters and shows that Paul is not just repeating the Psalm unchanged.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Ephesians 4:8 is one of the more interpretive and textually flexible reuses of an Old Testament passage in the New Testament. They note that the wording is adjusted in a way that fits the letter’s argument about Christ distributing gifts to the community. Scholars often describe this as a later christological adaptation of a victory-psalm text rather than a strict quotation.

cards.q:
NT: One Gospel alludes to this OT verse about bread from heaven in a discourse that compares manna and Jesus.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a retelling of Israel’s wilderness story and describes God feeding the people with manna.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 78 retells Israel’s history, especially the wilderness period, as a lesson about memory, disobedience, and God’s provision. Verse 24 says that God rained down manna and gave them the grain of heaven. In context, this is not a prediction about Jesus. It is part of a poetic retelling of the exodus generation’s story. John 6 later uses manna language in a much more direct christological way, comparing what God gave in the wilderness with Jesus as the true bread from heaven.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say John 6 uses wilderness food texts such as Psalm 78:24 and Exodus 16 as part of a larger interpretive field rather than relying on one isolated proof text. They note that manna becomes a symbolic bridge between Israel’s past and Jesus’s identity in the discourse. Scholars often describe this as typological or symbolic reuse of wilderness provision material.

cards.q:
NT: One Gospel quotes this OT line about divine teaching in a discussion about coming to Jesus.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to a restoration passage about Zion’s future children and peace after loss and humiliation.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 54:13 says that Zion’s children will be taught by the Lord and that their peace will be great. In context, the verse belongs to a restoration passage about rebuilding, renewal, and future blessing after devastation. It is not originally a saying about how individuals come to Jesus. In John 6, however, the verse is reused to explain why coming to Jesus depends on divine teaching and drawing.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say John 6:45 is a clear example of a restoration promise being given a new christological use. They note that Isaiah 54:13 originally speaks about Zion’s restored future, but John places that teaching promise inside a discourse about recognition of Jesus. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of restoration language within a new revelatory framework.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus uses this OT verse before his arrest to describe the coming scattering of his followers.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic judgment-and-purification section and speaks about the shepherd being struck and the flock being scattered.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 13:7 appears in a difficult prophetic section about judgment, mourning, purification, and crisis. The verse says that the shepherd will be struck and the sheep will be scattered. In its original setting, the line belongs to Zechariah’s own symbolic prophetic world and is tied to upheaval among God’s people. It is not originally narrated as a prediction about Jesus and the disciples on the night before the crucifixion. In the Gospels, though, Jesus applies the line directly to the immediate crisis about to unfold around him.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Zechariah 13:7 originally belonged to Zechariah’s own prophetic setting, not to the Gospel arrest scene in its first meaning. They note that the Gospels reuse the verse because its shepherd-and-scattering imagery fits the collapse of the disciples at Jesus’s arrest. Scholars often describe this as a later christological application of a prophetic crisis text.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT passage to redirect boasting away from human achievement and toward God.
OT: In its original setting, the passage warns against boasting in wisdom, strength, or wealth and instead points to understanding and knowing the Lord.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah 9:23–24 says that the wise should not boast in wisdom, the strong should not boast in strength, and the rich should not boast in wealth. Instead, the only proper boasting is in knowing and understanding the Lord. In context, Jeremiah is addressing Judah in a setting of judgment, corruption, and false confidence. The passage criticizes human pride and misplaced trust. Paul later uses that same language to attack boasting based on status, achievement, or human credentials in Christian communities.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Paul’s use of Jeremiah 9:23–24 preserves the core force of the original passage while relocating it into new debates about status and authority. They note that Jeremiah’s critique of human boasting becomes a powerful tool in Paul’s arguments about the cross, apostleship, and proper confidence. Scholars often describe this as direct prophetic reuse with a new communal target.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses OT language about heavenly beings worshiping in order to exalt the Son above the angels.
OT: The exact source is debated, but the wording reflects Greek-scripture traditions tied to a covenant song and possibly a royal psalm.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hebrews 1:6 says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.” That exact wording does not come neatly from the standard Hebrew text alone. It is closely connected to the Greek Septuagint form of Deuteronomy 32:43, and many readers also compare Psalm 97:7, which has similar worship language involving heavenly beings. This means the background is partly textual as well as literary. The New Testament is working with the Greek Bible here, not only with the Hebrew wording as it now stands.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 1:6 is one of the clearest examples where Septuagint wording strongly shapes New Testament interpretation. They usually note that Deuteronomy 32:43 is the main source, while Psalm 97:7 may also help explain the broader worship language. Scholars often describe this as a text-form-dependent christological reading rather than a straightforward citation from a single Hebrew verse.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses this servant passage to describe Jesus’s quiet, nonviolent, justice-bringing mission.
OT: In its original setting, the passage introduces the servant as one chosen by God to bring justice with gentleness rather than loud public force.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 42:1–4 is the opening servant passage in Isaiah. It describes a servant chosen and upheld by God, empowered by God’s spirit, and tasked with bringing justice. The servant is marked by gentleness: he does not cry out loudly, break a bruised reed, or quench a faintly burning wick. In context, the passage belongs to Isaiah’s servant material and is not originally identified with Jesus by name. It offers a portrait of a divinely chosen figure whose mission is patient, quiet, and justice-oriented.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 12:18–21 is one of the clearest places where the Gospel of Matthew explicitly frames Jesus through Isaiah’s servant imagery. They also note that the original identity of the servant in Isaiah remains debated and is not settled by the passage itself in a simple way. Scholars often describe Matthew’s use as a later christological interpretation of Isaiah’s servant text.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about beautiful feet to support the importance of announcing the good news.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language about good news reaching Zion after humiliation and exile-like loss.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 52:7 celebrates the messenger who brings good news, peace, and salvation to Zion. In context, the passage belongs to restoration language in which Jerusalem hears that God reigns and deliverance is coming. It is not originally about Christian missionaries. It is about the joyful announcement that God is acting to restore the people after suffering and humiliation. Paul later reuses the verse in Romans 10 to support the necessity of preaching.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 10:15 takes a restoration-messenger passage from Isaiah and gives it a new role in Paul’s argument about proclamation. They note that Paul keeps the good-news theme but changes the historical setting from Zion’s restoration to the spread of the gospel message. Scholars often describe this as a later missionary reuse of restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT passage about Jacob and Esau in his argument about divine choice.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic statement about Israel and Edom, not just about two individual brothers by themselves.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Malachi 1:2–3 says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” In context, this is not simply about the two brothers in Genesis as private individuals. It is about Israel and Edom as peoples, and it belongs to a prophetic argument about God’s dealings with nations after later history has already unfolded. The line is harsh and polemical, and it is meant to make a point about Israel’s standing in contrast to Edom. Paul later uses the verse inside a theological argument about election and divine freedom.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Romans 9:13 takes a prophetic statement about Israel and Edom and places it inside a more abstract argument about divine choice. They often stress that Malachi’s original setting is national and historical, not a philosophical treatise about predestination. Scholars commonly describe Paul’s use here as a significant theological extension of the original passage.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about mercy and compassion in his argument about God’s freedom in showing mercy.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the aftermath of a major rebellion, when Moses asks to see God’s glory and God speaks about divine mercy.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 33:19 comes after the golden calf disaster. Israel has sinned badly, Moses is interceding, and the relationship between God and the people is in crisis. In that setting, God says, “I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” In context, the line is tied to divine freedom and mercy after covenant failure. It is not originally part of a later debate about election in Romans, but Paul finds in it a powerful statement of God’s freedom.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Paul’s use of Exodus 33:19 in Romans 9 is a major example of theological rereading. They note that the original verse belongs to a narrative about mercy after rebellion, while Paul turns it into a central proof text about divine freedom and mercy more broadly. Scholars often describe this as later doctrinal use of a narrative statement.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses this servant line in connection with Jesus’s healing activity.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the suffering-servant poem and speaks about bearing griefs, sorrows, sicknesses, or pains.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 53:4 is part of the servant song and says that the servant bears griefs and carries sorrows. Depending on translation, the terms can also sound more directly like sicknesses and pains. In context, the verse belongs to a poetic description of the servant’s suffering and misunderstood burden-bearing. It is not originally a narrative about Jesus healing crowds. Matthew later applies the verse to Jesus’s healing ministry, not only to his death.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars point out that Matthew 8:17 is an important example of how early Christian writers could apply the same servant text in more than one way. Here the focus is on healing and burden-bearing rather than only on crucifixion or atonement. Scholars often describe this as a selective christological reuse of servant language with a healing emphasis.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus uses this servant line about being counted among transgressors on the night before his arrest.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the closing part of the suffering-servant poem and speaks about the servant being treated like the guilty while bearing sin.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 53:12 comes near the end of the servant song. It says that the servant was numbered with transgressors, bore sin, and interceded for transgressors. In context, the verse belongs to the larger poetic portrait of the servant’s humiliation, burden-bearing, and later vindication. It is not originally a scene set during Jesus’s final meal with his followers. In Luke, Jesus uses the line to say that scripture about him must be fulfilled as his arrest and suffering approach.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke 22:37 is one of the clearest places where Jesus is presented as explicitly identifying himself with Isaiah’s servant. They also note that the original servant passage in Isaiah is still debated in terms of its first referent. Scholars often describe Luke’s use as a direct later christological application of servant language.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus combines these two OT passages in the temple-cleansing scene.
OT: One text presents the temple as a house of prayer for all peoples, while the other condemns false confidence in the temple as a “den of robbers.”
cards.a: Matthew 21:13, Mark 11:17, Luke 19:46 vs Isaiah 56:7, Jeremiah 7:11

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 56:7 belongs to a hopeful passage about outsiders being welcomed and the temple serving as a house of prayer for all peoples. Jeremiah 7:11 belongs to the temple sermon, where Jeremiah attacks the false belief that the temple can protect people who continue in injustice and corruption. In their original settings, these two verses do different things: Isaiah emphasizes the temple’s intended openness and purpose, while Jeremiah condemns the corruption and false security attached to it. In the Gospels, Jesus brings both together in a single protest against what the temple has become.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say the temple-cleansing saying is a classic composite quotation. They note that Jesus’s action and words make sense only when both texts are heard together: Isaiah 56:7 supplies the positive ideal, while Jeremiah 7:11 supplies the judgment. Scholars often describe this as a later prophetic recombination used to turn temple protest into a scripturally charged symbolic act.

cards.q:
NT: The Gospels use this OT blessing line in the crowd’s acclamation during Jesus’s entry into Jerusalem.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to festival or temple-procession language and blesses the one who comes in the name of the Lord.
cards.a: Matthew 21:9, Mark 11:9, Luke 19:38, John 12:13 vs Psalm 118:26

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 118:26 says, “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.” In context, the line belongs to a liturgical psalm of thanksgiving and procession, likely used in temple or festival settings. It is a blessing formula inside worship, not originally a prediction about Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey. The Gospel writers use the line because it already carries public, celebratory, and sacred-procession language. In the triumphal entry, that liturgical blessing is turned into a public acclamation around Jesus.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the triumphal entry uses Psalm 118:26 as liturgical language repurposed for a messianic scene. They note that the verse’s original setting was festive and processional, which made it especially suitable for a public welcome scene. Scholars often describe this as later liturgical reuse in a christological key rather than the original intended meaning of Psalm 118:26 being specifically about Jesus.

cards.q:
NT: One apostolic sermon may also draw on this OT enthronement line in the same context where another verse from the same psalm is used for Jesus’s exaltation.
OT: In its original setting, the line speaks about God installing the king on Zion and belongs to royal enthronement language.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 2:6 says that God has installed the king on Zion, the holy hill. In context, the line is part of a royal enthronement psalm about divine backing for the king in the face of rebellious nations. It is not originally a resurrection text. But because Acts 13 uses Psalm 2 in a speech about Jesus’s exaltation, the enthronement setting of nearby lines also matters. Psalm 2:6 helps fill out the royal background behind the more famous sonship line in Psalm 2:7.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that New Testament use of Psalm 2 is often richer than the single quotation of verse 7 by itself. They point out that the surrounding enthronement material, including Psalm 2:6, helps explain why the psalm was so useful for early Christian claims about Jesus’s exalted status. Scholars often describe this as broader royal-psalm background rather than a separate explicit proof text.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic prayer uses this OT passage to interpret opposition to Jesus and the early movement.
OT: In its original setting, the lines describe nations and rulers resisting the Lord and the Lord’s anointed in a royal context.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 2 opens with nations raging and rulers plotting against the Lord and against the Lord’s anointed. In context, the language belongs to royal ideology and enthronement conflict. It is about resistance to God’s chosen king, not originally about Roman and Judean opposition to Jesus or the apostles. In Acts 4, the community takes that royal conflict language and applies it to the coalition against Jesus, reading present hostility through the psalm’s framework.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 4:25–26 is a strong example of later scriptural reuse that maps an older royal-psalm scene onto the story of Jesus and his opponents. They note that the original Psalm concerns a king in a royal setting, while Acts broadens it into a template for interpreting persecution and opposition. Scholars often describe this as a later political-theological rereading of royal language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT commandment in household instruction and highlights it as the first commandment with a promise.
OT: In its original setting, the command belongs to the Decalogue and concerns honoring parents within Israel’s covenant life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 20:12 says to honor father and mother and attaches a promise about life and well-being in the land. In context, this command belongs to the Ten Commandments and functions within Israel’s covenant order. It is not originally part of a Greco-Roman household code. In Ephesians, however, the commandment is taken out of Sinai’s national setting and applied directly to Christian family life, while the promise is also preserved in adapted form.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Ephesians 6:2–3 is a straightforward example of direct ethical reuse of Torah material. They also point out that the commandment’s original land-based promise is adapted to fit a broader Christian moral setting. Scholars often describe this as continuity with contextual adjustment rather than a radical reinterpretation.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about living by doing the commandments in arguments about law and righteousness.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to holiness legislation and says that the person who does these things will live by them.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Leviticus 18:5 appears in a section of holiness law dealing with how Israel is to live differently from surrounding peoples. The verse says that the person who keeps God’s statutes and rules will live by them. In context, this is covenantal legal instruction, not a critique of law or an argument against grace. Paul later uses the line in Romans and Galatians as part of his contrast between law-based doing and faith-based righteousness.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Paul’s use of Leviticus 18:5 is one of his more strategic reuses of Torah language. They note that the original verse positively affirms life through obedience within covenant law, while Paul puts it into a larger contrast between law and faith in his own theological argument. Scholars often describe this as later polemical or contrastive reuse of a legal text.

cards.q:
NT: Two New Testament passages use this OT line about every knee bowing and every tongue swearing allegiance.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a strong monotheistic declaration about the Lord alone, not originally to a statement about Jesus.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 45:23 comes in a section where God declares that there is no other God and that every knee will bow and every tongue will swear loyalty to the Lord. In context, the passage is a sweeping monotheistic statement about God’s unique sovereignty over all nations. It is not originally a christological text. Later New Testament writers use that same language in contexts about final judgment and Jesus’s exalted status.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars point to Isaiah 45:23 as one of the strongest examples of New Testament writings applying language originally said of God to Jesus. They note that Romans 14 keeps the verse in a judgment setting, while Philippians 2 places it inside a high christological hymn. Scholars often describe this as a major case of later christological reuse of strict monotheistic language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses a line of thought close to this OT wisdom text when warning that people reap what they sow.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to wisdom teaching about moral consequence, though the wording relationship is looser than with many direct quotations.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Proverbs 11:31 is part of Israel’s wisdom tradition, where actions have consequences and moral order is built into the world. The exact wording is not the same as Galatians 6:7, but the conceptual connection is close: what a person does has fitting results. In context, Proverbs is giving general instruction about how life works under God’s order, not making a specific prediction or offering a Pauline slogan. Galatians later uses similar wisdom logic to warn about behavior and outcomes.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the connection between Galatians 6:7 and Proverbs 11:31 is more conceptual than exact. They note that Paul draws on a broader wisdom principle rather than citing one verse in a strict quotation formula. Scholars often describe this kind of case as thematic sapiential reuse rather than a direct citation.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses OT anti-idolatry language in warning the one New Testament letter about sacrifices offered to idols.
OT: The background is not one single verse but a cluster of passages about idols, false worship, and sacrifices associated with foreign gods or powers.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 106:20 criticizes Israel for exchanging God’s glory for an image. Psalm 115:4–8 mocks idols as powerless human-made objects. Deuteronomy 32:17 says that the people sacrificed to demons or non-gods. In their original settings, these texts all attack idolatry, but they do so in different ways: historical reflection, satire, and covenant warning. Paul draws on that wider anti-idolatry world in 1 Corinthians 10, where he warns that participation in idol feasts is not spiritually neutral.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 10:20 is not best explained by one single Old Testament source. Instead, Paul draw from a larger scriptural field of anti-idolatry language, especially passages that connect false worship with powers opposed to God. Scholars often describe this as broad thematic reuse rather than a one-verse quotation.

cards.q:
NT: Apostolic speeches use this OT promise about a prophet like Moses in connection with Jesus.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to Moses’s promise of continuing prophetic mediation for Israel after his death.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 18:15–18 belongs to Moses’s promise that after his death, God will continue to guide Israel through prophets. The passage comes after warnings against divination and foreign religious practices. Its point in context is that Israel does not need forbidden ways of seeking revelation because God will raise up a prophet from among the people, like Moses, and put words in that prophet’s mouth. Originally, this is about ongoing prophetic mediation for Israel, not a direct single-person prediction about Jesus alone. In Acts, however, the passage is used christologically and treated as reaching its fullest meaning in Jesus.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Deuteronomy 18 originally addressed the continuation of prophecy in Israel rather than naming Jesus directly in its first context. They note that Acts narrows the passage christologically by presenting Jesus as the climactic prophet like Moses. Scholars often describe this as Mosaic-typology reuse or later christological rereading of a passage about prophetic succession.

cards.q:
NT: One Gospel uses this OT wilderness-serpent story as a comparison for Jesus being “lifted up.”
OT: In its original setting, the story is about judgment, repentance, and healing in the wilderness, not about a future crucifixion.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Numbers 21:8–9 comes from a wilderness story in which the people complain, are struck by serpents, and then receive a way of healing. Moses is told to make a bronze serpent and set it up so that those who look at it may live. In its original context, this is a story about judgment, repentance, and divine healing during Israel’s wilderness experience. It is not a prediction about crucifixion. In John 3, the image is turned into a comparison: just as the serpent was lifted up, so the Son of Man must be lifted up. The original story supplies the pattern, but the Gospel gives it a new symbolic meaning.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Numbers 21:8–9 was not originally about Jesus or the cross. They usually describe John 3:14–15 as typological reuse, where an earlier narrative event becomes a symbolic pattern later applied to Jesus. Scholars often note that John is less interested in original predictive meaning here than in analogy and theological transformation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament narrative quotes this OT servant passage in the scene with the Ethiopian official and links it to Jesus.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to the servant poem and describes silent suffering, humiliation, and removal by judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 53:7–8 belongs to the suffering-servant poem. It describes a servant who is oppressed, silent like a lamb before shearers, taken away by judgment, and cut off from ordinary justice. In Isaiah’s original setting, the servant’s identity is not explicitly named, which is why there has been so much debate over whether the servant is Israel, a faithful remnant, a prophetic figure, or some individual representative. The passage is poetic and compressed. It does not mention Jesus or Christianity in its original setting. In Acts, however, Philip is presented as giving an explicit christological interpretation of the passage.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars regard Acts 8 as one of the clearest places where the New Testament openly performs christological interpretation of Isaiah’s servant poem. They also note that the original referent of the servant in Isaiah remains debated and is not settled in a simple way by the text itself. Scholars often describe Acts 8 as an explicit later interpretation rather than a case where Isaiah 53:7–8 originally and unambiguously identified Jesus.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT servant line about wounds and healing in a moral and pastoral context.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the suffering-servant poem and speaks about affliction and healing in a debated servant passage.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 53:5 is part of the servant poem and says that the servant was wounded or pierced and that by his wounds healing comes. In context, this is poetic language inside a larger passage about affliction, rejection, burden-bearing, and later vindication. The line is not originally part of a Christian pastoral letter or a direct statement about Jesus. In 1 Peter, however, the verse is reused in a moral and pastoral context, where suffering, healing, and return are tied to the community’s life and conduct.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 2:24–25 is a strong example of later christological reuse of Isaiah’s servant language. They note that the letter uses Isaiah 53 not only to describe Jesus’s suffering, but also to shape Christian ethics and identity under pressure. Scholars often describe this as pastoral appropriation of servant imagery rather than the original passage being specifically about Jesus in its first context.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT servant line about deceitlessness and innocence in a pastoral-ethical setting.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the suffering-servant poem and emphasizes the servant’s innocence amid unjust suffering.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 53:9 says that the servant had done no violence and that no deceit was found in his mouth. In context, this line belongs to the suffering-servant poem’s insistence that the servant suffers despite innocence. The point in Isaiah is that the servant’s affliction is not explained by personal guilt in the ordinary sense. In 1 Peter, that same line is taken up to present Jesus as innocent in suffering and to make him a model for believers facing unjust treatment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Isaiah 53:9 originally belonged to the larger servant poem, where innocence intensifies the problem of the servant’s suffering. They note that 1 Peter reuses the verse in an explicitly christological and pastoral way. Scholars often describe this as later application of servant innocence language to Jesus and, through him, to the conduct of the Christian community.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT forgiveness text in his argument about righteousness and forgiveness.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a psalm celebrating forgiven sin and restored standing before God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 32 is a psalm about confession, forgiveness, and restored relationship with God. Verses 1–2 say that blessed are those whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, and to whom the Lord does not count iniquity. In the Psalm’s original setting, this is celebratory language about pardon after sin. It is not originally part of a technical Pauline argument about justification. Paul later uses the lines because they already speak in terms of non-counting sin and blessedness, which fit his wider argument in Romans 4.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 4:7–8 is a good example of Paul building theology from scriptural language that was not originally written as a formal doctrinal treatise. They note that Psalm 32 is a forgiveness psalm, while Paul makes it part of a sustained argument about righteousness, faith, and non-imputation of sin. Scholars often describe this as theological development from devotional and liturgical material.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT wisdom instruction about feeding an enemy in a section about overcoming evil with good.
OT: In its original setting, the saying belongs to practical wisdom about generosity toward an enemy.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Proverbs 25:21–22 advises a person to feed an enemy when that enemy is hungry and to give drink when thirsty. The saying concludes with the image of heaping burning coals on the enemy’s head, a phrase that has been understood in different ways, including shame, moral awakening, or intensified judgment. In its original setting, this is wisdom instruction about how to respond to hostility in a way that refuses simple retaliation. Paul later uses the passage inside a section about not repaying evil for evil and overcoming evil with good.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 12:20 preserves the basic moral direction of Proverbs 25:21–22 while giving it a sharper place inside Paul’s ethic of non-retaliation. They note that Paul does not radically rewrite the proverb, but he does place it in a larger argument about enemy-love, peace, and leaving vengeance to God. Scholars often describe this as direct ethical reuse of wisdom instruction.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing quotes this OT psalm passage in a section about speech, peace, and righteous living.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a psalm of deliverance that includes wisdom-like moral exhortation.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 34 is a praise psalm about deliverance, trust, and God’s care for the righteous. Verses 12–16 take on a wisdom-like tone, urging the hearer to keep the tongue from evil, seek peace, and do good, because the Lord’s eyes are on the righteous. In the Psalm’s original setting, this is moral exhortation inside a poem of thanksgiving and trust. It is not originally directed to a Christian audience under social pressure. In 1 Peter, the passage is reused to support an ethic of disciplined speech, peace, and righteous conduct.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 3:10–12 is an example of direct sapiential reuse of a psalm that already contains moral instruction. They note that the Psalm’s original ethical force remains largely intact, even though it is now applied within a Christian paraenetic setting. Scholars often describe this as continuity with contextual adaptation rather than a major reinterpretation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing draws on this OT passage when urging believers not to fear but to honor Christ.
OT: In its original setting, the passage tells people in a political crisis not to share the panic of those around them, but to regard the Lord as the one to fear rightly.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 8:12–13 comes from a time of political fear and instability. Judah is surrounded by threats, and the people are tempted to panic in the same way everyone else is panicking. Isaiah is told not to share that fear. Instead, the people are to regard the Lord as the one truly to fear and honor. In its original setting, the passage is about refusing public panic and misplaced fear during a national crisis. It is not originally a Christian exhortation about persecution. In 1 Peter, however, the same line is reused to tell believers not to fear hostile pressure and to set apart Christ as Lord.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 3:14–15 gives Isaiah 8:12–13 a striking christological turn. They note that the original passage tells people to fear and honor the Lord, while 1 Peter applies that language to Christ. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of a crisis text with high christological significance, since language first used of Israel’s God is reassigned to Jesus.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT line about casting out the slave woman and her son in an allegorical argument about covenants.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a family conflict in the Abraham story about inheritance, status, and the future of the household.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 21:10 belongs to the conflict between Sarah, Hagar, Isaac, and Ishmael in the Abraham story. Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be cast out because she does not want Ishmael sharing the inheritance with Isaac. In its original setting, the verse is about family tension, inheritance, and the future of Abraham’s household. It is not originally a symbolic statement about covenants or theological systems. Paul, however, turns the line into part of an allegorical contrast between slavery and freedom in Galatians 4.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Galatians 4 is one of Paul’s boldest examples of allegorical interpretation. They note that Genesis 21:10 originally belongs to a family story about Sarah and Hagar, but Paul reuses it as part of a symbolic argument about two covenants and two kinds of children. Scholars often describe this as a strong case of later interpretive transformation rather than a continuation of the original narrative meaning.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT line about the barren woman in the same symbolic argument about promise and freedom.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language about a once-desolate Zion becoming fruitful again.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 54:1 belongs to a restoration passage that follows the servant poem. Zion is pictured as a barren woman who is suddenly called to sing because she will become fruitful again. In its original setting, this is not about Sarah and Hagar or about Paul’s argument in Galatians. It is about restoration after devastation, shame, and loss. The image is communal and national: desolate Zion is promised renewed life and future abundance. Paul later brings that image into his contrast between slavery and freedom.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Galatians 4:27 is another example of Paul extending an Old Testament restoration passage into a new symbolic argument. They note that Isaiah 54:1 originally speaks about Zion’s renewed future, but Paul folds it into his allegory about the children of promise. Scholars often describe this as later figurative reuse of restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT creation line in his argument contrasting Adam and Christ.
OT: In its original setting, the line describes the first human becoming a living being in the creation narrative.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 2:7 describes the creation of the first human. God forms the human from the dust of the ground and breathes into him the breath of life, so that the human becomes a living being. In its original setting, the verse belongs to the creation narrative and explains the origin of human life. It is not originally part of a contrast between Adam and Christ. Paul later uses the line in 1 Corinthians 15 to set up a comparison between the first Adam and the last Adam, extending the meaning of the verse far beyond its original narrative setting.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 15:45 is a major example of Paul building theology from creation narrative. They note that Genesis 2:7 originally explains how the first human came to life, while Paul reuses it to construct an Adam-Christ contrast about mortality, embodiment, and resurrection. Scholars often describe this as theological development from narrative origins material.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line about winds and flames in a contrast between angels and the Son.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a creation hymn celebrating God’s rule over the world and heavenly servants.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 104 is a creation hymn celebrating God’s majesty and rule over the world. Verse 4 speaks about God making winds his messengers and flames of fire his servants, though the wording can also be understood differently depending on whether one follows the Hebrew or the Greek tradition. In its original setting, the line belongs to poetic praise of God’s command over creation and heavenly forces. It is not originally part of a contrast between angels and the Son. Hebrews later draws the line into that contrast, treating it as language about angels in service to God.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Hebrews 1:7 depends on a reading of Psalm 104:4 that suits the argument about angels as servant beings. They also point out that the verse is poetic and textually flexible enough to allow this use. Scholars often describe this as a later application of creation-hymn language within a christological hierarchy argument.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse repeatedly uses this OT line about ruling with a rod of iron.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a royal psalm about the anointed king’s power over rebellious nations.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 2 is a royal psalm about God’s anointed king and the rebellion of the nations. Verse 9 says the king will break or rule them with a rod of iron and dash them like pottery. In its original setting, this is royal enthronement language about firm dominion over hostile nations. It is not originally part of a Christian apocalypse. Revelation later reuses this verse several times because it already carried strong imagery of messianic authority, judgment, and rule over the nations.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Psalm 2:9 became one of the most important royal texts for the book of Revelation. They note that the verse’s language of iron rule and broken pottery is repeatedly transferred to Jesus and, in one passage, shared with the faithful. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic intensification of royal-psalm imagery.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT line about God’s name being dishonored among the nations because of the behavior of his own people.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to prophetic language about national humiliation and the scandal this creates among the nations.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 52:5 belongs to a passage about humiliation, oppression, and the dishonoring of God’s name among the nations because of what has happened to the people. In its original setting, the line is about Israel’s suffering and exile-like disgrace, not about hypocrisy within a later religious community. Paul, however, takes the line and uses it against those whose behavior causes God’s name to be dishonored. That means he shifts the verse from a setting of national humiliation to a setting of moral accusation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 2:24 is a good example of Paul reapplying prophetic language in a sharper moral direction. They note that Isaiah 52:5 originally concerns the dishonor attached to Israel’s condition among the nations, while Paul uses it to accuse his hearers of conduct that brings disrepute on God’s name. Scholars often describe this as a later ethical rereading of prophetic shame language.

cards.q:
NT: One major speech uses this OT passage to argue that God cannot be confined to a man-made house.
OT: In its original setting, the passage critiques simplistic temple thinking and emphasizes God’s transcendence and concern for the humble.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 66:1–2 says that heaven is God’s throne and earth is God’s footstool, so no human-built house can contain him. In context, the passage critiques simplistic temple thinking and shifts attention toward the kind of person God truly regards: the humble, contrite, and reverent. It is not originally part of Stephen’s speech in Acts. But because it already challenged overconfident reliance on sacred buildings, it becomes a natural text for Stephen’s argument that God is not confined to a temple made by human hands.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 7 uses Isaiah 66:1–2 to push a sharp critique of temple-centered thinking. They note that the original passage already relativized the temple by emphasizing God’s transcendence and concern for the humble. Scholars often describe Stephen’s use as a later polemical reuse of prophetic anti-triumphal temple language.

cards.q:
NT: The New Testament uses this OT vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds in scenes about exaltation, judgment, and final authority.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to an apocalyptic vision about beasts, kingdoms, and vindicated rule.
cards.a: Matthew 24:30, Matthew 26:64, Mark 14:62, Luke 21:27, Revelation 1:7 vs Daniel 7:13–14

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Daniel 7:13–14 belongs to an apocalyptic vision in which beastly kingdoms are judged and one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive authority, glory, and a kingdom. In its original setting, the imagery is symbolic and tied to Daniel’s larger vision of imperial oppression, judgment, and vindicated rule. The passage is not originally a Gospel prediction scene or a Christian apocalypse. Later New Testament writings use it because it already joins heavenly authority, vindication, and final dominion in one vivid image.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Daniel 7:13–14 is one of the most important Old Testament background texts for New Testament language about exaltation, judgment, and the Son of Man. They note that the original passage is apocalyptic and symbolic, not a straightforward narrative prediction about Jesus. Scholars often describe New Testament use of Daniel 7 as later christological appropriation of an apocalyptic kingdom vision.

cards.q:
NT: Paul combines these OT texts to explain a present condition of dullness, blindness, or non-perception.
OT: In their original settings, one text comes from covenant-memory language and the other from prophetic judgment, but both deal with people failing to understand what God is doing.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Romans 11:8 combines language from Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. Deuteronomy 29:4 says that despite all Israel has seen, God has not yet given them a heart to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear. Isaiah 29:10 speaks of a spirit of deep sleep and closed eyes in a setting of prophetic judgment. In their original contexts, these passages come from different settings—covenant memory and prophetic denunciation—but both deal with failure to perceive what God is doing. Paul brings them together to explain a present condition of hardening and non-perception.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 11:8 is a classic composite quotation. They note that Paul does not simply quote one verse, but fuses covenant language and prophetic judgment language into a single explanation of Israel’s present condition. Scholars often describe this as later scriptural blending used to support Paul’s argument about hardening.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT passage about a table becoming a trap in order to explain stumbling and judgment.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to an imprecatory lament in which the speaker calls for enemies to be judged.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 69 is a lament in which the speaker suffers hostility and cries out for God’s help. Verses 22–23 shift into imprecatory language, asking that the enemies’ table become a trap and that their eyes be darkened. In its original setting, this is not a calm doctrinal statement. It is part of a passionate prayer for judgment against opponents. Paul later reuses that language in Romans 11 to describe stumbling and hardening. So the original passage is a lament for justice, while Romans turns it into part of an explanation for Israel’s present situation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 11:9–10 is a strong example of Paul reusing imprecatory psalm language for theological argument. They note that Psalm 69 originally voices the suffering speaker’s plea for judgment, but Paul applies it to the issue of stumbling and non-response. Scholars often describe this as later theological reuse of lament and curse language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul alludes to this OT complaint by Elijah in order to frame a remnant argument.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a moment of prophetic despair in which Elijah believes he has been left alone.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: 1 Kings 19:10 comes from Elijah’s moment of deep despair after conflict with royal power and prophetic opposition. Elijah says that he alone is left and that the people have abandoned the covenant and killed the prophets. In its original setting, the line is not a statement of fact meant to define all future faithful communities. It is the complaint of an exhausted prophet who believes he has been left alone. Paul later uses Elijah’s complaint in Romans 11 as part of his remnant argument, pairing despair with God’s response that not all are gone.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Romans 11 uses Elijah’s complaint typologically rather than simply historically. They note that 1 Kings 19:10 is a cry of prophetic isolation, while Paul uses it to frame the idea that God still preserves a faithful remnant even when things look hopeless. Scholars often describe this as later narrative reuse built around the contrast between despair and divine preservation.

cards.q:
NT: Paul reuses this OT veil scene in a larger argument about covenant, reading, and transformed perception.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to the story of Moses veiling his face after encountering God’s glory.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 34:33–35 tells the story of Moses veiling his face after speaking with God. The shining of his face follows his encounter with divine glory, and the veil belongs to that narrative sequence. In its original setting, the passage is not about hardened reading, old covenants, or spiritual blindness. It is part of the Sinai story and the aftermath of Moses’s direct encounter with God. Paul later turns the veil into a symbolic way of speaking about covenant, reading, and transformed perception in 2 Corinthians 3.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 3 is one of Paul’s most creative rereadings of a Pentateuchal narrative. They note that Exodus 34 originally tells a story about reflected glory and a literal veil, while Paul transforms the veil into a theological symbol for misunderstanding and removal through turning to the Lord. Scholars often describe this as a major example of figurative and theological expansion from narrative material.

cards.q:
NT: Paul combines these OT covenant-presence texts to describe the community as God’s dwelling place.
OT: In their original settings, one text belongs to priestly covenant blessing language and the other to restoration vision language about God dwelling with a renewed people.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Leviticus 26:12 belongs to covenant blessing language and says that God will walk among the people and be their God. Ezekiel 37:27 belongs to a restoration vision after exile and says that God’s dwelling place will be with a renewed people. In their original settings, these passages come from different moments in Israel’s story: one from priestly covenant instruction and one from prophetic restoration hope. Paul combines them in 2 Corinthians 6:16 to describe the community as God’s dwelling place and to stress holiness and separation from impurity.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 6:16 is a classic composite quotation that merges covenant-presence language from more than one Old Testament source. They note that Paul takes words first addressed to Israel and applies them to the Christian community. Scholars often describe this as later identity-transfer reuse of covenant and restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul quotes this OT call to depart and be clean in a passage about separation from impurity.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to restoration and return language that calls the people to leave uncleanness behind.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 52:11 belongs to restoration language calling the people to depart from uncleanness as they leave behind the conditions of exile and disgrace. In its original setting, the verse is tied to return, purification, and preparation for restored life with God. It is not originally a direct command to a Christian congregation about separation from pagan practices. Paul later uses it in 2 Corinthians 6:17 as part of an exhortation about holiness, purity, and distinct communal identity.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 6:17 reuses return-from-exile language in a moral and communal way. They note that Isaiah 52:11 originally addressed a restoration setting, but Paul applies it to the life of the Christian community in relation to impurity and separation. Scholars often describe this as later ethical appropriation of restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing draws on this OT promise of divine presence and non-abandonment in a paraenetic setting.
OT: In its original settings, the wording belongs to leadership-transition scenes that assure God’s presence in the face of fear.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 31:6 and Joshua 1:5 both belong to leadership-transition settings where God’s presence is promised in the face of fear and uncertainty. The wording assures Moses’s successor and the people that God will not leave or forsake them as they move into a difficult future. In their original settings, these are not general sayings about money or contentment. Hebrews 13:5 reuses the promise in a paraenetic setting, connecting divine presence with courage, steadiness, and freedom from anxious attachment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Hebrews 13:5 takes a promise first spoken in leadership and conquest-transition contexts and applies it more broadly to the Christian community. They often describe this as later paraenetic reuse of divine-presence language, where a historically specific assurance becomes a general ground for trust and contentment.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line about not fearing what people can do in a section of closing exhortations.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a thanksgiving psalm about divine help and trust rather than fear.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 118:6 says, “The Lord is on my side; I will not fear. What can mortals do to me?” In its original setting, the line belongs to a thanksgiving psalm about deliverance, public praise, and trust in God’s help. It is not originally a closing exhortation in a Christian letter. Hebrews 13:6 uses the verse because it already gives strong language of confidence under threat. The original psalm speaks from a position of trust after or during deliverance, and Hebrews turns that trust into an exhortation for the community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hebrews 13:6 is a straightforward example of reusing trust language from a psalm in a paraenetic context. They note that Psalm 118:6 originally belongs to praise and thanksgiving, while Hebrews brings it into a setting of encouragement and communal perseverance. Scholars often describe this as later exhortational reuse of confidence language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT royal-judgment line in a scene of conquering messianic rule.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a vision of a Davidic ruler who judges with righteousness and strikes with the breath of his mouth.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 11:4 belongs to the vision of a Davidic ruler from the line of Jesse who judges with righteousness and strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth. In its original setting, the passage is about just rule, restoration, and the defeat of wickedness. It is not originally part of a Christian apocalypse. Revelation 19:15 later uses that royal-judgment imagery in its scene of conquering messianic rule, intensifying the violence and finality of the image in an apocalyptic setting.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 19:15 reuses Isaiah 11:4 as part of a broader cluster of royal and judgment texts. They note that the original Isaiah passage presents a just Davidic ruler, while Revelation transforms that image into a final apocalyptic warrior-king scene. Scholars often describe this as later apocalyptic intensification of messianic rule imagery.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT light imagery in its vision of the final city.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a restoration vision in which the Lord becomes everlasting light for a renewed Zion.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 60:19–20 belongs to a restoration vision in which Zion’s future is so transformed that the Lord becomes its everlasting light. The imagery is about security, glory, and the end of sorrow after humiliation and loss. In its original setting, the passage is addressed to restored Zion, not to the New Jerusalem of Revelation. Revelation 21–22 later reuses this light imagery in its final city vision, where there is no need for sun or moon because divine presence fills the place with light.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation’s final-city imagery depends heavily on restoration texts like Isaiah 60. They note that Isaiah 60:19–20 originally concerns Zion’s restored future, but Revelation extends that imagery into a cosmic and final-apocalyptic scene. Scholars often describe this as later new-creation reuse of Zion-restoration language.

cards.q:
