NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT line about a new heavens and a new earth in its final vision.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic picture of restored creation, renewed joy, and a transformed future after judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 65:17 says that God is creating new heavens and a new earth. In its original setting, this belongs to a prophetic vision of restored creation, renewed joy, long life, and reversal after judgment. The passage addresses the future of a restored people after disaster and humiliation. It is not originally part of a Christian apocalypse. Revelation 21:1 reuses the line because it already gives strong language for cosmic renewal, but it places that language into a much more final and universal end-time scene.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 21:1 depends heavily on Isaiah’s restoration language while also expanding it. They note that Isaiah 65:17 originally imagines a transformed future for God’s people after judgment, whereas Revelation turns the phrase into part of a final new-creation vision. Scholars often describe this as later apocalyptic reuse of restoration imagery.

wrongAnswers: Leviticus 17:11 / cultic blood principle behind Hebrews 9:22

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT promise about God dwelling with the people in its final city scene.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a restoration vision of reunified Israel, renewed covenant life, and divine presence after exile.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ezekiel 37:27 belongs to a restoration vision after exile in which God promises to dwell with a renewed and reunified people. The verse is part of a larger passage about covenant peace, sanctuary presence, and restored identity after national collapse. In its original setting, it is directed toward Israel’s restoration, not toward the final city scene in Revelation. Revelation 21:3 later uses the same dwelling language because it already expressed divine presence with a restored people, but it extends it into a final and cosmic horizon.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 21:3 is one of the clearest cases of later reuse of Ezekiel’s restoration-presence language. They note that Ezekiel 37:27 originally concerns Israel’s restoration after division and exile, while Revelation universalizes the imagery in its final vision of God dwelling with humanity. Scholars often describe this as new-creation expansion of restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT lament line about being killed all day long in a passage about suffering and assurance.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a communal lament about suffering even while remaining loyal to God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 44 is a communal lament in which the people protest that they are suffering even though they have not forgotten God or turned to false gods. Verse 22 says, “For your sake we are being killed all day long,” expressing the pain of suffering that seems undeserved. In its original setting, the line belongs to a national or communal cry for help. It is not originally part of Paul’s argument in Romans about suffering and assurance. Paul later uses the verse to show that hardship has long been part of the life of God’s people and does not separate them from God’s love.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 8:36 is a strong example of Paul reusing lament language to frame present suffering. They note that Psalm 44 originally voices communal distress and protest, while Paul incorporates it into an argument about perseverance and divine love. Scholars often describe this as later theological reuse of lament to normalize suffering within covenant life.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about generosity to the poor in a passage encouraging financial giving.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a wisdom-shaped psalm praising the righteous person’s generosity and stability.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 112 is a wisdom-shaped psalm praising the righteous person. Verse 9 says that such a person gives freely to the poor and that this generosity is part of enduring righteousness. In its original setting, the line belongs to a portrait of the stable, God-fearing, generous righteous person. It is not originally a fundraising text. Paul later uses the verse in 2 Corinthians 9 because it already connects generosity with righteousness and lasting fruit, making it useful in a passage encouraging financial giving.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 9:9 is a direct reuse of wisdom-shaped psalm language in support of communal generosity. They note that Paul preserves the basic force of the original passage but places it into a more specific appeal about giving and mutual provision. Scholars often describe this as straightforward ethical reuse of a righteousness-and-generosity text.

wrongAnswers: Leviticus 17:11 / cultic blood principle behind Hebrews 9:22

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about equal provision in the wilderness in a passage about fairness in giving.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the manna story, where no one had too much and no one had too little.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 16:18 belongs to the manna story in the wilderness. The point of the verse is that when the manna was gathered and measured, the one with much did not have too much, and the one with little did not have too little. In context, the verse is about God’s provision and the pattern of enough for each person in the wilderness. It is not originally a teaching about church finances. Paul later reuses it in 2 Corinthians 8 to support the idea of fairness and shared provision within the community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 8:15 is a good example of Paul drawing an economic principle out of a narrative about divine provision. They note that the original verse belongs to the manna story, while Paul applies its pattern of equitable sufficiency to the collection for believers. Scholars often describe this as later analogical reuse of a wilderness provision text.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about believing and therefore speaking in a passage about suffering and proclamation.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a thanksgiving psalm in which the speaker remembers distress and deliverance.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 116 is a thanksgiving psalm in which the speaker remembers distress, cries out to God, and celebrates deliverance. Verse 10 says, in effect, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” though the wording can vary between textual traditions and translations. In its original setting, the line belongs to a testimony of suffering and rescue. It is not a formal principle about apostolic ministry. Paul later uses it in 2 Corinthians 4:13 to connect faith and proclamation under pressure, placing his own ministry inside a similar pattern of trust, suffering, and speech.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that 2 Corinthians 4:13 reuses Psalm 116:10 because the psalm already ties faith, distress, and confession together. They say Paul does not radically change the basic force of the line, but he does place it into a new apostolic framework of suffering and proclamation. Scholars often describe this as later testimonial reuse of thanksgiving-psalm language.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus uses this OT line about mountains falling in a warning speech on the way to crucifixion.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to prophetic judgment language about terror, collapse, and national disaster.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hosea 10:8 belongs to a judgment oracle against Israel. The line about people saying to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall on us,” expresses terror in the face of national collapse and divine judgment. In its original setting, this is prophetic disaster language, not a saying spoken by Jesus on the way to crucifixion. Luke 23:30 later uses the same imagery because it vividly expresses the kind of catastrophic judgment and fear that Jesus is warning about.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke 23:30 reuses Hosea 10:8 as judgment language rather than as a prediction originally aimed at Jesus’s own situation. They note that Hosea’s verse belongs to national disaster imagery, while Luke places it into Jesus’s warning speech on the road to execution. Scholars often describe this as later prophetic reuse of disaster language in a new moment of crisis.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT creation-rest line in an argument about God’s rest still being open.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the creation story and describes God resting after finishing the work of creation.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 2:2 says that after finishing the work of creation, God rested on the seventh day. In its original setting, this is part of the creation story and marks the completion and rhythm of creation. It is not originally an argument about whether God’s rest is still open to later hearers. Hebrews 4:4 takes that creation-rest line and places it into a larger argument about Sabbath rest, promise, and the possibility of entering God’s rest in the present.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 4 is a striking example of theological expansion from a narrative line. They note that Genesis 2:2 originally describes God’s rest at creation, while Hebrews turns it into part of an argument about an ongoing rest still available to believers. Scholars often describe this as later theological rereading of the creation narrative.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses this OT grief line in the birth narrative, even though the larger original passage continues into hope and return.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to exile poetry about Rachel weeping, but the surrounding verses move toward restoration.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah 31:15 pictures Rachel, one of Israel’s matriarchs, weeping for her children because they are gone. In its original setting, this is exile poetry. Rachel is used as a poetic figure for the nation’s grief as the people are taken away by the Babylonians. From that perspective, it can feel as if the children are simply “no more.” But the larger passage does not end there. Verses 16–17 move toward hope, saying there is still a future and that the children will return from the land of the enemy. In Matthew, only the grief line is applied to Herod’s order to kill the male infants two years old and under near Bethlehem.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Jeremiah 31:15–17 originally refers to the trauma of exile and the promise of return, not to Herod’s massacre. They also note that Matthew uses only the weeping line and leaves the immediate restoration context unstated. Scholars often describe Matthew 2:18 as a later reuse of exile imagery rather than the original meaning of Jeremiah 31:15–17.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses this OT naming line for Jesus’s birth, even though the name and its setting belong to a larger crisis passage.
OT: In its original setting, the sign belongs to a political crisis and the name continues to matter in nearby material beyond one isolated verse.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 7:14 belongs to the political crisis faced by King Ahaz in the 8th century BCE. Judah is under threat from two kings, and Isaiah tells Ahaz that the child called Immanuel will function as a near-term sign that those enemies will soon be gone. The name continues to matter in nearby material, especially Isaiah 8:8 and 8:10, where “God with us” remains part of the crisis setting. In Hebrew, the word in Isaiah 7:14 means “young woman,” not specifically “virgin.” The Greek Septuagint uses a word that can be read as “virgin,” and that is the form Matthew follows. In its original setting, the sign is tied to Isaiah’s own time, not to a birth centuries later.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Isaiah 7:14–8:10 belongs to the Ahaz crisis and was not originally about Jesus. They note both the immediate historical timing and the difference between the Hebrew wording and the Greek Septuagint wording. Scholars often describe Matthew 1:23 as a later reinterpretation of the Immanuel passage through Greek scripture rather than the original meaning of Isaiah 7:14.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse combines this OT mourning-over-the-pierced-one imagery with cloud-coming imagery in an opening declaration about Jesus.
OT: In their original settings, these two passages belong to different prophetic and apocalyptic scenes, one about mourning and one about heavenly vindication.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Revelation 1:7 combines two very different Old Testament images. Zechariah 12:10 belongs to a prophetic scene of mourning, piercing, and future cleansing. Daniel 7:13 belongs to an apocalyptic vision in which one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive authority and dominion. In their original settings, these passages do not belong to the same scene. Revelation fuses them into a single declaration about Jesus, combining mourning-over-the-pierced-one imagery with heavenly vindication and cloud-coming language.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Revelation 1:7 is a classic composite scriptural construction. They note that the verse depends on both Zechariah 12:10 and Daniel 7:13, not on one source alone. Scholars often describe this as an apocalyptic blending of prophetic and visionary texts to create a christological declaration with more than one Old Testament root.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse builds its throne-room vision from several major OT vision texts rather than from a single source.
OT: In their original settings, these passages describe temple holiness, visionary creatures, heavenly court imagery, and judgment scenes.
cards.a: Revelation 4:1–11, Revelation 5:1–14 vs Isaiah 6:1–3, Ezekiel 1:4–28, Daniel 7:9–10

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Revelation 4–5 does not rest on one single Old Testament proof text. Its throne-room vision is built from several major vision passages. Isaiah 6 contributes temple holiness, seraphic praise, and the overwhelming presence of the Lord. Ezekiel 1 contributes the visionary creatures, radiant throne imagery, and the sense of divine glory beyond ordinary earthly categories. Daniel 7 contributes heavenly court and judgment imagery. In their original settings, these are distinct prophetic and apocalyptic scenes. Revelation combines them to create a new throne-room vision centered on God and the Lamb.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 4–5 is one of the clearest examples of large-scale scriptural saturation rather than neat quotation. They note that the author does not cite one verse directly so much as build an entire scene out of major Old Testament vision traditions. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic reuse through image-cluster composition rather than simple proof-text citation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT light imagery in its closing no-night vision.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a day-of-the-Lord passage about a uniquely transformed and luminous future.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 14:7 belongs to a difficult day-of-the-Lord chapter filled with conflict, transformation, and unusual cosmic imagery. The verse speaks of a unique day and unusual light, so that evening is not marked by normal darkness. In its original setting, this is part of Zechariah’s own prophetic vision of a transformed future centered on Jerusalem. Revelation 22:5 later draws on that no-night or altered-light imagery in its picture of the final city, where darkness is fully overcome by divine presence.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation’s no-night imagery draws not only on Isaiah but also on Zechariah 14:7. They note that Zechariah’s unusual light imagery becomes part of Revelation’s final-city symbolism. Scholars often describe this as later apocalyptic reuse of prophetic light language.

cards.q:
NT: New Testament arguments about Abraham and the nations can also be read against this OT promise line.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to the Abraham story before the Sodom episode and speaks broadly about blessing through Abraham.
cards.a: Acts 3:25, Galatians 3:8 vs Genesis 18:18, Genesis 12:3, Genesis 22:18

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 18:18 says that Abraham will become a great and mighty nation and that all nations of the earth will be blessed in him. Along with Genesis 12:3 and Genesis 22:18, it belongs to the wider Abraham-promise tradition. In its original setting, the verse appears before the Sodom episode and speaks broadly about Abraham’s significance in God’s purposes. It is not originally part of a later Christian argument about Gentile inclusion. New Testament writers later read this larger promise cluster as anticipating blessing flowing outward through Abraham into a wider community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts and Paul often draw not on a single Abraham verse in isolation but on a wider promise field built from Genesis 12, 18, and 22. They note that these passages originally belong to the patriarchal narrative and are later reread in more focused theological ways. Scholars often describe this as broader promise-horizon reuse rather than one-verse proof texting.

cards.q:
NT: Several New Testament writings draw on this OT judgment language to explain why speech or teaching does not lead to understanding.
OT: In their original settings, these passages belong to prophetic contexts where language itself becomes part of judgment against people who refuse to listen.
cards.a: Matthew 13:14–15, Mark 4:12, Luke 8:10, John 12:40, Acts 28:26–27, 1 Corinthians 14:21 vs Isaiah 6:9–10, Isaiah 28:11–12

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 6:9–10 comes from Isaiah’s call vision and speaks about a people who hear but do not understand and see but do not perceive. Isaiah 28:11–12 speaks of foreign speech and strange tongues as part of judgment on a people who refused to listen. In their original settings, both passages belong to prophetic contexts where language itself becomes part of judgment against resistant hearers. New Testament writers repeatedly draw on this pair or on this broader Isaianic field to explain why proclamation, teaching, or signs do not always produce understanding.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the New Testament repeatedly returns to Isaiah to explain failed reception. They note that this is broader than one exact quotation problem, since multiple writings reuse overlapping Isaianic hardening and judgment language in different settings. Scholars often describe this as repeated reuse of an Isaianic explanatory pattern rather than one isolated proof text.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse also echoes this OT image of living waters flowing from Jerusalem in its river-of-life scene.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a transformed-Jerusalem vision within a difficult day-of-the-Lord chapter.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 14:8 says that living waters will flow out from Jerusalem in a transformed future linked to the day of the Lord. Ezekiel 47:1–12 describes healing water flowing from the temple in a restoration vision after exile. In their original settings, these are different prophetic visions, but both imagine life-giving water as part of a transformed sacred future. Revelation 22:1–2 gather both streams together in its river-of-life scene, where the water comes from the throne of God and the Lamb in the final city.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 22 works through overlapping water-and-city imagery from more than one prophetic source. They note that Ezekiel 47 is the clearest major background, but that Zechariah 14:8 likely contributes to the larger image field. Scholars often describe this as composite prophetic reuse within a final new-creation vision.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line about flesh fading like grass and God’s word enduring forever.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a restoration message that contrasts human frailty with the permanence of God’s promise.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 40:6–8 belongs to the opening of Isaiah’s comfort section. The passage contrasts human frailty, which fades like grass or flowers, with the permanence of God’s word. In its original setting, this is restoration language addressed to people living under instability and loss. The point is that human life is fragile, but God’s promise endures. It is not originally a Christian statement about the gospel. First Peter later reuses the passage to emphasize the enduring word proclaimed to the community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 1:24–25 is a strong example of restoration language being redirected into Christian proclamation. They note that Isaiah 40 originally speaks in an exilic or restoration horizon, while 1 Peter makes the enduring word into part of its message about new life and the gospel. Scholars often describe this as later proclamation-oriented reuse of restoration language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT passage about trust, children, and signs in a christological argument about solidarity.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a prophet’s own family-sign context during a political and military crisis.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 8:17–18 belongs to a political crisis in Judah. Isaiah says that he will wait for the Lord, and then adds that he and the children given to him are signs and portents in Israel. In its original setting, this is about Isaiah’s own prophetic situation and household. The children are part of the prophet’s symbolic world during a time of danger, fear, and judgment. The passage is not originally about Jesus and believers. Hebrews later takes this prophetic household-sign language and applies it christologically, using it to describe Jesus in relation to those associated with him.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 2:13 gives Isaiah 8:17–18 a bold later reinterpretation. They note that the original passage refers to Isaiah and his children as signs in their own historical setting, while Hebrews reuses the wording to speak of Jesus and his people. Scholars often describe this as a strong example of figural or christological rereading of prophetic family-sign language.

cards.q:
NT: The passion narratives echo this OT mocking language about trusting in God and being delivered.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a lament scene where the speaker is scorned by onlookers.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 22:7–8 describes a speaker being mocked by onlookers who sneer at his trust in God and taunt him to seek rescue. In its original setting, this is part of a lament scene of humiliation and social contempt. The lines belong to the suffering voice of the Psalm’s speaker, not to a later crucifixion narrative. In the Gospels, however, this mocking language becomes a script for the ridicule directed at Jesus while he is on the cross.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the passion narratives use Psalm 22 not only as background mood but as a source for concrete verbal and dramatic elements. They note that Matthew 27:39–43 closely echoes Psalm 22:7–8 in order to cast Jesus as the suffering righteous one of Israel’s prayer tradition. Scholars often describe this as later lament reuse in the formation of the passion scene.

cards.q:
NT: One Gospel places this OT line on Jesus’s lips at death.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a psalm of trust spoken from within danger and distress.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 31 is a psalm of distress and trust. Verse 5 says, “Into your hand I commit my spirit,” and belongs to a prayer spoken from within danger, not after danger has already passed. In its original setting, the line expresses confidence in God’s care during suffering and threat. It is not originally a prediction about Jesus’s final words. Luke later places this line on Jesus’s lips at death, turning an existing scriptural prayer into the closing speech of the crucifixion scene.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke 23:46 is a clear example of prayer reuse rather than predictive fulfillment. They note that Psalm 31:5 was already a trust-prayer in Israel’s tradition, and Luke uses it to voice Jesus’s death in scriptural language. Scholars often describe this as the passion narrative being shaped through inherited prayer language.

cards.q:
NT: This OT servant line about the righteous one helping “many” is an important background for later New Testament atonement reasoning.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the climax of the suffering-servant poem and joins suffering, vindication, and benefit for others.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 53:11 belongs to the climax of the suffering-servant poem. The verse ties together suffering, righteousness, vindication, and benefit for “many.” In its original setting, it is part of the servant’s larger portrayal and remains inside the debated question of who the servant is in Isaiah. It is not originally a Pauline doctrinal statement. Later Christian interpretation found the verse important because it already held together the ideas of a righteous sufferer and many others benefiting from that sufferer’s experience.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars treat Isaiah 53:11 as an important background text for early Christian atonement reasoning, even when it is not always quoted as directly as some neighboring servant lines. They note that its conceptual role is large because it links righteousness, suffering, and benefit for others. Scholars often describe this as broader servant-horizon influence rather than one neat proof-text use.

cards.q:
NT: The triumphal-entry scene works through a layered pairing of donkey-king imagery and processional acclamation.
OT: In their original settings, one passage speaks of a humble king entering Zion and the other belongs to temple-procession praise language.
cards.a: Matthew 21:4–9, Mark 11:7–10, John 12:13–15 vs Zechariah 9:9, Psalm 118:25–26

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 9:9 speaks of Zion’s king arriving humbly on a donkey. Psalm 118:25–26 belongs to festival procession and blessing language, including the plea for saving help and the blessing of the one who comes in the name of the Lord. In their original settings, these texts are separate: one is prophetic royal imagery and the other is liturgical temple language. The triumphal entry scene brings them together so that Jesus’s arrival is framed as both royal and processional, with prophetic and liturgical overtones combined in one moment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the triumphal entry is best understood as a composite scriptural scene rather than as the fulfillment of one isolated verse. They note that Zechariah 9:9 supplies the humble-king imagery while Psalm 118:25–26 supplies the acclamation language. Scholars often describe this as a layered scriptural enactment or composite reuse.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing echoes this OT line about peace to those far and near in a passage about reconciliation.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language about healing and renewed relationship after judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 57:19 speaks of peace for those who are far off and those who are near in a context of healing, restoration, and renewed relationship after rebellion and judgment. In its original setting, the verse belongs to prophetic language about God repairing what has been broken. It is not originally a statement about Jew-Gentile reconciliation inside the church. Ephesians later uses the same far-and-near language in a more specific way to speak about reconciliation and unity in Christ.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Ephesians 2:17 gives Isaiah 57:19 a new communal application. They note that the original restoration language is redirected into a church-setting argument about bringing formerly separated groups together. Scholars often describe this as later expansion of prophetic peace language into ecclesial reconciliation.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT Redeemer-from-Zion passage in his difficult argument about Israel’s future.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to prophetic language about injustice, failure, and God’s own intervention to bring redemption.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 59:20–21 belongs to a prophetic chapter about injustice, failed righteousness, and the need for God to intervene because no human agent is adequate. The promise of a redeemer from Zion comes in a context of covenant renewal after moral and communal collapse. In its original setting, the passage addresses Zion and Israel’s restoration. It is not originally part of Paul’s argument in Romans 9–11. Paul later uses it in one of his most difficult passages about Israel’s future, hardening, and redemption.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 11:26–27 is a major example of Paul reusing a prophetic restoration text in a new theological argument. They note that Isaiah 59:20–21 originally belongs to Israel’s restoration horizon, while Paul incorporates it into his complex reasoning about Israel’s future. Scholars often describe this as later theological rereading of a restoration oracle.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing draws on this OT servant line about being a covenant and a light in mission and identity themes.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to servant material that joins Israel-focused covenant language with a wider horizon toward the nations.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 42:6 and Isaiah 49:6 both belong to Isaiah’s servant material. Isaiah 42:6 presents the servant as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations. Isaiah 49:6 says that restoring Israel alone would be too small a task and that the servant is also made a light to the nations so salvation reaches the ends of the earth. In their original settings, these lines belong to debated servant passages within Isaiah’s restoration horizon. They are not originally speeches about Jesus. Later Christian writers reuse them because they already join Israel-focused restoration with a wider international mission.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say later Christian use of Isaiah’s servant passages often draws on a broader servant field rather than on a single isolated verse. They note that language about covenant, light, and the nations became especially important for early christological and missionary interpretation. Scholars often describe this as later mission-oriented rereading of servant texts.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about the acceptable time and day of salvation in an urgent appeal.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language about help, covenant purpose, and divine timing.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 49:8 belongs to servant-related restoration language. The verse speaks about an acceptable time, divine help, covenant purpose, and the restoration of the land and people. In its original setting, it belongs to a future-oriented promise of recovery and divine faithfulness. It is not originally an apostolic appeal to a congregation to respond immediately. Paul later takes the line and turns it into an urgent present-tense call: now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 6:2 is a strong example of Paul relocating a restoration promise into a present moment of decision. They note that Isaiah 49:8 originally belongs to restoration and servant language, while Paul turns it into an immediate appeal. Scholars often describe this as later event-oriented or paraenetic reuse of restoration timing language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing combines several OT stone texts into a single christological argument about trust, rejection, and stumbling.
OT: In their original settings, these passages come from different prophetic and psalmic contexts and do not originally form one unified oracle.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: 1 Peter 2:6–8 combines three stone texts from different parts of the Old Testament. Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a foundation stone in Zion in a context of failed leadership and false security. Psalm 118:22 speaks of a rejected stone becoming central in a liturgical setting of reversal and vindication. Isaiah 8:14 speaks of the Lord becoming either sanctuary or stumbling stone in a time of political fear and judgment. In their original settings, these passages are separate and do not form one unified oracle. First Peter brings them together to create a single christological argument about trust, rejection, and stumbling.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 2:6–8 is one of the New Testament’s clearest composite stone catenae. They note that the author deliberately fuses several distinct Old Testament stone texts into one interpretive frame centered on Christ. Scholars often describe this as a classic example of composite quotation and christological scriptural blending.

cards.q:
NT: One Gospel draws on this OT gathering language in speaking about God’s scattered children being brought together.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language about sons and daughters being brought back from far away.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 43:6 belongs to restoration language in which God calls sons and daughters back from far away. In its original setting, the verse is about regathering, divine ownership, and the end of exile-like dispersal. It is addressed to Israel in a restoration horizon, not originally to the Gospel of John’s interpretation of Jesus’s death. John 11:51–52 later uses similar gathering language to speak of God’s scattered children being brought together through Jesus.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say John 11:51–52 reflects a broader restoration-text background rather than a neat one-verse proof text. They note that Isaiah 43:6 is one of the strongest candidates because of its language of bringing scattered children home. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of restoration-gathering imagery in a christological framework.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author also uses this OT line about throwing silver into the house of the Lord for the potter in the Judas-money scene.
OT: In its original setting, the line continues the symbolic shepherd passage and uses temple-and-potter imagery as part of a judgment drama.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 11:13 continues the symbolic shepherd scene by directing the silver to be thrown into the house of the Lord for the potter. In its original setting, the line is part of a symbolic drama of rejection, insultingly low valuation, and judgment. It does not originally describe Judas, a burial field, or a Gospel narrative. Matthew later uses this line because it brings together temple, silver, and potter imagery, all of which help shape the scene around Judas’s money and its aftermath.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 27:9–10 depends especially on Zechariah 11:13 for the temple-and-potter imagery, even though the wording and attribution remain complex. They note that this is one of the places where Matthew is working with a cluster of scriptural motifs rather than a single neat source line. Scholars often describe this as a later composite reuse problem with Zechariah as a central ingredient.

cards.q:
NT: New Testament writers use this OT Passover-blood line as an important background for interpreting Jesus’s death as protective and saving.
OT: In its original setting, the blood marks the Israelite houses so judgment passes over them during the exodus.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 12 belongs to the Passover narrative in the setting of Israel’s escape from Egypt. Verse 13 says the blood on the houses will be the sign so that judgment passes over the Israelites. Verse 46 says the Passover lamb’s bones are not to be broken. In their original setting, these are ritual and narrative details tied to the exodus, deliverance from slavery, and annual covenant memory. They are not originally predictions about Jesus. Later New Testament writers reuse these features because Passover already carried themes of deliverance, protection, sacrifice, and covenant identity.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Exodus 12 became one of the most important typological backgrounds for early Christian interpretation of Jesus’s death. They note that Paul’s “Christ our Passover” language and John’s unbroken-bones detail both depend on Passover imagery rather than on a direct original prediction about Jesus. Scholars often describe this as typological reuse of ritual and narrative material.

cards.q:
NT: Early Christian interpretation draws on this OT servant line about exaltation and being lifted high in order to hold suffering and vindication together.
OT: In its original setting, the line opens the servant poem with a paradox of high status followed by shocking suffering.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 52:13 opens the servant poem by saying that the servant will prosper, be exalted, and be lifted up very high. In its original setting, this creates an immediate tension with the shocking suffering and disfigurement described in the verses that follow. The line belongs to the servant poem’s paradox: humiliation and exaltation are held together from the beginning. It is not originally a Christian statement about Jesus. Later Christian interpretation found this opening especially important because it provided scriptural language for connecting suffering and vindication.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Christian use of the servant poem is not limited to its suffering language. They point out that Isaiah 52:13 already frames the servant’s story as one of exaltation after humiliation, which made it especially powerful for later christological interpretation. Scholars often describe this as broader servant-horizon reuse rather than reliance only on a few isolated suffering lines.

cards.q:
NT: Paul and one Gospel may draw on this OT birth-pains image in resurrection and new-life discussions.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to prophetic language about painful expectation that seems not to produce real deliverance.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 26:17–18 compares the people to a woman in labor who experiences pain but seems only to give birth to wind rather than real deliverance. In its original setting, the image expresses frustration, incomplete rescue, and the painful gap between hope and fulfillment. It belongs to a prophetic section about distress and longing before vindication. The passage is not originally about resurrection bodies. Later Christian readers could still find it useful because it already uses intense birth-and-deliverance imagery in a context of hoped-for reversal.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Isaiah 26:17–18 functions more as a thematic background than as a neat proof text for 1 Corinthians 15. They note that Paul’s resurrection argument works within a broader field of scriptural imagery about life, transformation, and failed or fulfilled expectation. Scholars often describe connections to this passage as horizon-level or image-cluster reuse rather than direct quotation.

cards.q:
NT: Later Jewish and Christian resurrection hope draws strongly on this OT line about the dead living and the earth giving up the departed.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to a prophetic section about distress, hoped-for vindication, and divine reversal.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 26:19 says that the dead shall live and those in the dust shall awake and sing. In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic section about distress, longing, and hoped-for vindication. It is one of the strongest resurrection-sounding lines in Isaiah. Isaiah 25:8 adds the image of God swallowing up death forever in a larger vision of victory, feast, and removed sorrow. These two passages do not originally form a Christian resurrection argument, but together they provided powerful language for later Jewish and Christian hope about divine reversal over death.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Isaiah 26:19 and Isaiah 25:8 form an important part of the wider scriptural horizon behind 1 Corinthians 15, even though Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8 more directly. They note that both passages belong to broader prophetic visions of reversal and victory. Scholars often describe this as resurrection-horizon reuse rather than exclusive dependence on one verse alone.

cards.q:
NT: Later Jewish and Christian resurrection hope draws strongly on this OT line about sleepers in the dust awakening to different outcomes.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to an apocalyptic vision of distress, vindication, judgment, and final reversal.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Daniel 12:2 says that many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt. In its original setting, the verse belongs to Daniel’s apocalyptic conclusion, where distress, deliverance, judgment, and vindication all come together. It is one of the clearest resurrection texts in the Old Testament. The verse is not originally part of the Gospel of John or Acts, but it became central for later Jewish and Christian reflection because it already combined resurrection with differentiated judgment outcomes.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Daniel 12:2 is one of the most important Old Testament backgrounds for New Testament resurrection language. They note that even when it is not quoted word-for-word, its apocalyptic framework strongly shaped later expectations about resurrection and judgment. Scholars often describe this as a major horizon-setting text rather than a merely occasional proof text.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT royal-psalm line about the nations as inheritance as part of its wider background for worldwide messianic rule.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to enthronement language for the anointed king and the scope of his dominion.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 2:8 promises the nations as inheritance and the ends of the earth as possession for the anointed king. In its original setting, the line belongs to royal enthronement language about the scope of the king’s dominion. It is not originally a Christian apocalypse text. Even so, it helped shape later messianic imagination because it joined kingship with worldwide rule. Revelation later uses that wider royal-psalm horizon alongside the more explicit rod-of-iron language from Psalm 2:9.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Psalm 2:8 is often less explicitly cited than nearby Psalm 2 lines, but it still matters as part of the larger royal background behind Revelation’s messianic rule imagery. They note that the psalm’s universal scope supports the later apocalyptic vision of worldwide dominion. Scholars often describe this as broader royal-psalm horizon reuse.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses new-name imagery that strongly resonates with this OT promise about Zion’s transformed identity.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to restoration language in which Zion is vindicated and receives a new name after shame and desolation.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 62:1–2 belongs to a restoration passage in which Zion’s vindication, righteousness, and transformed public identity are emphasized. The promise that Zion will receive a new name signals reversal, honor, and divine redefinition after shame and desolation. In its original setting, this is addressed to Zion’s restored future, not to the churches in Revelation. Revelation later reuses that new-name logic in its promises about transformed identity and belonging.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation’s repeated interest in new names resonates strongly with Isaiah 62. They note that the Isaianic passage originally concerns Zion’s restored identity, while Revelation extends that promise into a final symbolic and ecclesial register. Scholars often describe this as later apocalyptic reuse of restoration-identity language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses sealing imagery that strongly echoes this OT marking scene before judgment falls.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to a judgment vision in which those who grieve over abominations are marked for preservation.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ezekiel 9:4 belongs to a judgment vision in which a mark is placed on those who grieve over the abominations in Jerusalem so that they are distinguished before destruction falls. In its original setting, the mark is part of a terrifying and selective judgment scene. It is not originally an apocalyptic seal on the servants of God in the book of Revelation. Revelation later takes that protective-mark pattern and transforms it into a scene of end-time sealing before judgment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 7 strongly echoes Ezekiel 9:4. They note that both passages share the pattern of marking a protected group before judgment falls. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic image reuse, where an earlier visionary sign of preservation is expanded in a later end-time setting.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse reworks this OT temple-restoration vision on a very large scale in its final city scenes.
OT: In its original setting, the passage presents measured sacred space, renewed land order, divine presence, and a life-giving river after exile.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ezekiel 40–48 presents a long temple-restoration vision with measured sacred space, priestly order, renewed land arrangement, a life-giving river, and the return of divine glory. In its original setting, the vision offers an ordered future after exile and devastation, centered on renewed sanctuary presence. It is not originally the final city of Revelation. Revelation 21–22 later draws heavily on this visionary world, but also transforms it by removing the temple as a separate building and placing divine and Lamb presence directly at the center of the city.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Ezekiel 40–48 is one of the largest background horizons behind Revelation 21–22. They note that Revelation reuses numerous Ezekiel motifs while also decisively reshaping them. Scholars often describe this as large-scale apocalyptic rewriting rather than simple citation.

cards.q:
NT: The Gospels’ darkness-at-noon crucifixion scene is often read against this OT judgment image.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to prophetic disaster language about the sun going down at noon and daylight turning dark.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Amos 8:9 says that the sun will go down at noon and the earth will be darkened in broad daylight. In its original setting, this is prophetic disaster language. The verse belongs to a larger judgment oracle about social injustice, mourning, and coming catastrophe. It is not originally a prediction about Jesus’s crucifixion. The Gospel darkness-at-noon scene later uses that kind of prophetic imagery because it already expressed public disaster, judgment, and cosmic disturbance in vivid terms.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the darkness at noon in the crucifixion narratives is often read against prophetic judgment imagery such as Amos 8:9. They note that the connection is usually thematic rather than a strict quotation formula. Scholars often describe this as scriptural atmosphere or horizon-level reuse, where older catastrophe language helps interpret the theological weight of Jesus’s death.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses throne-and-books judgment imagery that strongly resonates with this OT courtroom vision.
OT: In its original setting, the passage belongs to an apocalyptic scene of heavenly judgment over beastly kingdoms.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Daniel 7:9–10 presents the Ancient of Days seated in judgment, with fiery imagery, books opened, and a heavenly court in attendance. In its original setting, the vision belongs to Daniel’s apocalyptic judgment over beastly empires and the transfer of dominion after oppressive kingdoms are judged. It is not originally the final judgment scene of Revelation. Revelation 20:11–12 later uses very similar throne-and-books imagery because Daniel had already supplied a powerful picture of heavenly judgment and opened books.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation’s judgment scenes depend heavily on Danielic apocalyptic imagery, especially Daniel 7:9–10. They note that Revelation does not merely quote Daniel, but reworks its courtroom symbolism in a final-apocalypse setting. Scholars often describe this as later apocalyptic reuse of Daniel’s heavenly judgment vision.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to support the idea that the nations will join in praising Israel’s God.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a royal thanksgiving song in which the speaker praises God among the nations after deliverance from enemies.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 18 is a royal thanksgiving psalm celebrating deliverance, victory, and God’s faithfulness to the king. Verse 49 says that the speaker will praise God among the nations and sing to God’s name. In its original setting, this is not a missionary program or a direct statement about Gentiles joining the covenant community. It is the victorious praise of a royal figure whose deliverance has public significance beyond Israel. Paul later reuses the line in Romans 15 because it helps him argue that the nations praising Israel’s God fits within Israel’s own scriptures.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 15 uses Psalm 18:49 as part of a catena designed to show that Gentile praise of God is scripturally grounded. They note that the original psalm is royal thanksgiving, not a direct Gentile-inclusion oracle. Scholars often describe Paul’s use as a later expansion of royal praise language into an argument about the nations’ place in worship.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to show the nations rejoicing together with God’s people.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a covenant warning song that ends with vengeance, vindication, and widened praise.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 32 is the Song of Moses, a long covenant poem about Israel’s future unfaithfulness, God’s judgment, and God’s eventual vindication. Verse 43, especially in its Greek form, includes language about the nations rejoicing with God’s people. In its original setting, the line belongs to a judgment-and-vindication song, not to Paul’s later church argument. But because the passage ends with widened praise and divine justice, it became important for later writers looking for scriptural support for a broader worshiping community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Romans 15:10 reflects the Greek textual form of Deuteronomy 32:43, which makes the nations’ rejoicing more explicit. They often point out that Paul is drawing from a covenant song whose original setting is judgment and vindication, not a direct Gentile-mission oracle. Scholars commonly describe this as later reuse of a widened praise line within a larger catena about Gentile inclusion.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this very short OT call to praise as support for the nations glorifying God.
OT: In its original setting, the line is already a direct summons for all nations and peoples to praise the Lord.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm and one of the clearest universal praise texts in the Psalter. It directly calls all nations and all peoples to praise the Lord because of God’s steadfast love and enduring faithfulness. In its original setting, this is already wider in scope than many other psalms. It does not need much reinterpretive stretching to function in a later argument about Gentile praise.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Psalm 117:1 is one of the strongest and most straightforward texts Paul could use in Romans 15. They note that unlike some of his more creative citations, this one already directly addresses the nations. Scholars often describe this as a case of relatively direct continuity between the psalm’s original force and its later Pauline use.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT root-of-Jesse text to support hope among the nations.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a Davidic restoration vision in which a ruler from Jesse’s line becomes a signal for the peoples.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 11:10 belongs to a larger vision of a Davidic ruler from the stump of Jesse. The chapter presents a just and spirit-filled ruler whose reign brings restoration, judgment on wickedness, and peace. Verse 10 adds that the root of Jesse will stand as a signal for the peoples and that nations will seek him. In its original setting, this is part of a royal restoration vision after political collapse. Paul later uses the verse because it already joins Davidic hope with the nations.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 15:12 is one of Paul’s strongest Gentile-inclusion citations because Isaiah 11:10 already names the nations directly. They note that the original passage is still a Davidic restoration text in Isaiah’s own world, but that its outward-facing horizon makes it especially suitable for Paul’s argument. Scholars often describe this as a relatively direct reuse of a royal-restoration text with international scope.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line to argue that Jesus is a priest in a category different from the Levitical system.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a royal psalm that joins kingship and priestly language in a striking way.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 110 is a royal psalm about enthronement, victory, and divine backing for the ruler. Verse 4 says that the ruler is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. In its original setting, this is unusual because it joins royal and priestly language in the same psalm. It is not originally a detailed treatise on heavenly priesthood. Hebrews later turns this one line into a major theological foundation for its argument that Jesus’s priesthood is different in kind from the Levitical priesthood.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews gives Psalm 110:4 a far larger role than it had in its original royal-psalm setting. They note that the psalm provided a compact but highly suggestive line joining priesthood and kingship, and Hebrews expands that into a sustained theology of Christ’s priesthood. Scholars often describe this as major theological development from a brief royal-psalm statement.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT oath to Abraham as support for the certainty of God’s promise.
OT: In its original setting, the line comes after the near-sacrifice of Isaac and emphasizes God’s sworn commitment to bless and multiply Abraham.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 22:16–17 comes after Abraham has shown willingness to offer Isaac, and God responds with a sworn oath. The promise emphasizes blessing, multiplication, and the continuation of Abraham’s line. In its original setting, this is not a general lesson about hope in Hebrews. It is part of the Abraham narrative and marks a climactic reaffirmation of the promise after a severe testing episode. Hebrews later uses it because the oath language makes the promise appear especially firm and unchangeable.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 6 uses Genesis 22 strategically because it contains not just promise language but oath language. They note that this helps Hebrews argue for the reliability and firmness of God’s commitment. Scholars often describe this as later theological reuse of patriarchal oath material rather than a major reinterpretation of the original story.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line to stress that the promised line was reckoned through Isaac.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the Abraham family story and clarifies which son carries the covenant line.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 21:12 comes during the conflict involving Sarah, Hagar, Isaac, and Ishmael. God tells Abraham not to be distressed and says that the line through which offspring will be named or reckoned will come through Isaac. In its original setting, the verse clarifies inheritance, promise, and lineage within Abraham’s family story. It is not originally part of a resurrection argument. Hebrews later uses it in the context of Abraham and Isaac to emphasize the promised line and the tension involved when that same Isaac is then offered up.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Hebrews 11:18 draws attention to Genesis 21:12 in order to heighten the dramatic force of the Akedah story: the promised son is the very one Abraham is asked to offer. They often describe this as later narrative-theological reuse, where a promise-line text is brought into a faith-and-testing argument.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT Sinai restriction to heighten the fear and distance of the old mountain scene.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the Sinai boundary laws that forbid approaching the holy mountain carelessly.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 19:12–13 belongs to the preparations for Sinai. The people are warned to set boundaries around the mountain and not to touch it, because the mountain has become dangerous through divine holiness. Even animals that touch it are to be killed. In its original setting, the passage stresses distance, fear, and the seriousness of approaching God’s holiness without authorization. Hebrews later uses this material to intensify its contrast between the terrifying Sinai scene and the different kind of access described in its new-covenant vision.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hebrews 12 uses Sinai material rhetorically, highlighting the fearsome and exclusionary features of the mountain scene in order to sharpen the contrast with the new covenant. They note that Exodus 19 originally functions within the Sinai narrative itself, but Hebrews reorganizes its force inside a larger theological comparison. Scholars often describe this as later contrastive reuse of covenant-theophany material.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing alludes to OT language about divine jealousy in a warning against divided loyalty and worldly attachment.
OT: In its original settings, the language belongs to covenant texts in which God’s jealousy guards exclusive allegiance and rejects idolatry.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 20:5 and Exodus 34:14 both describe God as jealous in the context of covenant loyalty and the rejection of other gods. In their original settings, this jealousy is not petty envy. It is covenant language about exclusive allegiance, especially in the face of idolatry. The point is that Israel cannot belong to the Lord while also giving loyalty elsewhere. James 4:5 is textually difficult, but it echoes this Old Testament jealousy theme in order to condemn spiritual double-mindedness and friendship with the world.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say James 4:5 is one of the harder New Testament scripture-use cases because it does not neatly quote one exact Old Testament verse. They often argue that it reflects a scriptural theme, especially the Exodus language about God’s jealousy and exclusive covenant claim. Scholars commonly describe this as thematic reuse of covenant-jealousy language rather than a clean citation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing appeals to this OT figure as an example of endurance and the eventual compassion of the Lord.
OT: In its original setting, the story is a wisdom drama about suffering, protest, divine speeches, and restoration, not a simple patience proverb.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The book of Job is a wisdom drama about devastating suffering, disputed explanations, protest, and divine response. Job loses family, health, and status, argues with his friends, and speaks boldly about his pain and confusion. In its original setting, the story is not mainly a neat lesson about quiet patience. It is a long and difficult exploration of suffering and justice. James 5:11 later uses Job as an example of endurance and points especially to the outcome that reveals the Lord’s compassion and mercy.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that James’s appeal to Job is selective. They point out that Job is not consistently passive or silent in the biblical book, but deeply argumentative and emotionally intense. Scholars often describe James 5:11 as a later paraenetic use of Job that highlights endurance and outcome more than the full complexity of the original wisdom drama.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT wisdom line to argue that even the righteous are saved through difficulty, raising the question of what will happen to the ungodly.
OT: In its original setting, the verse belongs to wisdom teaching about moral consequence and recompense.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Proverbs 11:31 belongs to Israel’s wisdom tradition and makes a comparison about recompense: if the righteous receive what is due on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner. In its original setting, the verse is a general wisdom statement about moral order and consequence. It is not originally about Christian suffering or persecution. First Peter later uses the line in a setting where believers are already experiencing hardship, and the saying becomes a way of framing their trials in relation to final judgment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 4:18 gives Proverbs 11:31 a sharper eschatological edge than it has in its original wisdom setting. They note that the verse is moved from general moral consequence into an argument about suffering, salvation, and judgment. Scholars often describe this as later paraenetic reuse of sapiential recompense language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line about casting burdens on the Lord in a closing call to humility and trust.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a lament about betrayal, anxiety, and the need to place one’s burden before God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 55 is a lament shaped by anxiety, hostility, and the pain of betrayal by a close companion. Verse 22 says to cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you. In its original setting, this is trust language spoken out of emotional distress and social threat. It is not originally a general church exhortation. First Peter later uses the same burden-casting logic in a paraenetic setting, joining humility with trust that God cares for the community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Peter 5:6–7 reflects psalmic trust language even when the wording is adapted. They note that Psalm 55:22 supplies a strong background for the call to cast anxiety on God. Scholars often describe this as later paraenetic reuse of lament-and-trust language.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing cites a Jewish apocalyptic judgment line about the Lord coming with countless holy ones to execute judgment.
OT: Part of the background reaches beyond the Hebrew Bible into Jewish literature, while also echoing older Sinai and divine-coming imagery from Israel’s scriptures.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jude 14–15 quotes a judgment saying most directly known from 1 Enoch 1:9, where the Lord comes with many holy ones to execute judgment on the ungodly. That line itself echoes older scriptural imagery such as Deuteronomy 33:2, where the Lord comes in majesty with holy ones in a Sinai-like setting. The result is layered tradition: ancient divine-appearing imagery is developed in Jewish apocalyptic literature and then cited in Jude. So the background is not limited to one Old Testament verse alone.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Jude 14–15 is one of the clearest places where the New Testament directly cites non-canonical Jewish literature. They note that 1 Enoch 1:9 is the immediate source, while older biblical traditions such as Deuteronomy 33:2 likely stand behind it. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic chain-tradition reuse rather than a simple OT quotation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing strings together three notorious OT rebellion figures as a warning pattern.
OT: The examples come from different narratives—murder, corrupt gain, and revolt against divinely appointed leadership—and are fused into one denunciation.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jude 11 names Cain, Balaam, and Korah together. Cain comes from Genesis 4 as the brother who murders Abel. Balaam comes from Numbers 22–24 and later traditions as a figure associated with corrupt gain and leading others astray. Korah comes from Numbers 16 as the leader of a revolt against Moses and Aaron. In their original settings, these are separate narratives with different concerns. Jude fuses them into one warning pattern about false teachers and destructive rebellion.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Jude 11 is a compact example of typological clustering, where several notorious scriptural figures are brought together to create a single polemical profile. They note that Jude is not quoting one passage but invoking a bundle of rebellion traditions. Scholars often describe this as composite narrative reuse in the service of denunciation.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT lion-and-scepter imagery for a victorious messianic figure.
OT: In its original setting, the lines belong to Jacob’s blessing over Judah and point to tribal rulership and enduring authority.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 49:9–10 belongs to Jacob’s blessings over his sons. Judah is compared to a lion, and the passage speaks of the scepter not departing from Judah. In its original setting, this is tribal and dynastic language about authority and rule associated with Judah. It is not originally part of an apocalyptic vision of Jesus. Revelation later uses this imagery because lion and rulership themes already made Judah a powerful symbolic source for messianic identity.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 5:5 draws on the royal and tribal symbolism of Genesis 49 in a highly concentrated way. They note that the original blessing is not a Christian apocalypse text, but it became important in later Jewish and Christian messianic interpretation. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic reuse of patriarchal rulership imagery.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse presents a victory song that evokes both the song of Moses and later covenant-song traditions.
OT: The background is not one verse but a cluster of Israel’s great songs of deliverance, judgment, and divine kingship.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 15 is the song sung after deliverance through the sea, praising God’s victory over Pharaoh and celebrating divine kingship. Deuteronomy 32 is the Song of Moses, a covenant poem about unfaithfulness, judgment, and eventual vindication. In their original settings, these are distinct songs with different moods and purposes, but both became major scriptural reservoirs of deliverance and judgment imagery. Revelation 15:3 evokes “the song of Moses” in a way that gather this wider song tradition into its own apocalyptic victory hymn.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 15:3 is not best reduced to one exact Old Testament verse. They note that it likely draws on a broader mosaic of Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32 themes rather than one direct quotation. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic song-cluster reuse built from Israel’s foundational deliverance and covenant songs.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse describes the final city in measurements that echo both temple and restored-city imagery.
OT: The background includes perfect-cube holy-space dimensions and idealized city measurements from restoration visions.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: 1 Kings 6:20 describes the inner sanctuary, the holy of holies, as a perfect cube. Ezekiel 48:16 gives idealized city measurements in Ezekiel’s restoration vision. In their original settings, these passages concern temple holiness and restored spatial order after crisis. Revelation 21:16 later describes the New Jerusalem with equal length, width, and height, giving the whole city holy-of-holies dimensions. That means the final city itself takes on the character of the most sacred space.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 21:16 is one of the clearest symbolic architectural reuses in the book. They note that the perfect-cube form strongly evokes the holy of holies, while restoration-measurement traditions from Ezekiel also stand in the background. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic transformation of temple symbolism into city symbolism.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses tree-of-life imagery that combines Eden and restoration-river symbolism.
OT: The background joins primal garden imagery with prophetic healing-tree imagery from a restored temple landscape.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 2:9 places the tree of life in the garden of Eden at the beginning of the biblical story. Ezekiel 47:12 describes trees nourished by the temple river whose fruit and leaves bring life and healing in a restoration vision after exile. In their original settings, these are very different scenes: one primal and one restorative. Revelation 22:2 combines them so that Eden’s tree of life and Ezekiel’s healing trees merge into a final image of restored and healed creation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 22:2 is a classic example of apocalyptic fusion. They note that the verse does not merely repeat Genesis or Ezekiel, but combines Eden imagery and restoration-river imagery into one final new-creation scene. Scholars often describe this as synthetic reuse of beginning-of-Bible and restoration-vision symbolism.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to argue that God remains true even if human beings prove false.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a penitential prayer in which the speaker confesses guilt and acknowledges God’s justice in judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 51 is a penitential psalm about sin, confession, and the need for mercy. Verse 4 says that God is justified in speaking and blameless in judging. In its original setting, this is the speaker’s admission of guilt and recognition that God is right. It is not originally a general argument about universal human falsehood. Paul later uses the line in Romans 3 to support a broader claim: God’s truth and justice stand firm even when human beings fail or prove unfaithful.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 3:4 lifts a confessional line from Psalm 51 into a wider theological argument about divine faithfulness. They note that the original verse belongs to a personal penitential setting, while Paul generalizes its force in a discussion of sin and God’s truthfulness. Scholars often describe this as later argumentative reuse of penitential language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to argue that Abraham’s calling already pointed beyond one ethnic line to many nations.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the covenant-renaming scene in which Abram becomes Abraham because he will be father of many nations.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 17:5 belongs to the covenant-renaming scene where Abram becomes Abraham. The name change is explained by the promise that he will become the father of many nations. In its original setting, this is part of the patriarchal covenant narrative, tied to descendants, covenant obligations, and future multiplication. It is not originally a Pauline argument about faith and Gentile inclusion. Paul later uses the verse because the wording about many nations fits his wider claim that Abraham’s significance extends beyond one people.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 4:17 is a good example of Paul building a broader theological case from a narrative covenant line. They note that Genesis 17:5 originally explains Abraham’s new name inside the patriarchal story, while Paul turns it into support for an international promise horizon. Scholars often describe this as later theological expansion of covenant-naming language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about countless descendants to frame Abraham’s hope against hope.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the covenant scene in which Abraham is shown the stars as a sign of the scale of the promised offspring.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 15:5 belongs to the covenant scene where Abraham is brought outside and told to look toward the heavens and count the stars, if possible. The stars serve as a vivid image of the scale of the promised offspring. In its original setting, the verse is part of the patriarchal promise story and addresses Abraham’s uncertainty about descendants. It is not originally a general lesson about faith under impossibility. Paul later uses it in Romans 4 to highlight Abraham’s trust in the face of apparent hopelessness.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Romans 4 turns the Abraham narrative into a model of faith under impossible conditions. They note that Genesis 15:5 originally functions inside the promise story itself, while Paul uses it to sharpen the theme of trusting divine promise against visible circumstances. Scholars often describe this as later paradigmatic reuse of patriarchal promise imagery.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to argue that not all physical descendants are counted in the same way within the promise line.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the Abraham family story and clarifies that the covenant line is reckoned through Isaac.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 21:12 comes during the conflict involving Sarah, Hagar, Isaac, and Ishmael. God tells Abraham not to be distressed and says that the offspring line will be reckoned through Isaac. In its original setting, the verse clarifies inheritance, promise, and lineage inside Abraham’s family story. It is not originally a later theological claim about corporate election or the people of God. Paul later uses it in Romans 9 because it helps him distinguish between mere biological descent and the line of promise.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 9:7 is a classic example of Paul turning a family-line text into a broader argument about promise and identity. They note that Genesis 21:12 originally settles a narrative question within Abraham’s household, while Paul gives it a much larger theological role. Scholars often describe this as later theological reuse of patriarchal lineage language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT promise line about the appointed time of a birth in his argument about promise and election.
OT: In its original setting, the words come from the scene where Sarah is promised a son despite her age and doubt.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 18:10 and 18:14 belong to the scene where Sarah is told that she will have a son at the appointed time, even though the promise seems impossible because of age. In its original setting, the passage is about divine promise overcoming human limitation and disbelief. It is part of the patriarchal narrative, not originally a Pauline argument about election. Paul later uses the line in Romans 9 to stress that Isaac’s birth depended on promise rather than ordinary expectation or entitlement.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 9:9 draws from the birth-promise scene to sharpen the distinction between promise and ordinary descent. They note that the original passage is narrative and dramatic, but Paul extracts from it a theological point about how the promised line comes into being. Scholars often describe this as later doctrinal use of patriarchal birth-promise material.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT oracle about two brothers before birth in his argument about divine choice.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to Rebekah’s pregnancy oracle and speaks of two nations and the reversal of expected status.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 25:23 comes during Rebekah’s troubled pregnancy, when she receives an oracle explaining that two nations are in her womb and that the older will serve the younger. In its original setting, this is both a family oracle and a statement about larger peoples descending from the twins. It is not a philosophical treatise on election. Paul later uses the line in Romans 9 because it allows him to emphasize divine choice before the twins have acted.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Romans 9:12 takes a narrative oracle about Jacob and Esau and gives it a sharper theological role than it has in Genesis itself. They often stress that the original setting includes national dimensions, not only individual ones. Scholars commonly describe Paul’s use as a significant theological extension of a birth-oracle narrative.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT salvation line about calling on the Lord in a way that overlaps with his application of “Lord” language to Jesus.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic passage about deliverance in the day of the Lord.

notes.label: Context
