notes.text: Joel 2:32 says that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic passage about cosmic signs, divine judgment, and deliverance in the day of the Lord. The “Lord” in Joel is Israel’s God within Joel’s own prophetic horizon. Paul later reuses the line in Romans 10 as part of a larger argument where calling on the Lord overlaps with calling on Jesus, which gives the verse a much sharper christological role than it had in Joel itself.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 10:13 is one of the more significant examples of Paul applying to Jesus a verse whose original referent is the Lord in Joel. They note that the original passage concerns divine deliverance in a prophetic judgment context, while Paul uses it in a gospel-and-confession framework. Scholars often describe this as high christological reuse of prophetic salvation language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to say that God will destroy the wisdom of the wise.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a prophetic judgment against human schemes, false confidence, and religious blindness.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 29:14 says that the wisdom of the wise will perish and the discernment of the discerning will be hidden. In its original setting, the verse belongs to a prophetic critique of blindness, hypocrisy, and political or religious scheming in Judah. It is not originally a statement about Greek philosophy or Christian preaching. Paul later uses the line in 1 Corinthians 1 because it fits his argument that God overturns human standards of wisdom through the message of the cross.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 1:19 reuses Isaiah 29:14 in a way that preserves its anti-human-scheming force while shifting the argument into Paul’s contrast between worldly wisdom and divine wisdom. Scholars often describe this as later prophetic reuse in a polemic against self-assured human understanding.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses a composite-sounding OT line about what no eye has seen or ear heard in speaking about what God has prepared.
OT: The wording is not a neat match to one verse, but it reflects restoration and divine-action language from later prophetic material.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 64:4 speaks about no one having heard or seen a God besides the Lord who acts for those who wait for him. Isaiah 65:17 begins a restoration promise about new heavens and a new earth. Paul’s wording in 1 Corinthians 2:9 does not exactly match one single verse, but it reflects this wider Isaianic world of divine action, hiddenness, and promised future. In its original settings, the material is about God’s unique action and restoration, not a New Testament doctrine of revealed wisdom.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 2:9 is not a simple citation of one verse but a composite or free scriptural paraphrase, most likely drawing on Isaiah 64 and possibly resonating with nearby restoration material such as Isaiah 65. Scholars often describe this as a good example of Pauline scriptural fusion rather than exact quotation.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to say that God catches the wise in their craftiness.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a speech in this passage where God is praised for overturning the plans of the cunning.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Job 5:13 appears in one of Eliphaz’s speeches. The line says that God catches the wise in their craftiness and frustrates the schemes of the cunning. In its original setting, this is part of wisdom-style theology inside the larger debate of the book of Job. Because Job is a contested dialogical book, not every line in it simply functions as final divine truth in context. Paul later uses the line in 1 Corinthians because it works well in his attack on self-confident human wisdom.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Paul’s use of Job 5:13 is interesting because it comes from a speech by Eliphaz rather than from God’s own speeches or the narrator’s explicit evaluation. They often describe this as selective sapiential reuse, where Paul extracts a useful line from the larger argumentative world of Job for his own polemic against human wisdom.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line in a warning against idolatry, feasting, and reckless behavior.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the golden calf story and describes a celebratory scene that turns into covenant betrayal.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 32:6 comes from the golden calf episode. The people sit down to eat and drink and rise up to revel after making an idol while Moses is on the mountain. In its original setting, this is not just a casual party scene. It is part of one of the most serious covenant-breaking moments in the wilderness story, where feast, idolatry, and disloyalty come together. Paul later uses the line in 1 Corinthians 10 because it gives a vivid scriptural example of how communal celebration can become spiritually corrupt.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 10 treats Israel’s wilderness failures as typological warnings for the church. They note that Exodus 32:6 is especially useful because it compresses idolatry and revelry into one memorable line. Scholars often describe this as later paraenetic reuse of a major covenant-failure narrative.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT episode in a warning about sexual immorality and divine judgment.
OT: In its original setting, the story belongs to Israel’s involvement with Moabite worship and the deadly consequences that follow.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Numbers 25:1–9 tells the story of Israel becoming involved with Moabite women and being drawn into the worship of Baal of Peor. In its original setting, the narrative is about both sexual entanglement and idolatrous compromise. A plague follows, and the episode becomes one of the Bible’s stark warnings about covenant disloyalty. Paul later uses this story in 1 Corinthians 10 because it combines bodily behavior, false worship, and judgment in a way that serves his warning to the community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Paul’s use of Numbers 25 in 1 Corinthians 10 shows how wilderness traditions could function as moral and theological precedents for early Christian communities. They note that the original story combines idolatry and sexual misconduct, making it especially potent for Paul’s purposes. Scholars often describe this as typological warning reuse of a wilderness judgment narrative.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT wilderness complaint story in a warning against testing the Lord.
OT: In its original setting, the people speak against God and Moses, and fiery serpents become part of the judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Numbers 21:5–6 belongs to the wilderness traditions in which the people complain against God and Moses, rejecting the provision they have been given. In response, fiery serpents appear as judgment. In its original setting, this is a story about impatience, distrust, and rebellion during the journey. It is not originally a sermon to a church. Paul later uses it because it gives a concrete example of what it looks like to test divine patience and reject God’s provision.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that 1 Corinthians 10 reuses multiple wilderness judgment stories together, not only one. They say Numbers 21 is especially useful because it dramatizes the danger of complaint and testing. Scholars often describe this as cluster-typology, where several wilderness failures are lined up as warnings for a new community.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses OT wilderness grumbling traditions in a warning against complaint and destruction.
OT: In its original setting, the background belongs to the rebellion after the spies’ report, where grumbling against Moses and God leads to judgment.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Numbers 14 tells the story of Israel’s rebellion after the spies’ report. The people grumble, reject the land, and speak against Moses and Aaron. Later in the chapter, judgment falls on those who helped spread the fearful report. In its original setting, this is part of the larger wilderness pattern of distrust and refusal to move forward under God’s leadership. Paul later uses grumbling language in 1 Corinthians 10 to warn that complaint is not a small matter when it reflects unbelief and resistance.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Paul’s wilderness catena in 1 Corinthians 10 works by evoking a whole pattern of rebellion, not always one exact verse. They note that Numbers 14 is a likely major background because it centers on grumbling, refusal, and judgment. Scholars often describe this as thematic reuse of rebellion traditions rather than one neat citation.

cards.q:
NT: A disputed Pauline instruction about silence and submission is often read against this OT line about desire, rule, and post-fall order.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the judgment scene after Eden and speaks about the altered relationship between woman and man.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 3:16 belongs to the judgment scene after the disobedience in Eden. The verse addresses pain, desire, and the man’s rule over the woman as part of the fractured order that follows the fall. In its original setting, this is not a church-order instruction or a letter about assembly practice. It is part of a narrative about consequence and disruption in human relationships. Later readers have sometimes brought it into discussions of gender hierarchy and submission, including debates around 1 Corinthians 14:34–35.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the connection between 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 and Genesis 3:16 is interpretive rather than a direct quotation. They note that some later traditions read the Pauline language through Eden and post-fall order themes, while others debate whether this is the best background at all. Scholars often describe this as a contested background proposal rather than a clean citation case.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT legal standard to frame the seriousness of repeated testimony and accountability.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to Israel’s legal requirements for establishing a matter by multiple witnesses.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 19:15 says that a matter is established by two or three witnesses. In its original setting, this is legal instruction within Israel’s judicial system. The rule is there to prevent arbitrary accusations and to require adequate confirmation before judgment is rendered. It is not originally about apostolic visits or church discipline. Paul later uses this legal standard in 2 Corinthians 13:1 as a way of framing his coming visit and the seriousness of repeated warnings and evidence.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 13:1 is a straightforward case of legal reuse. They note that Paul takes an Israelite judicial principle and applies it analogically to his relationship with the Corinthians. Scholars often describe this as direct adaptation of Torah legal standards for communal and disciplinary purposes.

cards.q:
NT: Paul turns the Hagar-and-Sarah material into a symbolic contrast between slavery and freedom.
OT: In its original setting, the material belongs to the Abraham family narratives, where conflict, inheritance, promise, and birth all unfold in story form rather than allegory.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 16–21 contains the intertwined stories of Hagar, Sarah, Ishmael, and Isaac. In their original setting, these are narrative episodes about family conflict, promise, fertility, inheritance, and the future of Abraham’s household. They are not originally an allegory of covenants. Paul later rereads this material symbolically in Galatians 4, using the two mothers and two sons to construct a contrast between slavery and freedom, flesh and promise, present Jerusalem and the Jerusalem above.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Galatians 4:21–31 is one of Paul’s most overtly allegorical or figurative scriptural rereadings. They note that the Genesis narratives do not present themselves this way in their original form. Scholars often describe Paul’s use as a major example of theological transformation of patriarchal narrative into symbolic argument.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT generation language to urge believers to stand out as blameless amid a crooked world.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the Song of Moses and describes a corrupt and twisted generation in a covenant-judgment context.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 32:5 belongs to the Song of Moses, a covenant poem about Israel’s corruption, unfaithfulness, and coming judgment. The line about a crooked and twisted generation belongs to that sharp indictment. In its original setting, this is not a church encouragement passage. It is a judgment description within a national covenant song. Paul later reuses the language in Philippians 2:15, but he does so to urge believers to be blameless and visibly different within a dark moral environment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Philippians 2:15 reuses Deuteronomy 32 in a strikingly contrastive way. They note that language originally used to condemn a corrupt generation is reapplied to describe the setting in which believers should shine. Scholars often describe this as later paraenetic reuse of covenant-judgment language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses OT peace language ironically in warning that sudden destruction can come when people feel secure.
OT: In their original settings, these lines belong to prophetic critiques of leaders who say “Peace” when there is no real peace.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Jeremiah 6:14 and Ezekiel 13:10 both attack leaders who say “Peace” when there is no peace. In their original settings, the point is that false reassurance hides real danger and prevents honest confrontation with judgment. These are prophetic critiques of superficial healing and deceptive security. Paul later uses similar peace-and-safety language in 1 Thessalonians 5:3 to warn that sudden destruction can break in precisely when people think everything is stable.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Thessalonians 5:3 reflects a wider prophetic pattern as a multi-source reuse. They note that Jeremiah and Ezekiel provide especially strong background for the irony of false peace language before judgment. Scholars often describe this as thematic prophetic reuse in an eschatological warning setting. This card should be read as prophetic-pattern reuse: Paul draws on the familiar scriptural irony of false peace before judgment.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT armor image in describing readiness, faith, love, and hope.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a divine-warrior scene in which God puts on righteousness and salvation in response to injustice.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 59:17 belongs to a dramatic passage in which God sees injustice and acts as a divine warrior. God puts on righteousness like a breastplate and salvation as a helmet. In its original setting, this is not advice to believers about personal conduct. It is a theophanic scene about God’s own intervention because no human agent is sufficient. Paul later reuses the armor imagery in 1 Thessalonians 5:8, adapting it from divine-warrior language into exhortation for believers to live alertly and faithfully.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Paul’s armor language draws on Isaiah’s divine-warrior imagery but relocates it into communal exhortation. They note that imagery first used of God becomes applied to believers as part of moral and eschatological readiness. Scholars often describe this as transformed reuse of divine-warrior symbolism.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line to say that the Lord knows who truly belong to him.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the Korah rebellion and introduces a test of who is truly chosen in a dispute over leadership.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Numbers 16:5 comes from the Korah rebellion, where Moses responds to a challenge against his and Aaron’s leadership. He says that the Lord will show who belongs to him and who is holy. In its original setting, the line belongs to a high-stakes leadership conflict and a judgment story about rebellion against divinely recognized authority. It is not originally a general statement about church identity. Second Timothy later reuses the line because it offers a concise way of grounding communal stability in God’s knowledge and recognition.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Timothy 2:19 uses Numbers 16:5 as part of a compact scriptural slogan about true belonging and purity. They note that the original verse comes from a rebellion narrative, while the New Testament application broadens it into a community-marking principle. Scholars often describe this as later paraenetic reuse of a rebellion-and-recognition text.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT line about a figure who was taken by God so that he did not see death.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the genealogy before the flood and marks out one figure as unusually close to God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 5:24 says that Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more because God took him. In its original setting, the verse appears in the genealogy before the flood and stands out from the repeated pattern of birth and death. The line is brief and mysterious, but it clearly marks Enoch as exceptional. It is not originally a developed argument about faith. Hebrews later uses the verse because it provides a concise example of someone whose life with God is portrayed as ending in divine translation rather than ordinary death.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hebrews 11 gives Genesis 5:24 a faith-oriented reading by drawing out the implications of Enoch’s closeness to God. They note that the original verse is sparse and genealogical, while Hebrews turns it into a model of pleasing God by faith. Scholars often describe this as interpretive expansion from a brief narrative notice.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT deathbed scene as an example of faith expressed in blessing and worship.
OT: In its original setting, the material belongs to Jacob’s final days, including blessing Joseph’s sons and bowing in weakness at the end of life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 47:31 and Genesis 48 belong to Jacob’s final days in Egypt. He asks Joseph to bury him in the ancestral land, then blesses Joseph’s sons, crossing his hands in a surprising act of preference. In its original setting, this material is about family continuity, promise, land, and blessing at the end of Jacob’s life. It is not originally framed as a formal lesson on faith. Hebrews later reads these final acts as examples of trusting God’s future promises even at the point of death.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Hebrews 11 often re-reads patriarchal end-of-life scenes as concentrated acts of faith. They say Jacob’s blessing and worship in Genesis become, in Hebrews, evidence of confidence in promises not yet fully seen. Scholars often describe this as faith-focused reuse of patriarchal deathbed narrative material.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT request about bones and departure as an example of faith in future deliverance.
OT: In its original settings, the material belongs first to Joseph’s deathbed expectation and later to the exodus generation carrying his bones out of Egypt.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 50:24–25 records Joseph’s final statement that God will surely visit the people and bring them up from Egypt, followed by his request that his bones be carried with them. Exodus 13:19 later notes that Moses takes Joseph’s bones during the exodus. In their original settings, these passages are about long-term trust in divine promise, land, and future deliverance. They are not originally a formal theological argument. Hebrews later uses Joseph’s request as a clear sign of confidence in a future God-act not yet visible in Joseph’s lifetime.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 11:22 highlights one of the most forward-looking details in the Joseph story. They note that Joseph’s concern about his bones is really concern about God’s promise and the future return. Scholars often describe this as a strong example of promise-oriented rereading of patriarchal narrative detail.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT birth narrative detail as an example of fearless faith.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to Moses’s infancy story under Pharaoh’s killing order, where his parents hide him after seeing that he was a beautiful child.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 2:2 tells the story of Moses’s birth under Pharaoh’s policy of killing Hebrew boys. His mother sees that he is a fine or beautiful child and hides him for three months. In its original setting, this is a vulnerable infancy story within a larger setting of oppression and threatened survival. It is not originally a generalized lesson about faith. Hebrews later turns the act of hiding Moses into an example of faith that resists fear in the face of royal command.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 11 often reinterprets narrative courage as faith, even where the original story does not explicitly frame it that way. They note that Exodus 2:2 is a concise narrative detail, while Hebrews expands it into a paradigm of fearless trust. Scholars often describe this as faith-centered rereading of rescue narrative material.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing reads Moses’s rejection of Egyptian status as a deliberate act of faith and identification.
OT: In its original setting, the material belongs to Moses’s early adulthood, palace background, and break with Egypt after the killing of an Egyptian.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 2:10–15 presents Moses growing up in Pharaoh’s daughter’s household, then killing an Egyptian after seeing a Hebrew being beaten, and finally fleeing Egypt. In its original setting, this material is narrative and politically charged. It shows Moses caught between identities and reacting decisively against oppression, but it does not explicitly present his actions as a worked-out doctrine of faith. Hebrews later reads this early-life material as a rejection of Egyptian privilege in favor of solidarity with God’s people.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hebrews 11 gives the Moses story a more inward and faith-driven interpretation than Exodus itself spells out. They note that the Exodus narrative is more dramatic and ambiguous in places, while Hebrews sharpens its theological meaning. Scholars often describe this as interpretive condensation of narrative complexity into a faith exemplar.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT Passover action as an example of faith in the face of coming judgment.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the night of the Passover, where blood on the houses marks protection from the destroyer.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 12:21–23 belongs to the Passover narrative on the night before the exodus. The Israelites are told to apply blood so that the destroyer will pass over their houses. In its original setting, this is part of a ritualized moment of crisis, judgment, and deliverance. It is not originally a theological chapter on faith. Hebrews later uses the act of keeping the Passover and applying the blood as a concrete expression of trusting God’s warning and promise before the deliverance is visible.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 11 highlights actions that embody trust before outcomes are seen, and the Passover night fits that pattern well. They note that Exodus presents the blood rite as obedience in a moment of danger, while Hebrews reads it explicitly through the category of faith. Scholars often describe this as faith-oriented reuse of exodus ritual action.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT crossing scene as a corporate example of faith.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the sea-crossing narrative where deliverance comes through parted waters and Egypt is overwhelmed.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 14:21–31 tells the story of Israel passing through the sea on dry ground while the pursuing Egyptians are drowned. In its original setting, this is one of the foundational deliverance narratives in Israel’s story, combining fear, salvation, divine power, and judgment on oppressors. It is not originally framed as a chapter on faith examples. Hebrews later reads the crossing as a collective act of trust in God’s saving action, in contrast to the Egyptians’ fatal attempt to do the same thing.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 11 transforms major salvation-history events into exempla of faith. They note that the sea crossing in Exodus is already a central act of deliverance, but Hebrews highlights the trusting response dimension more explicitly. Scholars often describe this as communal faith-rereading of foundational exodus narrative.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT siege story as an example of faith expressed through obedience before visible victory.
OT: In its original setting, the story belongs to the conquest narrative where Jericho falls after ritual circling and divine intervention.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Joshua 6:1–20 tells the story of Jericho’s fall. The people march around the city in the instructed pattern, and the walls collapse after ritual obedience rather than ordinary siege methods. In its original setting, this is conquest narrative shaped by divine command and divine intervention. It is not originally framed as a reflection on faith. Hebrews later rereads the episode by emphasizing the trust involved in acting according to God’s word before the visible result appeared.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hebrews 11 highlights obedience to divine instruction as a central expression of faith, and Jericho fits that pattern especially well. They note that Joshua narrates conquest and miracle, while Hebrews distills from it a paradigm of trusting action before fulfillment. Scholars often describe this as faith-exemplar reuse of conquest narrative.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses this OT outsider figure as an example of faith expressed through risky allegiance.
OT: In its original settings, the story belongs to the Jericho narrative, where a woman shelters spies, confesses Israel’s God, and is spared in the city’s fall.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Joshua 2 tells the story of Rahab hiding the Israelite spies in Jericho and confessing that the Lord has given the land to Israel. Joshua 6:22–25 later reports her rescue when the city falls. In their original settings, these passages belong to the conquest narrative and focus on protection, allegiance, and reversal. Rahab is an outsider who acts decisively in light of what she believes about Israel’s God. Hebrews later uses her as an example of faith shown in risky action before the outcome is visible.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 11’s use of Rahab fits its pattern of highlighting action that embodies trust. They note that the Joshua story is not originally a chapter on faith heroes, but Hebrews rereads it through that lens. Scholars often describe this as faith-centered reuse of conquest narrative with special emphasis on outsider inclusion.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing compresses a whole range of OT judges-and-kings stories into a rapid summary of victories, weakness turned to strength, and acts of faith.
OT: In their original settings, these stories are varied and often morally complex, but they are later gathered into one sweeping list of remembered triumphs.
cards.a: Hebrews 11:32–34 vs Judges 6–8, Judges 11, Judges 13–16, 1 Samuel 16–17, 1 Samuel 1–3, 1 Samuel 7

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hebrews 11:32–34 names Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, then summarizes a long range of deeds: conquering kingdoms, enforcing justice, escaping danger, and becoming strong out of weakness. In their original settings, these figures come from very different narratives with varied moral and theological textures. Some are exemplary in one respect and deeply flawed in another. Hebrews compresses that complexity into a rapid memory-list focused on trust, endurance, and divine action through imperfect people.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars note that Hebrews 11:32–34 is highly selective. It does not retell these narratives in full, but abstracts from them the elements that fit its faith-centered purpose. Scholars often describe this as summary-catena reuse of salvation-history traditions, where morally mixed stories are condensed into exemplary memory.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing alludes to OT stories of women receiving back their dead by resurrection.
OT: In their original settings, the stories concern prophetic miracle narratives in which Elijah and Elisha restore children to life.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: 1 Kings 17:17–24 tells how Elijah restores the widow’s son to life, and 2 Kings 4:18–37 tells how Elisha restores the Shunammite woman’s son. In their original settings, these are prophetic miracle stories that highlight divine power, prophetic authority, and restoration from devastating loss. Hebrews later alludes to them briefly as examples of women receiving back their dead. The point is not to retell the miracle stories in detail, but to place them in a wider chain of remembered faith and deliverance.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Hebrews 11:35 moves very quickly across different scriptural memories, and the widow stories from Elijah and Elisha are widely seen as the clearest background for the first half of the verse. Scholars often describe this as compressed allusive reuse of prophetic miracle traditions.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing evokes OT and later Jewish memories of prophets being persecuted, killed, and rejected.
OT: The background is not one clean verse but a cluster of traditions about violence against God’s messengers.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Hebrews 11:37 speaks of people being stoned, sawn in two, and killed by the sword. The Old Testament contains several relevant persecution memories, including Zechariah son of Jehoiada being stoned in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22 and the prophet Uriah being struck down in Jeremiah 26:20–23. Elijah’s complaint in 1 Kings 19:10 also reflects the larger memory of prophets being rejected and killed. The line about being sawn in two is more often connected with later Jewish tradition about Isaiah than with a canonical Old Testament passage. So the background is a cluster of prophetic persecution traditions rather than one neat citation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Hebrews 11:37 is allusive and tradition-rich as tradition-based reuse. They note that some elements come from canonical persecution stories, while others likely reflect broader Jewish martyrdom traditions. Scholars often describe this as cumulative reuse of prophetic suffering memory rather than direct quotation.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic sermon uses this OT promise of “holy and sure” blessings to David in connection with resurrection and enduring kingship.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a restoration invitation in which covenant promises associated with David are extended in renewed form.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 55:3 belongs to a restoration invitation calling people to come, listen, and receive life. The verse speaks of an everlasting covenant and of the “steadfast” or “holy and sure” mercies associated with David. In its original setting, the line belongs to restoration language and the renewal of covenant blessing, not to a resurrection sermon in Acts. Acts 13 later uses the verse because enduring Davidic blessings fit the claim that Jesus’s resurrection secures a lasting, non-decaying kingship.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 13:34 gives Isaiah 55:3 a more sharply messianic and resurrection-oriented role than it has in Isaiah itself. They note that the original verse belongs to a broad restoration invitation, while Acts narrows it toward the risen Jesus as the bearer of enduring Davidic promise. Scholars often describe this as later Davidic-restoration reuse in resurrection preaching.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic mission speech treats servant-language about light to the nations as a mandate for mission.
OT: In its original settings, the servant texts join restoration for Israel with a wider horizon toward the nations.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 42:6 and Isaiah 49:6 both belong to the servant passages in Isaiah. They present the servant as a light to the nations and join Israel-focused restoration with a wider international horizon. In their original settings, these are not speeches by Paul and Barnabas. They belong to Isaiah’s own servant world, where the servant’s identity remains debated. Acts 13 treats that servant-language as directly relevant to apostolic mission, extending the servant’s outward-facing role into the work of proclaiming to the nations.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 13 broadens servant-language by applying it not only to Jesus but also to the apostolic mission associated with him. They note that Isaiah’s original servant texts already point outward to the nations, which makes them especially reusable in mission contexts. Scholars often describe this as mission-extension reuse of servant material.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT lampstand-and-olive-tree imagery to portray two witnesses.
OT: In its original setting, the vision belongs to restoration-era leadership symbolism involving temple rebuilding and divine supply.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Zechariah 4 presents a vision of a lampstand and two olive trees in a post-exilic setting tied to leadership, temple rebuilding, and divine enablement. The imagery concerns restored community life and the sustaining work of God’s spirit. In its original setting, the vision is not about two end-time witnesses in Revelation. Revelation 11 later takes the lampstand-and-olive-tree imagery and retools it into a symbolic portrayal of prophetic testimony under apocalyptic pressure.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Most critical scholars say Revelation 11:4 is a clear reuse of Zechariah 4, but with major reinterpretive shifts. They note that Zechariah’s original restoration-leadership imagery becomes a new apocalyptic witness-symbol in Revelation. Scholars often describe this as transformed reuse of restoration vision symbolism.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses this OT feast-for-birds judgment image in a climactic battle scene.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to an oracle against Gog where carrion birds are invited to a sacrificial feast after divine victory.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ezekiel 39:17–20 belongs to the oracle against Gog, where birds and wild animals are summoned to feast on the fallen after God’s victory. In its original setting, this is judgment imagery connected to divine triumph over hostile nations and the vindication of Israel. It is not originally part of the Christian apocalypse. Revelation 19 later reuses this gruesome feast image in its own final battle scene, intensifying the sense of total judgment.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 19:17–18 depends heavily on Ezekiel 39’s carrion-feast imagery. They note that Revelation often reworks Ezekiel by placing restoration and judgment images into a more final apocalyptic frame. Scholars often describe this as direct apocalyptic reuse of prophetic battle-judgment symbolism.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse identifies the great enemy using a blend of ancient serpent and dragon imagery.
OT: The background joins Eden’s serpent with later prophetic monster language about God defeating a twisting sea-creature.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 3 introduces the serpent in Eden as the cunning creature who deceives the humans. Isaiah 27:1 speaks of the Lord punishing Leviathan, the fleeing or twisting serpent, in a cosmic judgment setting. In their original settings, these are different kinds of texts: one primal narrative, one prophetic monster image. Revelation 20:2 later fuses them by naming the enemy as the dragon, that ancient serpent, and Satan, blending Edenic and cosmic-opposition imagery into one apocalyptic adversary.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation’s serpent-dragon imagery is strongly synthetic. They note that it combines Genesis’s primal serpent with prophetic chaos-monster traditions such as Isaiah 27:1. Scholars often describe this as composite apocalyptic reuse of multiple enemy-imagery streams rather than a one-verse quotation.

cards.q:
NT: The passion narratives place this OT lament line on Jesus’s lips at the moment of crucifixion.
OT: In its original setting, the line opens a lament in which the speaker feels abandoned by God while still appealing to God for help.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 22:1 opens with the cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” In its original setting, this is the beginning of a lament psalm, not a prediction about crucifixion. The speaker feels abandoned, mocked, and endangered, but the psalm later turns toward trust and praise. Matthew and Mark place this line on Jesus’s lips at the cross, drawing the crucifixion scene into the language of Israel’s lament tradition.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the Gospel use of Psalm 22:1 is part of the broader passion narrative’s reliance on lament psalms. They note that the original psalm gives voice to suffering and appeal, while the Gospels use it to frame Jesus’s death scripturally. Scholars often describe this as passion-story shaping through inherited prayer language.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic speech combines OT lines about a desolate dwelling and another taking an office in connection with Judas’s replacement.
OT: In their original settings, the lines come from psalms of complaint and judgment against enemies, not from a direct prediction about Judas.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Acts 1:20 combines language from Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8. Psalm 69 is a lament where the speaker asks for judgment against enemies, including that their camp become desolate. Psalm 109 is an imprecatory psalm asking that an enemy’s position or office be taken by another. In their original settings, these are not about Judas by name. Acts reuses them to interpret Judas’s death and the need to appoint another witness in his place.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 1:20 is a clear composite use of psalmic judgment language. They note that the original psalms concern enemies of the speaker, while Acts applies their language to Judas and the apostolic office. Scholars often describe this as later ecclesial reuse of lament and imprecation texts.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses this OT line to explain Jesus’s teaching in parables.
OT: In its original setting, the line introduces a wisdom-like historical psalm that retells Israel’s past as instruction.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 78:2 says that the speaker will open the mouth in a parable and utter dark sayings from of old. In its original setting, the psalm is not about Jesus’s teaching ministry. It introduces a long reflection on Israel’s history, failures, and God’s faithfulness, using the past as instruction for later generations. Matthew 13:35 applies this line to Jesus’s parabolic teaching, presenting his use of parables as scripturally meaningful.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 13:35 reuses Psalm 78:2 by taking introductory wisdom language from a historical psalm and applying it to Jesus’s teaching style. They note that the original psalm’s concern is instructive retelling of Israel’s past, not prediction of a future teacher. Scholars often describe Matthew’s use as a later christological application of wisdom-parable language.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses this OT line to defend praise coming from children in the temple scene.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a creation praise psalm where even the weakest voices display God’s strength.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 8:2 says that praise or strength is established from the mouths of babes and infants. In its original setting, this line belongs to a psalm marveling at God’s glory in creation and at the surprising dignity of humans. It is not originally about children praising Jesus in the temple. Matthew later applies the line to the children’s praise after Jesus enters Jerusalem and acts in the temple, using the psalm to validate praise from unexpected voices.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 21:16 gives Psalm 8:2 a new christological setting. They note that the original psalm praises God’s majesty in creation, while Matthew uses its language to defend the praise directed toward Jesus. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of creation-praise language in a temple controversy scene.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses OT language about being hated without cause to interpret opposition to Jesus.
OT: In their original settings, the lines belong to laments where the speaker complains of unjust hostility from enemies.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 35:19 and Psalm 69:4 both include language about enemies hating the speaker without cause. In their original settings, these are lament texts about unjust hostility, social threat, and appeal to God for vindication. They are not originally predictions about Jesus’s opponents. John 15:25 uses the phrase to interpret the rejection of Jesus as part of a familiar scriptural pattern: the righteous or faithful sufferer is hated without just cause.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say John 15:25 draws on a lament tradition rather than one isolated proof text alone. They note that Psalm 35 and Psalm 69 both provide close background for the phrase. Scholars often describe this as later reuse of righteous-sufferer lament language to frame opposition to Jesus.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT command about coveting to explain how the law exposes sin.
OT: In its original setting, the command belongs to the Decalogue and forbids desire for what belongs to one’s neighbor.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 20:17 and Deuteronomy 5:21 command against coveting what belongs to one’s neighbor. In their original settings, the command belongs to the Decalogue and addresses inner desire as well as social harm. It is not originally part of Paul’s autobiographical or theological argument about law and sin. Romans 7:7 uses the command because it is especially suited to show how law can reveal desire and make sin recognizable.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 7:7 is a key example of Paul using Torah to analyze the relation between commandment, desire, and sin. They note that the commandment originally functions within Israel’s covenant law, while Paul makes it part of a larger argument about how sin exploits the command. Scholars often describe this as later theological reuse of Decalogue material.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT wisdom-like line to argue that God knows human thoughts are futile.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a psalm calling for justice against the arrogant and violent.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 94:11 says that the Lord knows human thoughts and that they are mere breath or futile. In its original setting, the psalm appeals to God as judge against arrogant evildoers who think God does not see. The line is not originally a classroom statement about philosophy. Paul later uses it in 1 Corinthians 3:20 as part of his critique of human wisdom and factional pride within the community.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 3:20 continues Paul’s larger argument against self-assured human wisdom. They note that Psalm 94:11 originally belongs to a justice psalm, while Paul adapts its judgment on human thought to a church setting marked by boasting. Scholars often describe this as later wisdom-and-judgment reuse of psalm language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line about the earth belonging to the Lord in a discussion of food, conscience, and freedom.
OT: In its original setting, the line opens a psalm about God’s ownership of the world and the requirements for entering sacred space.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 24:1 says that the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord. In its original setting, the line opens a psalm that moves from God’s ownership of creation to the question of who may ascend the Lord’s hill. Paul quotes it in 1 Corinthians 10:26 during a discussion about food sold in the marketplace, conscience, and idolatry. The original claim about divine ownership becomes a basis for freedom, while still operating inside Paul’s larger concern about idolatrous settings.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Corinthians 10:26 is a fairly direct reuse of Psalm 24:1, but in a surprisingly practical context. They note that Paul takes a broad theological claim about God’s ownership of the world and applies it to ordinary eating decisions in a mixed religious environment. Scholars often describe this as practical ethical reuse of creation-ownership language.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus cites OT commands about honoring parents and the penalty for reviling them during a dispute about tradition and responsibility.
OT: In their original settings, the commands belong to covenant law concerning family obligation and serious dishonor toward parents.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 20:12 commands honoring father and mother as part of the Decalogue. Exodus 21:17 gives a severe legal penalty for cursing or reviling parents. In their original settings, these laws are about family obligation, social order, and covenant life. In Matthew 15 and Mark 7, Jesus cites them while criticizing a practice that allows religious tradition to excuse neglect of parents. The OT commands become the basis for exposing a conflict between human tradition and moral obligation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say this Gospel dispute shows Jesus using Torah against a tradition that is portrayed as undermining Torah’s ethical demand. They note that the Decalogue command and the related legal penalty are brought together to sharpen the charge. Scholars often describe this as direct legal-ethical reuse of covenant law in controversy.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses this OT line to stress that no one has first given to God in a way that puts God in debt.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to God’s speeches and emphasizes divine freedom and unmatched sovereignty.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Job 41:11 comes from God’s speeches near the end of the book of Job. The line asks who has first given to God, that God should repay them. In its original setting, it belongs to a larger display of divine freedom, power, and sovereignty, especially through the imagery of Leviathan. Paul uses the line in Romans 11:35 at the close of a dense argument about mercy, Israel, Gentiles, and divine wisdom. The point becomes that God is not obligated by prior human claims.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 11:35 uses Job’s divine-speech language to underscore the unsearchability and independence of God’s purposes. They note that Job 41:11 originally appears in a theophanic response to Job, while Paul places it in a doxological conclusion. Scholars often describe this as later theological reuse of divine-sovereignty language.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses OT potter-and-clay language to challenge the idea that humans can put God on trial.
OT: In their original settings, these prophetic images criticize reversed thinking, where the formed thing questions the maker.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 29:16 and Isaiah 45:9 both use potter-and-clay imagery to expose the absurdity of created or formed things challenging the one who made them. In their original settings, the imagery appears in prophetic critiques of distorted thinking, resistance, and failure to recognize God’s authority. Paul uses the same kind of image in Romans 9:20 while discussing divine freedom, mercy, and election. The prophetic image becomes part of Paul’s argument that human beings are not in a position to accuse God of injustice.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 9:20 draws on a broader prophetic potter-clay tradition rather than one isolated verse alone. They note that Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9 both provide close conceptual background. Scholars often describe Paul’s use as later theological reuse of prophetic creator-creature imagery.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing uses a wake-up-and-rise saying about light shining on the sleeper.
OT: The wording blend restoration light imagery with resurrection-like awakening language.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Ephesians 5:14 has no exact single Old Testament source, but it strongly works from Isaiah 60:1, which calls Zion to arise and shine because light has come, and Isaiah 26:19, which speaks of the dead awakening and singing. In their original settings, these passages belong to restoration and hoped-for reversal after judgment and distress. Ephesians uses similar language in a moral exhortation about leaving darkness and living in light.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Ephesians 5:14 is a composite or hymn-like adaptation of scriptural language rather than a single-verse quotation. They often point to Isaiah 60:1 and Isaiah 26:19 as major backgrounds. Scholars commonly describe this as liturgical or paraenetic reuse of restoration and awakening imagery. This card should be read as composite scriptural reuse: restoration light and awakening language are reshaped into a call to leave darkness and live in light.

cards.q:
NT: A Gospel author uses OT darkness-and-light language to frame Jesus’s ministry in Galilee.
OT: In its original setting, the passage speaks of hope and reversal for northern regions that had experienced humiliation and distress.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 9:1–2 speaks of people who walked in darkness seeing a great light, especially in connection with regions associated with Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee of the nations. In its original setting, the passage belongs to hope after humiliation and oppression in the northern territories. It is not originally a direct narrative about Jesus moving to Capernaum. Matthew applies the passage to Jesus’s Galilean ministry, treating that ministry as the arrival of light in a region associated with darkness.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 4:15–16 is a classic example of Matthew’s geographic and typological use of scripture. They note that Isaiah 9 originally addresses historical distress and hope in Israel’s northern regions, while Matthew uses it to frame Jesus’s ministry location. Scholars often describe this as later christological rereading of restoration light imagery.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus points to healing and good-news signs as evidence of what is happening through his ministry.
OT: In their original settings, the background passages belong to restoration hopes involving healed bodies, renewed creation, and good news to the afflicted.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 35:5–6 describes blind eyes opened, deaf ears unstopped, and the lame leaping as part of a restoration vision where wilderness and weakness are transformed. Isaiah 61:1 speaks of good news to the poor or afflicted. In their original settings, these passages belong to restoration hope after crisis, not to a checklist for identifying Jesus. Matthew and Luke use the imagery when Jesus responds to questions about his identity, pointing to healing and good news as signs of restoration breaking in.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22 draw from a cluster of Isaianic restoration texts rather than one single passage. They note that the healing signs and good-news language come from Isaiah’s vision of renewal. Scholars often describe this as later christological reuse of restoration-sign imagery.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament apocalypse uses OT key-of-David imagery to describe authority to open and shut.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to a palace-office oracle about transferring authority to a royal steward.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 22:22 belongs to an oracle about Eliakim receiving authority in place of Shebna. The key of the house of David is placed on his shoulder, and what he opens or shuts cannot easily be reversed. In its original setting, this is about royal administrative authority in Judah, not a direct prediction about Jesus. Revelation 3:7 reuses the image to describe the authority of the holy and true one who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Revelation 3:7 transfers royal-steward authority imagery from Isaiah 22 into a christological setting. They note that the original passage concerns a historical palace office, while Revelation uses the key image for eschatological authority. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic and christological reuse of royal-administrative symbolism.

cards.q:
NT: Paul echoes OT wisdom warnings against being wise in one’s own eyes.
OT: In their original settings, these lines belong to wisdom instruction that challenges pride, self-confidence, and refusal to fear the Lord.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Proverbs 3:7 warns against being wise in one’s own eyes and instead calls for fear of the Lord and turning away from evil. Proverbs 26:12 criticizes the person who is wise in their own eyes as nearly hopeless. In their original settings, these sayings belong to wisdom instruction about humility, teachability, and moral perception. Paul echoes this wisdom pattern in Romans 12:16 as part of practical instruction for communal life.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Romans 12:16 reflects wisdom tradition more than a single exact quotation. They note that Proverbs repeatedly warns against self-wise arrogance, and Paul adapts that moral pattern for his community. Scholars often describe this as later ethical reuse of sapiential humility language. This card should be read as wisdom-tradition reuse: Paul adapts a recurring Proverbs warning against self-wise arrogance for communal ethics.

cards.q:
NT: Paul uses creation-light and restoration-light imagery to describe God shining light in human hearts.
OT: The background joins the first divine command of light with later imagery of light breaking into darkness.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 1:3 says, “Let there be light,” in the creation narrative. Isaiah 9:2 speaks of people walking in darkness seeing a great light. In their original settings, these passages are different: one concerns creation itself, the other hope after distress. Paul’s language in 2 Corinthians 4:6 draws on this broader scriptural field of divine light, creation, and revelation. The result is an image of God’s creative action now shining in human hearts.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 2 Corinthians 4:6 is a broad scriptural reuse but an allusive blend of creation and revelation imagery. Genesis 1:3 is usually seen as the strongest background, with prophetic light texts such as Isaiah 9 also contributing to the wider field. Scholars often describe this as broad scriptural-horizon reuse rather than direct citation. This card should be read as broad scriptural-horizon reuse: Paul blends creation-light and revelation-light imagery to describe God’s transformative action.

cards.q:
NT: The Synoptic apocalyptic discourse uses OT cosmic-collapse imagery to describe upheaval around coming judgment.
OT: In their original settings, these images belong to prophetic day-of-the-Lord and nation-judgment language, not one single end-times timetable.
cards.a: Matthew 24:29, Mark 13:24–25, Luke 21:25–26 vs Isaiah 13:10, Isaiah 34:4, Joel 2:10

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 13:10, Isaiah 34:4, and Joel 2:10 all use cosmic-disruption imagery: darkened sun, dimmed moon, falling or dissolving heavens, and trembling creation. In their original settings, these images are attached to prophetic judgment scenes involving Babylon, nations, or the day of the Lord. The language is poetic and apocalyptic in force, not a literal astronomy report. The Synoptic apocalypse draws on this imagery to portray the seriousness of coming judgment and divine intervention.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say the Synoptic cosmic signs depend on a broad prophetic image-field rather than a single Old Testament source. They note that prophetic judgment texts often use cosmic language to describe historical or theological catastrophe. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic reuse of day-of-the-Lord imagery.

cards.q:
NT: The Synoptic apocalyptic discourse uses gathering-language for the elect from the ends of the earth.
OT: In its original background, this language belongs to restoration hopes of scattered people being brought back from far places.
cards.a: Matthew 24:31, Mark 13:27 vs Deuteronomy 30:4, Isaiah 27:13, Zechariah 2:6

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 30:4 speaks of God gathering the scattered people even from the ends of the heavens. Isaiah 27:13 imagines a great trumpet and the return of exiles to worship the Lord. Zechariah 2:6 speaks of scattering to the four winds. In their original settings, these passages belong to exile, scattering, return, and restoration language. Matthew and Mark reuse this restoration-gathering imagery in an apocalyptic setting, where the elect are gathered from the ends of the earth.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 24:31 and Mark 13:27 draw on a broad restoration-gathering tradition rather than one exact quotation. They note that exile-and-return imagery is transformed into end-time gathering language. Scholars often describe this as apocalyptic expansion of restoration motifs.

cards.q:
NT: An infancy narrative uses OT Elijah-return language to describe the mission of a Gospel author the Baptist.
OT: In its original setting, the passage looks toward prophetic return before the day of the Lord and the turning of hearts.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Malachi 4:5–6 promises that Elijah will be sent before the great and terrible day of the Lord, turning the hearts of parents and children. In its original setting, the passage closes the prophetic book with a warning about coming judgment and the need for covenant restoration. Luke 1:17 applies this Elijah-return language to John the Baptist, presenting John as the preparatory figure who turns people back before the arrival of what the narrative sees as decisive divine action.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke 1:17 participates in a wider early Jewish expectation that Elijah would return before the eschatological moment. They note that Malachi originally speaks of Elijah’s return in a day-of-the-Lord context, while Luke identifies John as fulfilling that preparatory role. Scholars often describe this as later typological identification of John with Elijah tradition.

cards.q:
NT: A birth-song uses OT royal, light, and deliverance imagery to describe hoped-for redemption.
OT: The background draws from promises of Davidic strength, healing light, and light dawning on people in darkness.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Luke 1:68–79, often called the Benedictus, is saturated with Old Testament language rather than built from one quotation. Psalm 132:17 speaks of a horn for David. Malachi 4:2 speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing. Isaiah 9:2 speaks of light dawning on those in darkness. In their original settings, these passages belong to Davidic promise, judgment-and-healing hope, and restoration after darkness. Luke gathers this language into a song about redemption, covenant mercy, and guidance into peace.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke’s infancy hymns are scripturally saturated compositions rather than simple quotation chains. They note that the Benedictus draws on multiple Old Testament themes: Davidic promise, exodus-like redemption, prophetic light, and covenant mercy. Scholars often describe this as broad scriptural-horizon reuse in liturgical narrative form.

cards.q:
NT: An infancy narrative cites OT firstborn-consecration law in connection with Jesus being presented.
OT: In its original setting, the law belongs to exodus memory and the dedication of firstborn males to the Lord.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 13:2 and 13:12 command that the firstborn be consecrated to the Lord. In their original setting, these laws are tied to the exodus and especially to the rescue of Israel’s firstborn during the Passover event. The consecration of the firstborn becomes a ritual memory of deliverance from Egypt. Luke 2:23 cites this law when narrating Jesus’s presentation, placing Jesus’s infancy inside the rhythms of Israel’s covenant and exodus-shaped practice.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke 2 uses Torah observance to locate Jesus and his family within faithful Jewish practice. They note that Exodus 13 originally belongs to exodus memorial law, not to a messianic prediction. Scholars often describe Luke 2:23 as narrative legal reuse rather than fulfillment of a prophecy.

cards.q:
NT: An infancy narrative cites OT purification-offering law involving birds.
OT: In its original setting, the law belongs to postpartum purification requirements and includes a provision for those who cannot afford a lamb.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Leviticus 12:6–8 gives instructions for purification after childbirth, including an offering of a lamb and a bird, or two birds for someone who cannot afford a lamb. In its original setting, this is priestly law about ritual purification, not a prophecy about Jesus. Luke 2:24 cites the bird offering in the presentation narrative, suggesting that Jesus’s family participates in the ordinary legal practices of Israel and, perhaps, occupies modest economic status.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Luke 2:24 is an example of legal citation used for characterization and setting rather than prediction. They note that the Leviticus passage is ritual law, while Luke uses it to show Torah observance and possibly social modesty. Scholars often describe this as narrative reuse of priestly legal material.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic speech uses this OT royal enthronement line to argue for Jesus’s exaltation.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to royal language in which the Lord invites a kingly figure to sit at his right hand.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Psalm 110:1 says that the Lord tells the speaker’s lord to sit at his right hand until enemies are made a footstool. In its original setting, the line belongs to royal enthronement language and has been widely debated in terms of its historical referent and speaker. Acts 2:34–35 uses the verse in Peter’s Pentecost speech to argue that Jesus has been exalted to God’s right hand. The royal enthronement image becomes a resurrection-and-exaltation proof.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Psalm 110:1 is one of the most important Old Testament texts for early Christian exaltation theology. They note that Acts 2 uses it to distinguish David from the exalted Jesus and to argue that the psalm points beyond David. Scholars often describe this as later christological reuse of royal enthronement language.

cards.q:
NT: A major speech retells this OT call to leave country and kin in the story of Abraham.
OT: In its original setting, the line begins the patriarchal journey by calling Abram away from familiar land and family toward a place God will show.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 12:1 is the call of Abram to leave his country, kindred, and father’s house for the land God will show him. In its original setting, this begins the Abraham cycle and launches the promise story that will shape Israel’s later identity. Acts 7:3 uses the line in Stephen’s retelling of Israel’s history, emphasizing that the story of God’s people begins with movement, displacement, and divine initiative rather than with the temple or settled land.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 7 uses Israel’s scriptures in a selective historical retelling. They note that Genesis 12:1 originally begins the Abraham narrative, while Stephen’s speech uses it to frame a broader argument about God’s activity outside fixed sacred geography. Scholars often describe this as narrative reuse in a theological history speech.

cards.q:
NT: A major speech retells this OT prediction that Abraham’s descendants would be strangers, enslaved, and later delivered.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the covenant scene where Abraham is told the future of his descendants before they possess the land.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 15:13–14 tells Abraham that his descendants will be strangers in a land not theirs, enslaved and oppressed, but that God will later judge the oppressing nation and bring them out. In its original setting, this is part of the covenant scene that looks ahead to Egypt, exodus, and delayed land possession. Acts 7:6–7 quotes this material in Stephen’s historical speech to show that Israel’s story included long displacement before settlement.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 7 foregrounds the parts of Israel’s story that happen outside the land and before the temple. They note that Genesis 15:13–14 originally explains the future of Abraham’s descendants, while Acts uses it to stress that divine promise and presence precede national institutions. Scholars often describe this as strategic narrative reuse of patriarchal covenant material.

cards.q:
NT: A major speech retells this OT burning-bush scene where God appears, names suffering, and sends Moses.
OT: In its original setting, the passage begins Moses’s commission and reveals divine concern for Israel’s oppression in Egypt.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Exodus 3:2–10 tells of the burning bush, where God Moses, declares the ground holy, identifies himself with the ancestors, says he has seen Israel’s suffering, and sends Moses to Egypt. In its original setting, this is Moses’s call and commission narrative. Acts 7 retells the scene in Stephen’s speech, using it to highlight that God appeared to Moses outside the promised land and initiated deliverance before later institutions existed.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Stephen’s speech in Acts 7 uses the Moses story to challenge a narrow temple-centered view of divine presence. They note that Exodus 3 originally presents Moses’s commission, while Acts emphasizes the location and mobility of God’s revelation. Scholars often describe this as theological retelling of foundational exodus narrative.

cards.q:
NT: A major speech uses this OT line to argue that God cannot be contained by a human-made house.
OT: In its original setting, the passage contrasts God’s cosmic throne with human-built sacred space and points instead to humility before God.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Isaiah 66:1–2 says that heaven is God’s throne and earth is God’s footstool, asking what house humans could build for God. In its original setting, the passage critiques simplistic confidence in sacred buildings and emphasizes God’s concern for the humble and contrite. Acts 7:49–50 uses the passage at the climax of Stephen’s speech to argue that the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 7 uses Isaiah 66:1–2 as a major anti-temple-triumphalism text. They note that Isaiah already relativizes the temple by emphasizing God’s transcendence, while Acts deploys that language polemically in Stephen’s speech. Scholars often describe this as prophetic critique reused in a temple-controversy setting.

cards.q:
NT: An apostolic council speech uses this OT restoration text to support Gentile inclusion.
OT: In its original setting, the passage promises restoration after judgment and the rebuilding of David’s fallen booth.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Amos 9:11–12 promises that David’s fallen booth will be raised and repaired after judgment. The Hebrew wording speaks of possessing the remnant of Edom and the nations called by God’s name, while the Greek tradition supports a reading about the rest of humanity seeking the Lord. Acts 15:16–18 uses the passage in the Jerusalem council to argue that the inclusion of Gentiles fits scripture. The text is therefore a key case where restoration, textual tradition, and mission argument meet.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Acts 15:16–18 depends strongly on the Greek form of Amos 9:11–12, which differs in important ways from the Hebrew. They note that this makes the passage central for studying how textual tradition affects New Testament argument. Scholars often describe the Acts use as a Septuagint-shaped rereading of restoration language for Gentile inclusion.

cards.q:
NT: One New Testament writing pairs an OT labor law with a Jesus tradition about workers deserving wages.
OT: The OT piece comes from a law about not muzzling a threshing ox, which is then placed beside later tradition about human labor.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: 1 Timothy 5:18 contains two sayings: the Deuteronomy law about not muzzling an ox while it treads grain, and the saying that the worker deserves wages, known from Luke 10:7. The Old Testament source is Deuteronomy 25:4, a practical law about fair treatment of a working animal. In 1 Timothy, that law is paired with a Jesus tradition and applied to elders who labor well. This makes the passage important for how scripture and early Jesus tradition are placed side by side.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say 1 Timothy 5:18 is significant because it combines Torah and a Jesus saying under the heading of scripture or authoritative citation. They note that Deuteronomy 25:4 supplies the OT legal principle, while Luke 10:7 or a shared Jesus tradition supplies the wage saying. Scholars often describe this as a mixed authority citation rather than a simple OT-only quotation.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus cites this OT divorce provision before challenging the way it was being used.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to legal material regulating divorce and remarriage in ancient Israelite society.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 24:1 refers to a man writing a certificate of divorce and sending his wife away. In its original setting, the passage regulates a divorce situation and especially the complications of remarriage afterward. It is not a command to divorce, but a legal framework for a social reality. Matthew 5:31 cites the provision and then challenges a casual or permissive use of divorce, reframing the issue around faithfulness and harm.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 5:31–32 reflects an interpretive debate over how Deuteronomy 24 should function. They note that the Deuteronomy passage regulates divorce rather than simply endorsing it. Scholars often describe Matthew’s use as restrictive ethical reinterpretation of Torah divorce law.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus summarizes OT oath material before urging speech that does not depend on oath-making.
OT: In their original settings, these laws require truthful vows and warn against swearing falsely by God’s name.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Leviticus 19:12 forbids swearing falsely by God’s name. Numbers 30:2 requires a person to do what they vow. Deuteronomy 23:21 warns against delaying to fulfill a vow made to the Lord. In their original settings, these laws do not ban all oaths; they regulate truthfulness, seriousness, and faithfulness in speech before God. Matthew 5:33 gathers this oath tradition and then pushes toward a simpler ethic of truthful speech without manipulative swearing.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 5:33 is not quoting one single verse but summarizing a Torah tradition about vows and truthful speech. They note that the original laws assume oath-making can occur, while Matthew’s teaching restricts or transcends that practice. Scholars often describe this as synthetic ethical reinterpretation of oath legislation.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus cites this OT retaliation formula before teaching non-retaliation.
OT: In its original setting, the formula belongs to legal material aimed at proportionate justice rather than unlimited revenge.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: The formula “eye for eye” appears in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20, and Deuteronomy 19:21. In its original legal settings, the principle limits punishment to proportionate justice; it is not a blank check for personal revenge. Matthew 5:38 quotes the formula and then moves toward non-retaliation in personal conflict. The passage therefore shifts from a legal principle of measured justice to an ethic of refusing retaliatory escalation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 5:38–42 reinterprets lex talionis in a non-retaliatory direction. They note that the Torah formula originally constrained vengeance by proportionality, while Matthew’s teaching addresses personal response to injury and humiliation. Scholars often describe this as ethical transformation of legal justice language.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus combines creation texts in a dispute about marriage and divorce.
OT: In their original settings, the lines belong to creation narratives about humanity as male and female and the formation of a new kinship bond.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Genesis 1:27 says that God created humanity male and female. Genesis 2:24 says that a man leaves father and mother and clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh. In their original settings, these lines belong to the creation narratives and explain human identity, kinship, and union. Matthew 19 and Mark 10 combine them in a dispute about divorce, using creation as a deeper frame than later divorce regulation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Jesus’s argument in Matthew 19 and Mark 10 reads marriage through creation before turning to Mosaic divorce law. They note that the Gospel argument combines Genesis 1 and 2 to ground the claim in created order. Scholars often describe this as creation-text reuse in legal-ethical controversy.

cards.q:
NT: Jesus identifies this OT command as the greatest commandment.
OT: In its original setting, the line belongs to the Shema context and calls Israel to total covenant love for the Lord.

notes.label: Context
notes.text: Deuteronomy 6:5 commands love for the Lord with all one’s heart, soul, and might. In its original setting, the line follows the Shema and belongs to Israel’s core covenant confession and instruction. It calls for total allegiance to the Lord and is meant to shape daily life, teaching, and memory. Matthew 22:37 quotes it as the greatest commandment, placing love of God at the center of Torah interpretation.

notes.label: Scholarly Note
notes.text: Many critical scholars say Matthew 22:37 reflects a very direct and central use of Deuteronomy 6:5. They note that the verse already had major importance in Jewish covenant piety, and the Gospel places it at the top of the commandment hierarchy. Scholars often describe this as direct ethical and theological reuse of the Shema tradition.
